The psychological mind-twisting production will run through Sept. 13 at the 117-seat community theater, 700 W. Weatherbee Road in Fort Pierce. FORT PIERCE — A brilliant mathematician’s death leaves behind a mysterious proof — and questions about genius, mental illness and who deserves the credit. The Pineapple Playhouse will open its 2026-27 season Aug. 28 with “Proof,” David Auburn’s Pulitzer Prize-winning drama. The play follows Catherine, a young woman who spent years caring for her brilliant but mentally ill father. After his death, a groundbreaking mathematical proof is discovered, raising questions about its authorship and Catherine’s sanity. The psychological mind-twisting production will run through Sept. 13 at the 117-seat community theater, 700 W. Weatherbee Road in Fort Pierce. The schedule includes 10 performances, with 2 p.m. Michael Pisacane will direct the production, marking his fifth time directing at the theater. “‘Proof’ won both a Tony Award and a Pulitzer Prize in 2005, and was recently revived on Broadway with an all-star cast, including Don Cheadle,” Pisacane said. Jessica Lesko, a veteran actor and director, will lead the cast as Catherine. The cast also includes Martin Fitzpatrick, Caroline Remillard and Ray Balsamo. The Pineapple Playhouse presents six mainstage productions each season, along with a holiday show. The nonprofit community theater has operated for more than 50 years. Its mission is to provide a gathering place for the community and serve as a creative center “where stories are brought to life.” For performance dates, tickets and information, visit pineappleplayhouse.com or call 772-465-0366. Lucie Police Department is investigating after an 86-year-old woman died in a two-vehicle crash. Officers responded at approximately 2:30 p.m. Thursday at the intersection of Southwest Savona Boulevard and Southwest Lawndale Avenue, east of Interstate 95. The preliminary investigation indicates that a 2026 Honda HR-V, driven by a 17-year-old boy, was traveling northbound on Southwest Savona Boulevard approaching the intersection with SW Lawndale Avenue. A 2006 Hyundai Elantra, driven by Marie R. Martin, was traveling westbound near the stop sign on Southwest Lawndale Avenue. Investigators determined that Martin entered the intersection and failed to yield the right-of-way to the northbound Honda, resulting in the Honda striking the driver's side of the Hyundai. This caused the Honda to T-bone the Hyundai. Martin was extricated by St. Lucie Fire Rescue and was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital with critical injuries. Martin later succumbed to her injuries. The 17-year-old driver was not injured in the crash. Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app.

An 86-year-old woman died after police said she pulled into the path of an SUV and was struck in a Port St. Lucie intersection Thursday afternoon. The crash happened at about 2:30 p.m. at Southwest Savona Boulevard and Southwest Lawndale Avenue, according to the Port St. Investigators said Marie R. Martin was driving a 2006 Hyundai Elantra west on Lawndale Avenue when she entered the intersection from near a stop sign and failed to yield to a northbound 2026 Honda HR-V. The Honda, driven by a 17-year-old boy, struck the driver’s side of Martin’s car, police said. Body-camera video recorded after the crash shows the Hyundai off the roadway near a cluster of palm trees, with visible damage to its driver’s side and emergency crews working around the vehicle. The Honda also came to rest on the grass nearby, close to vegetation and a roadside sign. Lucie police officers and St. Lucie County Fire District personnel can be seen at the scene, along with fire engines, rescue vehicles and traffic cones blocking part of the intersection. Debris and emergency equipment were scattered across the grass between the two vehicles. See also: Chief: Five West Palm Beach police leaders fired following 'double-dipping' probe Martin had to be extricated from the Hyundai before she was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital with critical injuries, police said. She later died despite efforts to save her. The teenage driver of the Honda was not injured. The Police Department’s Traffic Homicide Unit continues to investigate the crash.

Martin County is weighing changes to its local shark fishing ordinance after the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission directed the county to align its rules with state regulations. It's a move that has drawn significant public concern.The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission asked the county to bring its ordinance in line with state law, which preempts counties from regulating saltwater fishing.WATCH WPTV'S COVERAGE BELOW:"There is a state statute that has essentially preempted the powers from the county to regulate salt water fishing that includes shark fishing. Preemption meaning the state says, 'county you can't control this anymore,'" Assistant County Attorney Melissa Petrick said.State law requires a saltwater fishing license and a special permit for shark fishing. It also allows shark fishing within 1,000 feet of a guarded beach at all hours.Among those opposing the changes is Jessica Veatch, whose then-3-year-old daughter Violet was attacked by a bull shark on Bathtub Beach in Martin County 9 years ago."I hear a scream that goes Mommy," Veatch said. "I come up out of the water and all I can see is the blood filling the water and I lifted her up out of the water and saw what was left of her leg."Veatch said she believes nearby fishing activity may have lead to the attack.."We noticed some young men that were spearfishing on the reef," Veatch said. "That is what provoked the attack on my daughter."Veatch said she was alarmed to learn the county may now be forced to eliminate its local shark fishing regulations."They're currently treating our shoreline like a Pavlov's dog experiment with an apex predator and I don't think that's going to work out in anybody's best interest," Veatch said.Indian River Keeper Jim Moir raised concerns about the potential impact of the changes at the Tuesday commission meeting."These animals are incredibly important to our ecosystems. The angler offshore are complaining bitterly daily about how many of their caught fish are being depraved by sharks. Attracting more sharks to the coast is not only bad for human safety, but it's bad for angling, its bad for our public awareness, it's bad for the sharks," Moir said.County attorneys suggested the ordinance does not need to be eliminated entirely."We can rework the ordinance and then instead of eliminating everything we can just reference the illegality of things under state law," Petrick said.County commissioners voted to table the discussion, directing staff to review concerns raised by the community and commissioners and draft new ordinance language.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Residents at Sanctuary at Winterlakes Apartments in Port St. Lucie said they have been living with unresolved maintenance issues and that their requests for help are being ignored.WATCH BELOW: 'I pay my rent on time. I would just like to be in my house and not have mold in it,' Cheryl Jones tells WPTV's Tyler HatfieldAlison Malio walked me through her apartment, pointing out what she believes is structural damage in her bedroom."I thought it might be structural," Malio said.She also showed damage she described as rot near the foundation."It looks like it's welting. It's welting like rot, rot on it in the foundation, rot," Malio said.Malio also said her freezer seal was damaged and has cost her thousands of dollars in lost food."I've had to throw away over like $1,500 in the last year and a half, two years, $1,500 worth of meat or frozen food," Malio said.Malio also showed a cockroach problem inside her apartment and building. She said pest control only comes once every 13 weeks."I replace the adhesive ones about three times a week, because they get so full," Malio said.Malio said she and her neighbors submit maintenance requests through an online portal, but she claims those requests go unanswered or get deleted — and are sometimes marked complete even when no work has been done."It's been like six, seven years of nothing but them just doing nothing to help us, nothing to help, I'll call them. They don't get back to me. They don't get back to me," Malio said."I have cameras and a ring doorbell, so I know if they come in to look at it and I can tell when it's not done, because it's not done," Malio said.Across the parking lot, neighbor Cheryl Jones said her air conditioning was out for nine weeks."It was too hot in here to cook. You know, I could make breakfast with my coffee maker and the toaster, but I mean, I couldn't cook a meal," Jones said.Jones said maintenance eventually fixed the air conditioning, but mold had grown inside her apartment.Jones sent a report from a company that tested her unit and found evidence of mold, recommending that drywall, insulation and other materials be removed.Jones said she sent that report to property management."I haven't heard nothing from them, nothing. Not a phone call, not an email back, nothing," Jones said. I would just like to be in my house and not have mold in it."I reached out to property management with the neighbors' concerns. Management sent a statement saying they are looking into the issues and that they "prioritize the safety and well-being of our tenants."The full statement reads:When asked why she doesn't move, Malio said she can't afford to. Jones said the same."I have nowhere to go. I can't afford to go anywhere else," Jones said.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. A Netflix docuseries is drawing renewed national attention to a Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office detective who interviewed accused killer Wade Wilson — also known as the Deadpool Killer — months before Wilson murdered two women in 2019, sparking widespread calls for the detective's termination.WATCH WPTV's COVERAGE BELOW:The series has focused scrutiny on Detective Louis Potter, who investigated rape and assault allegations against Wilson in February 2019. An internal affairs investigation later found Potter failed to conduct a thorough sex crimes investigation — a conclusion that has fueled a public petition calling for his firing that has grown to more than 16,000 signatures.Wilson's former girlfriend, Kelly Matthews, told WPTV she reported to law enforcement that Wilson had beaten, kidnapped, and raped her. She described the injuries she says she suffered during the attack. "Ligature marks on my wrists and ankles, I had red marks around my neck, a bite mark on my cheek and my ear, a busted lip, bloody nose," Matthews said.Matthews said she sought medical attention and reported the attack to law enforcement within hours."I had begged the detective to arrest him. Literally just detain him, pick him up or whatever and he refused and then he told me after the fact that he had already met up with him and done DNA and stuff," Matthews said.Potter did collect Wilson's DNA. But according to PBSO records, 34 days later, he closed the case — before the lab results came back."He even agreed in his report that my injuries were consistent with my story but then he turned around and just closed everything," Matthews said.In his report, Potter wrote there were no witnesses, no evidence, and that Wilson denied the allegations, concluding there was no probable cause to make an arrest.The Netflix series drew widespread attention to Potter's tone during his interrogation of Wilson, with viewers questioning whether he was too quick to accept Wilson's denials.During the interrogation, Potter told Wilson: Wilson responded: Matthews said she did not know what Potter had said during that interrogation until she watched the Netflix documentary. "I didn't know he had said any of that stuff until I saw the documentary," she said.Just days after Wilson murdered two women in October 2019, WPTV sat down with Matthews, who described the earlier attack. Years later, after watching Wilson's murder trial, Matthews filed a complaint against Potter. "Had Detective Potter arrested my ex, he likely wouldn't have gone on to murder two women," Matthews wrote in the complaint.That complaint triggered an internal investigation.WPTV obtained a copy of that report. In the report it says PBSO investigators concluded Potter failed to conduct a thorough sex crimes investigation. They found he closed the case before reviewing DNA results, and when those results came back — confirming Wilson's DNA was found at the scene — Potter failed to follow up. Investigators also found he failed to seek an arrest for dating violence.The internal affairs report found Matthews' account was corroborated by her injuries and evidence collected from the vehicle where the alleged crimes occurred, including a pocket knife and torn clothing — all factors the report says point to probable cause.Former State Attorney Dave Aronberg, who was in office in 2019, said the case never landed on his desk. He called the outcome a tragedy."The Wade Wilson matter is just a tragedy, because there are so many steps, if things had gone a different direction, that perhaps these victims would still be alive," Aronberg said.When asked whether the case was mishandled, Aronberg urged caution about judging decisions in hindsight, but said his office would have taken a closer look had the case been referred. "You don't want to be a Monday morning quarterback, because we're looking at this with the perspective of hindsight," Aronberg said."Clearly she does appear to be very credible. The fact that he's had a rap sheet, he's done this before, that would have come into play at a variety of levels," Aronberg said.Over the phone, PBSO said detectives need probable cause before referring a case to the State Attorney's Office — evidence Potter claimed did not exist. But the internal affairs report found Matthews' account did have substantial probable cause.Aronberg said Potter's discipline may hinge on whether he was required to consult with the State Attorney's Office before closing the case."If he was required to consult with the State Attorney's Office before dropping a charge like this, then this would be a violation of that policy, and he has been sanctioned for violations," Aronberg said.WATCH WPTV's PREVIOUS COVERAGE:Potter was suspended without pay for 120 hours. In a statement, PBSO said Potter "used poor discretionary judgment in the handling of a criminal case without following established agency procedures," adding that he was reassigned to administrative duties and received appropriate discipline.Years after the alleged rape and the murders, Potter when questioned if he would change how he handled the case said no. Aronberg pushed back on that position. "I don't think it's helpful to say that you know nothing could have been done differently when clearly things could have," Aronberg said.Matthews raised broader concerns about what Potter's approach could mean for other potential victims."Who knows how many women he's done this to, or men. Because he even says in the report he would do it the same way like if anyone else had this happen," Matthews said.Since the series aired, Matthews said she feels a sense of relief that the full story is now public."Ever since the Netflix thing came out I feel like I can breathe and I'm like OK, everyone knows the truth, everything's out there," Matthews said.PBSO has said it will not fire Potter over renewed attention to the case. Potter plans to retire Friday, July 31, and has not responded to requests for comment.Matthews said the experience has left a lasting impact on her trust in law enforcement."I was always taught as a kid to go to law enforcement and trust them and it ended up tainting my trust in law enforcement for awhile, because these are supposed to be the people that are going to protect you and he didn't," Matthews said.Full statement from PBSO below:This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Nestled in West Palm Beach's Northwood district, Nine Lives Cafe offers a bright, welcoming space that creates an uplifting atmosphere portraying its positive initiative of finding shelter cats their forever homes.The cafe's origin story begins with a search that came up empty. Co-owner Jada Thornton had fallen in love with the concept while volunteering at a cat cafe in North Carolina. When Thornton and co-owner Razmig Panossian were living in Boston hoping to find a similar experience, they found nothing. Hoping West Palm Beach might offer what Boston lacked, they were disappointed once again – but this time, they took action."We took a leap of faith and decided to open a cat cafe," Thornton explained, embarking on what would become an 18-month journey to bring their vision to life.Creating Nine Lives Cafe wasn't just about opening a business; it was about building something meaningful from the ground up. With Thornton's interior design background and Panossian's construction expertise, they designed and built the entire space themselves."The time did go by fast because we were able to get a lot of support from Furry Friends (Humane), from various other people in the community, mentors." Thornton said. "So it's been a pleasurable process, honestly."The spot features two distinct areas: the main "Cat Heaven" room where visitors can interact with the cats, and a separate coffee area divided by glass. This layout allows even those with cat allergies to enjoy the experience, watching the felines while sipping coffee and enjoying pastries in a cat allergy-safe environment.The $25 entry fee to interact with the cats provides an hour-long "feline therapy session," though most visitors end up staying much longer. "Nobody wants to leave," Thornton said. "They come in here, they stay for hours." The fee supports their nonprofit mission, covering cat care, facility maintenance, and staffing until each cat finds its forever home.Behind the cozy atmosphere lies a serious mission. Palm Beach County faces a staggering euthanasia rate of at least 800 cats monthly, making Nine Lives Cafe's work crucial for local animal welfare. The cafe partners primarily with Furry Friends Animal Rescue, providing a bridge between shelter life and permanent homes."These rescue (cats) are just as lovable and their stories are amazing. They're survivors, so they know how to love," Thornton said, speaking from personal experience with their own rescue cats.The cafe environment offers significant advantages for both cats and potential adopters. Unlike a traditional shelter setting, 'Cat Heaven' provides a home-like environment where felines can roam freely, play, and display their true personalities. This setting helps cats become better socialized while giving visitors a genuine sense of each animal's character."When you're hanging out with the cats, you get to see how they are because they act like it's their home," Panossian explained. "So you get an idea, a good sense of what their personality is like."In true Palm Beach fashion, Nine Lives offers "Paw-lates" – 60-minute mat-based classes that combine classical contemporary flow with feline therapy. The connection isn't coincidental— Joseph Pilates drew inspiration from cats when developing his exercise methodology."It's kind of like a full circle moment for the Pilates world," Thornton explained. The intimate classes, held in dimmed lighting with closed blinds, create a therapeutic environment. The cafe has already facilitated a handful of adoptions– a promising start toward their goal of maintaining 10-12 adoptable cats alongside a few resident cats who provide consistency and companionship.The coffee program at Nine Lives is overseen by David McLennan, the cafe's head of coffee, who brings over 20 years of experience serving coffee everywhere from super yachts to estates to his own coffee shops. McLennan and his wife discovered Nine Lives through Instagram and were immediately drawn to the concept that combined their two passions: cats and coffee."We both love cats and we love coffee, and so this just seemed like a natural thing to reach out to them and see if I could be involved in their coffee program," McLennan explained. The cafe features a specially sourced blend from New York that McLennan describes as "lovely and approachable" with chocolatey, velvety and fruity notes. The menu includes all the classics – hot and iced coffees, mochas, and lattes – along with high-quality matcha. "You can come here as the cafe itself and enjoy the view of the cats."As Nine Lives settles into its role as West Palm Beach's first cat cafe, the team remains focused on their dual mission: providing exceptional experiences for visitors while saving lives. Reservations can be made online at https://ninelivescafe.co/ or visitors can walk in for availability at 2032 North Dixie Highway.Follow Nine Lives Cafe on Instagram @ninelivescafe.com

Federal prosecutors said a Los Angeles man was sentenced to life in federal prison for selling fentanyl that caused the death of a Treasure Coast man, then continuing to traffic the deadly drug just two days later. District Judge Aileen Cannon imposed the sentence on Alfonso Guerrero, 39, of Los Angeles, after a federal jury convicted him in May 2026 of conspiracy to possess with intent to distribute fentanyl resulting in death and distribution of fentanyl resulting in death. “A tenth of a gram of fentanyl, about the size of a small pinch of salt, was enough to kill David Eller,” U.S. Reding Quiñones for the Southern District of Florida said in a statement. “This was not a small drug deal. Guerrero sold the fentanyl that killed his friend and, just two days later, was caught carrying more fentanyl for distribution. Today’s life sentence is the consequence of that deadly conduct and his long record of violence and crime. Together with the DEA and our local law enforcement partners, we will trace fatal doses back to the dealers who sold them and hold those dealers fully accountable.” According to court records and evidence presented at trial, the U.S. Attorney’s Office said Guerrero sold fentanyl in Indian River County. On May 16, 2023, prosecutors said he exchanged 0.1 gram of fentanyl — commonly known as “a point” — for another controlled substance known as “molly.” Officials said the drug transaction was captured on a doorbell camera. Hours later, Eller was found dead inside his Vero Beach home. Investigators recovered drug paraphernalia, including a small piece of burnt aluminum foil that the victim used to receive the fentanyl from Guerrero on the victim’s front porch, near his body. Two days later, on May 18, 2023, prosecutors said Guerrero was arrested and found in possession of additional quantities of fentanyl intended for distribution. Officials said Guerrero’s extensive criminal history included documented gang membership and prior convictions for attempted robbery with a firearm in California, aggravated assault in Georgia, and cocaine and fentanyl possession offenses in Florida.

Lucie police officer resigned in April following allegations of neglect during a March incident at the Treasure Coast Church of God Worship Center on Savona Boulevard, according to an internal affairs report. The report alleged Officer Mathew Brown came across a car with a man inside, looked, and then immediately left the scene. Fifteen minutes later, another officer spotted the same car and discovered the man inside had died by suicide. Officer Brown arrived as backup but allegedly did not inform anyone about his earlier encounter with the vehicle and later claimed he did not see anything. A woman was killed and a man was found dead Saturday evening following what investigators believe was a domestic-related shooting in Port St. Lucie Police Department officers responded around 7:40 p.m. Saturday to the 2000 block of SE Oxmoor Terrace after receiving multiple 911 calls reporting possible gunshots and a domestic disturbance.When officers arrived, they found an adult woman suffering from a gunshot wound. She was airlifted to a local hospital, where she was later pronounced dead.Officers also found an adult man dead at the scene. Investigators said he appeared to have died from a self-inflicted gunshot wound.The scene remains an active crime scene as detectives continue processing evidence and interviewing witnesses.Based on the preliminary investigation, police believe the incident was an isolated, domestic-related shooting and said there is no known threat to the public.Detectives cautioned that the facts and circumstances surrounding the case remain subject to change as the investigation continues.Residents should continue to expect a heavy police presence in the area of SE Triumph Road and SE Veterans Memorial Parkway while investigators remain on scene. Motorists are encouraged to avoid the area and use alternate routes whenever possible.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. A student receives a back-to-school haircut at Fort Pierce Beauty Academy. A client receives a fresh look at Fort Pierce Beauty Academy. FORT PIERCE — A fresh haircut can help students walk into a new school year with a little more confidence. The Academies of Cosmetology is offering free back-to-school haircuts for school-age children at its three Treasure Coast campuses through Aug. Families do not need appointments or advance registration. Students and parents may walk in, sign in and wait for the next available barbering or cosmetology student, much as they would at a traditional barbershop or salon. Kris Evangelista said the schools have long offered discounted back-to-school haircuts, but began offering them for free only within the past few years. “It’s always been discounts for the kids for back to school, but I believe this is the second or third year we’re doing the free cuts,” Evangelista said. All students at the three campuses are expected to participate, with instructors supervising the work to ensure children receive quality haircuts. Families may request a specific student stylist if they choose. Evangelista said the service is especially meaningful because a haircut can make a difference in how children feel when they return to school. “It’s a fresh year, fresh haircut,” Evangelista said. “It boosts their confidence, their self-esteem.” The promotion has become popular with families, including regular clients who return each year and bring relatives and friends. Evangelista said the academies do not plan to turn anyone away. Michael Prevette owns the Academies of Cosmetology, where Evangelista assists. Evangelista said the academies also plan to continue their community outreach beyond the back-to-school season by hosting free spring and fall festivals. The free back-to-school haircuts are at Beauty and Massage Institute, 1375 U.S. 1, Suite 2, Vero Beach, 772-978-7178; Port St. Lucie Beauty Academy, 10036 South U.S. Lucie, 772-337-4747; and Fort Pierce Beauty Academy, 3028 South U.S. 1, Fort Pierce, 772-464-4885. The Florida Department of Health in Palm Beach County has issued a health alert, no-swim advisory and no-irrigation advisory following a wastewater spill connected to a lift station on Singer Island.According to the health department, the spill entered Park Avenue from Lift Station 10 in Riviera Beach.Officials said drinking water is not affected.Until more is known about possible bacterial contamination, residents and visitors are urged to avoid contact with affected waterways in the area.The City of Riviera Beach is coordinating water quality testing and cleanup efforts with the Florida Department of Environmental Protection.Health officials warn that water contaminated with high levels of fecal bacteria can cause illness, infections and skin rashes.Anyone who comes into contact with the water should wash thoroughly, especially before eating or drinking. The health department said children, older adults and people with weakened immune systems may be at greater risk and should avoid exposure altogether.For more information about the health advisory, residents can contact the Florida Department of Health in Palm Beach County at 561-837-5900 or 561-881-1888 after hours.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. A prosecutor says they have dropped charges against Gregory Allen Davis, 49, of Port St. Lucie in an incident June 24 in Port St. Lucie when Davis ordered three juveniles out of their car at gunpoint and told them to get on the ground at the intersection of SW Morelia Lane and SW Acapulco Terrace. Minutes earlier, one of the teens had fired an Orbeez toy gun at the car that Davis and his fiancee were in. An Orbeez toy gun shoots soft water-absorbing beads. According to a prosecutor, the reason they dropped the charges against Davis is because in Florida, citizens have the right to make a citizen's arrest if they see that a felony has been committed in their presence. The felony that Davis saw was the teen firing a gun at his vehicle. "Basically, under Florida law, a citizen has a right to make a citizen's arrest if they observe a felony, occur in their presence. So that's basically what happened here. When someone effects a citizen's arrest, basically, they have the same powers as a police officer would, at least temporarily," said Jason Bruin, Assistant State Attorney, 19th Judicial Circuit. Bruin says if the case had gone to a jury, they would've returned a verdict of not guilty. Davis, in this case, gets out of the vehicle and holds the the people that were in that car at gunpoint. No, we don't recommend that people take the law into their own hands like that. Let the police do their job. Call the police, let the police do their job," Bruin said. Davis was charged with three counts of false imprisonment and three counts of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon. Those six charges carry a maximum sentence of 30 years in prison if convicted. "I am very grateful as I am a father of three and everything I do is for my kids. The thought of being away from them is horrifying. I have a daughter that is the same age as the person who did the shooting, and I spend my time teaching my children not to do dumb things like that. Obviously I would never want anyone to ever get hurt. Especially over what they consider to be a prank. I believe behavior like this starts with the parents. It is our job to teach our kids right from wrong and be their parent first and their friend second," Davis said in a text message to CBS12 News, reacting to the fact that the charges against him were dropped. Lucie County sheriff's deputy was fired after an Internal Affairs investigation found she created a social media post that mocked Sheriff Richard Del Toro's "Standards of Performance." According to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office Internal Affairs report, on Oct. 10, 2025, Sheriff Richard Del Toro was made aware of a Facebook post on Deputy Tina Speicker's personal social media account featuring an image titled "Standards of Power." The report says the image closely resembled Del Toro's "Standards of Performance," which was introduced after he was sworn into office. The Standards of Performance outlined eight performance expectations for employees, agency divisions and the Sheriff's Office's core values. See also: PSL police seek missing 14-year-old girl last seen Tuesday night The report says Speicker's Facebook post mirrored the "Standards of Performance" but replaced the original language with phrases depicting domination, manipulation and exploitation. Investigators alleged the post was intended to disparage the Sheriff's Office and Sheriff Del Toro and violated agency rules and regulations. According to the Internal Affairs report, Speicker's "Standards of Power" graphic stated: Top-down domination. Keep everyone beneath you guessing who's next to take the blame. Set confusion for others to follow. The less they know, the more control you have. Display a ruthless work ethic with a focus on self-preservation. Take credit for wins, redirect the failures. Demonstrate selective respect. Favor those who serve your goals; silence those who don't. Being unfair-strategically. Tip the scales to your advantage. Remain obsessive and paranoid. Control every detail, question every motive. Be committed to manipulation and influence. Knowledge is leverage trade it like currency. You own what you exploit and sign off to survive. The Internal Affairs investigator identified several similarities between the "Standards of Power" graphic and Del Toro's "Standards of Performance," including that both contained eight principles, used similar wording and sentence structure, began each bullet point with the same first word and featured a similar two-tone outline. Investigators concluded the graphic was intended to parody the Sheriff's official standards. During the investigation, the Sheriff's Office interviewed Sheriff Del Toro, agency supervisors, other deputies and Speicker. The IA report states Speicker acknowledged posting the graphic to her Facebook page but said it was intended as commentary on Congress and the federal government shutdown. The report also found Speicker gave inconsistent statements during multiple interviews, leading investigators to sustain allegations of criticism of orders or policies, conduct unbecoming, violating the code of ethics for public officers and employees, and false testimony. As a result of the investigation, Speicker was terminated on June 12, 2026. The investigation concluded that Speicker violated Sheriff's Office policies regarding criticism of orders or policies, conduct unbecoming, the code of ethics for public officers and employees, and false testimony.

Two sharks were spotted along the Atlantic Ocean shore — one that washed up dead and another of fishermen struggling with a hooked one. Both incidents occurred Friday, with video sent to WPBF. Jensen Beach resident and avid beach walker Kathy Green was walking along Normandy Beach on Hutchinson Island in St. Lucie County when she filmed a group of fishermen struggling with a 12-foot shark they had hooked. The fishermen unhooked the deadly beast and released it back into the water. Shark expert and conservationist Jim Abernethy believes it was a great white shark by looking at the video. Also Friday, a hammerhead shark was spotted dead just south of the Jupiter Beach Resort. Christopher Ray, a musician, submitted video to WPBF. Later that day, Fish Wildlife removed the shark. Shark Week 2026 ran from July 26 to Saturday on the Discovery Channel. Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission has ordered Martin County, which also includes Hutchinson Island, to follow rules about people fishing for fish or sharks from the beach or shoreline. Shark fishing requires a state saltwater fishing license to fish within 1,000 feet of the guarded beach boundaries at any time. Under the current county ordinance, shark fishing is prohibited within 1,000 yards of the county's four guarded beaches: Jensen, Stuart, Bathtub and Hobe Sound. On Tuesday, commissioners postponed making a decision and asked attorneys to review the law.

The Martin County School District has approved a consolidation of bus routes that officials say will save $255,000 without affecting students or eliminating any driver positions. The school board voted Tuesday unanimously to reduce the number of bus routes by 3, bringing the total from 58 to 55 ahead of the upcoming school year. District officials say all bus stops will remain the same and students will not be impacted by the change. WATCH WPTV'S COVERAGE BELOW: "Right now, we have 55 routes and roughly 56 drivers. So we have all of our routes covered," Superintendent Michael Maine said. The $255,000 in savings reflects a reduced transportation budget and will not be redirected to a specific expense, according to the school district. Parents have mixed reactions. Marino Reyes and Tiffany Gugumuck expressed support for the financial decision. "I think that's a great thing. A quarter million dollars that's a lot of money just for that one situation there. So many other needs that we can put the money towards," Reyes and Gugumuck said. Parent Ken Winstanley wondered what the change means for the budget. "Where's the money gonna go to?" Winstanley said. Michael Skinner, the President of the local AFSCME labor union chapter, voiced concerns during public comment on behalf of the bus drivers. "As what my feedback from the bus drivers were is that their routes or their buses are always full and cutting routes are not actually a good idea," Skinner said. Transportation Director Ruth Spires pushed back on that concern, noting that the buses hold a maximum of 77 passengers and are not operating at capacity. Spires also confirmed that no drivers were let go as part of the consolidation. "We were already challenged with a shortage last year. So the routes that were merged—consolidated—yes, the drivers were already covering. So no one was cut at all," Spires said. Drivers will be paid for any additional hours they work as a result of the consolidation, Spires explained. The district said it is confident it will maintain the same level of service with fewer buses on the road. Volunteers remove litter from Stuart Beach during the 2025 International Coastal Cleanup. For Hometown News STUART — Thousands of pieces of plastic, fishing line and other debris collect along Martin County’s shoreline, but volunteers will have a chance to turn the tide in a single morning. Keep Martin Beautiful will coordinate the 2026 International Coastal Cleanup on Saturday, Sept. 19, bringing residents together to remove litter from local beaches, shorelines and waterways. Last year, volunteers collected nearly 3,000 pieces of microplastic from Martin County’s shoreline during the event. For more than three decades, Keep Martin Beautiful has served as the county’s local coordinator for the worldwide cleanup effort. Each year, more than 1,000 volunteers, including individuals, families, businesses, youth groups and civic organizations, roll up their sleeves to remove litter from the shorelines. In addition to bottles and food packaging, volunteers collect cigarette butts, plastic foam fragments, discarded fishing line and microplastics. The pollutants travel through storm drains and waterways, threatening marine life and damaging coastal habitats. “Our beaches and waterways are at the heart of what makes Martin County such a special place to live,” said Tiffany Kincaid, Keep Martin Beautiful executive director. “The International Coastal Cleanup gives everyone an opportunity to make a real difference. In just one morning, volunteers can create a lasting impact while helping preserve these beautiful places for future generations.” Volunteers are encouraged to register through the Keep Martin Beautiful website and download the free Clean Swell™ app before the event. The app allows participants to record the litter they collect, providing data to Keep Martin Beautiful and the Ocean Conservancy. The information helps scientists identify pollution trends, guide conservation efforts and develop ways to reduce marine debris. Volunteers of all ages are welcome. Whether participating for the first time or returning year after year, every volunteer helps protect Martin County’s coast and becomes part of one of the world’s largest volunteer efforts to keep oceans and waterways healthy. Sponsors include WM, Martin County, Ashley Capital, Hutchinson Shores Resort Spa, Surfing’s Evolution Preservation Foundation, CSA Ocean Sciences, Lucido Associates, Indian Riverkeeper, Ecological Associates, Coastal Waste Recycling, The Guardians of Martin County, Jenkins Landscape, Live With Grace, Ram Real Estate, Solar Electric Power Company, the city of Stuart and the Firefly Group. Keep Martin Beautiful is a nonprofit organization founded in 1994. Its programs include litter prevention, recycling promotion, beautification projects, the Great American Cleanup and Adopt-A-Road and Adopt-A-Street programs. Recycled fishing line is transformed into a friendship bracelet during a hands-on activity presented by Coastal Connections at the Vero Beach Museum of Art. VERO BEACH — Discarded fishing line will find new purpose as friendship bracelets when art and marine conservation come together at the Vero Beach Museum of Art. The museum and Coastal Connections will team up for a free Second Saturday program beginning at 10 a.m. 8, with hands-on activities, gallery tours and lessons about protecting local marine life. Activities also include docent-led mini-tours, studio art projects and opportunities to learn about protecting local marine life. Coastal Connections will lead a hands-on activity in the Laura and Bill Buck Atrium, where visitors can make friendship bracelets using recycled fishing line collected from local waterways. Participants also can learn about the organization’s Fishing Line Recycling Program. The museum has adopted the fishing line recycling tube at the Riverside Park boat ramp. to 1 p.m., families can take short, docent-led gallery tours through the Museum Studios family program. Visitors can then participate in “Nature in Layers,” an art activity for children connected to the museum’s exhibitions. Guests also can tour the museum’s summer exhibitions throughout the day. “James Prosek: At Work” is on view in the Holmes Gallery, while “Jill Nathanson: Chromatic Phrases” is displayed in the Schumann and Titelman galleries. “Our partnership with VBMA is a great example of how we are working with our community to introduce everyone to marine conservation and environmental protection in unique ways,” explained Kendra Bergman, founder and executive director of Coastal Connections. “Collaborations like these are key to meeting our mission and watching one of the greatest conservation success stories unfold within our lifetime.” Second Saturday includes free museum admission throughout the day. Additional programs may include performances, lectures, films and other arts and humanities offerings on select Saturdays. Coastal Connections was founded in 2017 with a mission of advancing the survival of sea turtles by educating and connecting people to the environment. North America’s soccer body on Thursday rejected FIFA president Gianni Infantino’s plan to sell stakes in the World Cup to private equity investors, joining European nations in opposition.UEFA member federations agreed Thursday to boycott all FIFA competitions in protest at Gianni Infantino's plan to sell stakes in the World Cup to private equity investors."UEFA and its national associations will not participate in FIFA competitions," the European soccer body said after an urgent online meeting of the 55 members.RELATED STORY | FIFA's Infantino sets deadline to members in Kushner-backed World Cup planOn Thursday, all 41 Concacaf members met and have rejected Gianni Infantino's FIFA Forward Enterprise plans.“During the meeting," CONCACAF said in a statement, "the membership expressed deep concerns about the lack of due process surrounding the proposal, the artificially short deadline imposed, and the absence of any review or approval by the relevant FIFA governance bodies."They released the following statement following the meeting.U.S. Soccer reiterated it's stance on it's social media platforms.The strategy meeting was called to counter FIFA president Infantino's offer of $20 million to each of its 211 global members that has to be accepted by mid-September.Infantino's secret proposal was revealed Tuesday to spin off its commercial operations in a $20 billion operation 20% owned by private investors. More than 100 women's college basketball players have teamed up to form a union for college athletes as part of their growing push to collectively bargain with their schools, an organizing group announced Friday.The United College Athletes Association said as part of the push, members of the Oregon State women's team filed a petition with state regulators, marking a formal effort to seek collective bargaining rights under state law.RELATED STORY | NCAA transfer portal rules, NIL could change under new bipartisan Senate billThe announcement comes two years after a group of women's basketball players co-signed letters to Southeastern and Big Ten Conference leaders in 2024, requesting a formal collaboration process on issues affecting college athletics.Since those efforts were denied, more than 100 female athletes have signed union authorization cards with the UCAA, agreeing to representation in collective bargaining.The announcement comes a few days after the College Football Players Association revealed that Stanford has become the first football team to organize a player-led chapter — another effort by college athletes to unionize.The UCAA says its mission is to represent and protect athletes through collective bargaining, ensuring that college sports are safe, fair, sustainable and that athletes have a say in decision-making."As interim president of the UCAA, I'm proud to help lead a movement that gives college athletes a real voice in the decisions that shape our lives and careers," University of Maryland basketball player Oluchi Okananwa said in a statement.RELATED STORY | NCAA accuses DraftKings of trademark infringement in March Madness marketingNCAA leaders have long opposed the idea of players becoming employees of their schools, though the idea isn't universally opposed by college leaders. Tennessee athletic director Danny White has been among those who have said collective bargaining is the only real solution to the problems that confront schools that are now paying millions to their players.Attempts to create unions for college athletes at Dartmouth and Southern California stalled in 2024 due to the changing landscape in college sports and the then-incoming Trump administration's new National Labor Relations Board, which wasn't expected to approve the moves.

West Palm Beach Police Chief Tony Araujo announced Friday the termination of five command-level officers following a nearly two-year administrative investigation into overtime misconduct, marking the latest development in what has rocked the department since 2020.WATCH BELOW: 3 West Palm Beach police captains among those fired in probe"Yesterday, following a thorough, nearly two-year administrative investigation, and after careful review of the findings, I made the difficult decision to terminate five command-level officers," Araujo said during a Friday morning press conference.The firings — which included three captains, a major and an assistant chief — come as the culmination of an investigation that began after a 2020 audit commissioned by the city uncovered nearly $20,000 worth of "double dipping" on timecards and thousands of hours of questionable overtime payments within the police department. The controversy dates back to 2020 when a third-party audit examined the finances of multiple city departments. The audit revealed what officials called "pretty egregious" overtime spending patterns within the police department that had gone undetected for years.The investigation eventually led to the firing of former Police Chief Frank Adderley and placed seven officers on administrative leave related to financial misconduct. The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office was brought in to handle the administrative investigation to ensure impartiality.The press conference Friday morning comes after the union pushed back against the terminations, claiming a "different standard" was applied to the fired captains compared to other officers involved in the overtime scheme. The union had previously filed a lawsuit alleging violations of the Police Officers' Bill of Rights, though that lawsuit was subsequently withdrawn."I respect the union. They have their own opinion. They have their own interpretation. I'm going to respectfully disagree," Araujo said. "But again, we're going to leave that to the continued due process that will take place, and I don't begrudge the union for advocating for their membership."WATCH THE FULL PRESS CONFERENCE BELOW:Araujo emphasized that the terminations were part of a broader effort to rebuild trust and accountability within the department. He said the department has strengthened training, reviewed overtime practices, and implemented better supervision of extra duty assignments.The chief acknowledged the department had been on accreditation probation when he arrived, a status that city leadership was unaware of at the time. He said those issues have since been corrected.Araujo indicated the department may need to conduct promotions to fill the vacant leadership positions.The chief stressed that despite the misconduct by some officers, the majority of the department's personnel continue to provide professional service to the community."We have good people at the West Palm Beach Police Department. Be certain of that; we have good leadership," Araujo said. "We can't look at the department as a whole and make a decision of the whole just based on the few."Fraternal Order of Police Union President Adam Myers, who represents the three captains, said a criminal investigation by the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office found no criminality and determined it was an administrative matter."Initially, there was a criminal investigation by the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office. They found there was no criminality and basically said it was an administrative issue," Myers said.Myers said the internal affairs report found the city had installed software designed to prevent officers from clocking two simultaneous shifts. Because the command staff members were salaried rather than hourly employees, they used what is called flex time — time earned from working beyond their regular schedule — to offset the extra hours. Myers said the practice was approved and directed by Adderley, who was chief at the time."They would put in vacation hours to take themselves off, so that it would allow the other program to let them pick up their job, and then they go back and take out the time because they aren't hourly employees," Myers said.Investigators found that because the software only checked for scheduling conflicts when a job was selected — and not after leave was removed — the overlapping hours remained. The report said at least four command staff members later admitted to using that process. The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office, which conducted the internal affairs investigation, called it a vulnerability that undermined the purpose of the system.Myers said the outcome has been difficult for the officers involved."If you follow the direction you're given by your supervision all the way to the top of the agency, and then to be reviewed and found that that's improper because it's a differing opinion is hard," Myers said.Araujo pushed back on that characterization."I'm going to respectfully disagree, but again, we're going to leave that to the continued due process that will take place," Araujo said.Araujo said the department's focus remains on rebuilding trust."Public trust is not something we inherit. It's something we earn," Araujo said.The union will pursue arbitration on behalf of the officers.

Back-to-school rush is on in Palm Beach County — and pediatricians say appointments are filling up fast“Lots of examinations,” Dr. Amanda Thomas told WPTV.WATCH BELOW: 'They said okay he needs this, this and that done before he even begins,' Christine Montalvo tells WPTV's Joel LopezThat's how Thomas, a pediatrician at Bluebird Kids Health in West Palm Beach, describes the annual back-to-school rush now underway across Palm Beach County.With the first day of school just over a week away, families are scrambling to complete their school entry health requirements before students head back to class. More than 3,000 people responded to a WPTV Facebook post regarding our recent coverage of wages and rents in South Florida — and the message was clear: rising housing costs are pushing South Florida residents to a breaking point.WATCH BELOW: Rising rents consuming 50% of income for many South Florida residentsBelow is a snapshot of some of the responses to the Facebook post:"The challenge is high prices and low wages," one person said. "I'm wondering if these landlords were looking for a place, what their thoughts would be," another person said. "So what is going to be done about this?" another commenter said, which doesn't seem easy to answer. Ned Murray at the Jorge M. Perez Metropolitan Center at Florida International University, many renters in South Florida are now using 50% of their income on rent, far above the traditional baseline of 30%. "Things really begin to break down, and that is increasing rapidly, and in fact here in South Florida, including Palm Beach (County) we have $320,000 renters who are now in that 50 percent and over category," Murray said.Tackling affordability in housing is being talked about a lot lately, and it is on the minds of local elected officials. "It is the most difficult thing we have to deal with; it is the one thing we get calls about every single day," Palm Beach County Commissioner Bobby Powell said. "What we can do is when we allocate funds we can make sure that rents don't go over a certain amount," Powell said. "There are some units we approved on July 7 that won't be over 60 percent of the area median income."

The western communities of Palm Beach County continue to grow, and residents will soon have another big-box store to do their shopping.Real estate developer Minto Communities USA announced Friday the sale of a 24-acre parcel in Westlake to Walmart Supercenter, which is planning to build a 188,779-square-foot superstore.Approved by the city council in April, Minto said the store will sell groceries, have a pharmacy, garden center, automotive center and vision center. The store will also have a separate area for a convenience store and gas station.The new Walmart will be located in Town Center West, just west of Seminole Pratt Whitney Road, close to 60th Street North. Minto Communities said the store will be adjacent to a future Lowe's Home Improvement store, which will also serve as a regional headquarters."Walmart gives Westlake homeowners another place to shop for everyday essentials, right in their own backyard," Senior Vice President of Minto Communities USA John Carter said in a statement. "Bringing in major brands like Walmart and Lowe's is a clear vote of confidence in our community’s growth and long-term value."The company did not say when construction would begin on the Walmart or when it would be ready to serve shoppers.Minto is also building single-family homes, estate homes and townhomes in Westlake with prices starting in the $300,000s.

Federal prosecutors said a Los Angeles man was sentenced to life in federal prison for selling fentanyl that caused the death of a Treasure Coast man, then continuing to traffic the deadly drug just two days later.U.S. District Judge Aileen Cannon imposed the sentence on Alfonso Guerrero, 39, of Los Angeles, after a federal jury convicted him in May 2026 of conspiracy to possess with intent to distribute fentanyl resulting in death and distribution of fentanyl resulting in death."A tenth of a gram of fentanyl, about the size of a small pinch of salt, was enough to kill David Eller," U.S. Reding Quiñones for the Southern District of Florida said in a statement. "This was not a small drug deal. Guerrero sold the fentanyl that killed his friend and, just two days later, was caught carrying more fentanyl for distribution. Today’s life sentence is the consequence of that deadly conduct and his long record of violence and crime. Together with the DEA and our local law enforcement partners, we will trace fatal doses back to the dealers who sold them and hold those dealers fully accountable."According to court records and evidence presented at trial, the U.S. Attorney's Office said Guerrero sold fentanyl in Indian River County. On May 16, 2023, prosecutors said he exchanged 0.1 gram of fentanyl — commonly known as "a point" — for another controlled substance known as "molly." Officials said the drug transaction was captured on a doorbell camera. Hours later, Eller was found dead inside his Vero Beach home. Investigators recovered drug paraphernalia, including a small piece of burnt aluminum foil that the victim used to receive the fentanyl from Guerrero on the victim's front porch, near his body.Two days later, on May 18, 2023, prosecutors said Guerrero was arrested and found in possession of additional quantities of fentanyl intended for distribution.Officials said Guerrero's extensive criminal history included documented gang membership and prior convictions for attempted robbery with a firearm in California, aggravated assault in Georgia, and cocaine and fentanyl possession offenses in Florida.

Renters in Martin County say keeping up with the cost of living is a challenge, while a local real estate agent said that the market is neither rising nor falling — for now.Renters on the Treasure Coast told WPTV reporter Tyler Hatfield on Friday that the cost of living is putting a strain on their finances, even as a local real estate expert says the rental market has leveled off.Jesse Espinosa, a renter in Martin County, said the price of rent is taking a toll.WATCH BELOW: Treasure Coast renters say costs are straining budgets"I mean, living on your own, you got rent, food. An 86-year-old woman died after police said she pulled into the path of an SUV and was struck in a Port St. Lucie intersection Thursday afternoon. The crash happened at about 2:30 p.m. at Southwest Savona Boulevard and Southwest Lawndale Avenue, according to the Port St. Investigators said Marie R. Martin was driving a 2006 Hyundai Elantra west on Lawndale Avenue when she entered the intersection from near a stop sign and failed to yield to a northbound 2026 Honda HR-V. The Honda, driven by a 17-year-old boy, struck the driver’s side of Martin’s car, police said. Body-camera video recorded after the crash shows the Hyundai off the roadway near a cluster of palm trees, with visible damage to its driver’s side and emergency crews working around the vehicle. The Honda also came to rest on the grass nearby, close to vegetation and a roadside sign. Lucie police officers and St. Lucie County Fire District personnel can be seen at the scene, along with fire engines, rescue vehicles and traffic cones blocking part of the intersection. Debris and emergency equipment were scattered across the grass between the two vehicles. See also: Chief: Five West Palm Beach police leaders fired following 'double-dipping' probe Martin had to be extricated from the Hyundai before she was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital with critical injuries, police said. She later died despite efforts to save her. The teenage driver of the Honda was not injured. The Police Department’s Traffic Homicide Unit continues to investigate the crash.

A suspected burglar dressed for happy hour instead of a police lineup is now known across St. Lucie County as the Flamingo Bandit. The nickname comes courtesy of the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office , which is searching for a man photographed wearing a tropical shirt dominated by a giant pink flamingo. Some criminals try to blend in, the agency wrote. This one apparently took fashion advice from a Jimmy Buffett concert. But deputies said the man’s alleged itinerary involved burglary, not boats, beaches or frozen drinks. Investigators said the suspect entered a residence on July 28 and stole a laptop, miscellaneous food and a key to the home. Deputies allege he then returned later that same day and used the stolen key to get inside a second time. The sheriff’s office shared an image of the flamboyantly dressed suspect, hoping his difficult-to-miss wardrobe will help someone identify him. While we can appreciate a memorable wardrobe, we can’t overlook burglary, the agency wrote. Anyone who recognizes the man or has information about the case is asked to call the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office at 772-462-7300 or email Deputy V. Ancewicz at PatrolTips@stluciesheriff.com . As the sheriff’s office put it, Crime doesn’t get a free pass just because it’s dressed for paradise.

A Fort Pierce resort says an abandoned sailboat that washed ashore three weeks ago is damaging property, slamming into other boats, and costing them thousands in business, but state law prevents them from moving it. "This is a danger to people and personal property," said Joe Zebrowski, general manager of Dockside Marina and Resort. The sailboat washed ashore near On The Edge Bar and Grill, and Zabrowski and his team quickly secured it. However, Zabrowski said the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC) informed him that the boat cannot be moved. The agency is giving the owners 60 days to claim the vessel, and the resort is also prohibited from moving it. "I did a good deed, but no deed goes unpunished," Zebrowski said. The FWC used a chain to secure the sailboat, but Zebrowski said it hasn’t stopped the vessel from causing problems. "It kept it from floating away but didn’t keep it from whipping back and forth," he said. Zebrowski explained that the sailboat has slammed into a docked boat, destroyed a piling, and forced the restaurant to block off several tables near the vessel, which has significantly impacted their revenue. "These are our prime tables. They probably cost us about 25 percent of our overall business for the past month," Zebrowski said. According to state law, moving a boat that has washed ashore onto private property without proper permission can expose individuals to legal liabilities or even charges of theft. "There needs to be a carveout in however the law takes care of situations like this that takes care of people who are innocent and stop protecting an owner who has abandoned his boat that I don’t think is registered or has insurance," Zebrowski said. The FWC confirmed to WPBF that no one can touch the boat except its owners. WPBF is working to contact the owners of the boat for comment. The FWC is working on providing a more detailed statement. Renters in Martin County say keeping up with the cost of living is a challenge, while a local real estate agent said that the market is neither rising nor falling — for now.Renters on the Treasure Coast told WPTV reporter Tyler Hatfield on Friday that the cost of living is putting a strain on their finances, even as a local real estate expert says the rental market has leveled off.Jesse Espinosa, a renter in Martin County, said the price of rent is taking a toll.WATCH BELOW: Treasure Coast renters say costs are straining budgets"I mean, living on your own, you got rent, food. Two sharks were spotted along the Atlantic Ocean shore — one that washed up dead and another of fishermen struggling with a hooked one. Both incidents occurred Friday, with video sent to WPBF. Jensen Beach resident and avid beach walker Kathy Green was walking along Normandy Beach on Hutchinson Island in St. Lucie County when she filmed a group of fishermen struggling with a 12-foot shark they had hooked. The fishermen unhooked the deadly beast and released it back into the water. Shark expert Jim Abernethy believes it was a great white shark. Also Friday, a hammerhead shark was spotted dead just south of the Jupiter Beach Resort. Christopher Ray, a musician, submitted video to WPBF. Later that day, Fish Wildlife removed the shark. Shark Week 2026 ran from July 26 to Saturday on the Discovery Channel. Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission has ordered Martin County to follow rules about people fishing for fish or sharks from the beach or shoreline. Shark fishing requires a state saltwater fishing license to fish within 1,000 feet of the guarded beach boundaries at any time. Under the current county ordinance, shark fishing is prohibited within 1,000 yards of the county's four guarded beaches: Jensen, Stuart, Bathtub and Hobe Sound. On Tuesday, commissioners postponed making a decision and asked attorneys to review the law.

Lead sponsors supporting the Education Foundation of Martin County’s Your Classroom Connection programs are, from left, Patty McAuley of Seacoast Bank; Tami Karol of Tami Karol Insurance; Kelley Decowski of RE/MAX of Stuart; Dr. Ajay Goyal of Diagnostic Radiology Center of the Treasure Coast; Lisa Rhodes of the Education Foundation of Martin County; and Dr. Vincent Napoli of Napoli Orthodontics. STUART — Martin County residents can help teachers prepare for the new school year by adopting a classroom, funding a project or donating supplies through the Education Foundation of Martin County. As Martin County students prepare to return to school Aug. 10, the Education Foundation of Martin County is inviting residents, civic groups, nonprofits and businesses to help meet classroom needs through three online programs. Adopt-A-Class allows supporters to adopt a specific classroom or school program with a donation of $100 or more. Classrooms and programs may be adopted multiple times, and the foundation hopes to have every classroom adopted at least once during the school year. To adopt a class and make a donation to a classroom or program, visit www.educationfoundationmc.org/p/251/adopt-a-class . Through Fund-A-Project, teachers can post requests for classroom projects designed to support student learning. Donors can select and fund specific educational projects. To view teacher requests, visit www.educationfoundationmc.org/p/285/fund-a-project . Bulletin Board Listings connect community members with nonmonetary classroom needs. Participants may volunteer their time or donate materials, gently used equipment, books, magazines, shoe boxes and other reusable supplies. Community members also may offer subject-matter expertise or advisory board support. To support the Bulletin Board, visit https://www.educationfoundationmc.org/p/284/community-opportunities . “Every great classroom innovation begins with an idea,” said Chanda Leon, a pre-AICE biology teacher at Martin County High School and the Education Foundation’s 2025-2026 Martin County Teacher of the Year. “Too often, that idea never becomes reality because of cost. Adopt-a-Classroom and Fund-a-Project have helped to remove financial barriers, allowing me the opportunity to convert creative solutions into meaningful learning experiences for my students.” The foundation said 100 percent of donations go directly toward classroom needs because program sponsors cover administrative costs. Lead sponsors include Napoli Orthodontics, the Kelley Decowski Team at RE/MAX of Stuart, Tami Karol Insurance, Diagnostic Radiology Center of the Treasure Coast, Seacoast Bank, and Rosenthal, Levy, Simon Sosa Injury Lawyers. Other sponsors include Precision Site Contracting, Stuart Pediatric Dentistry, Sullivan Electric Pump, Searcy Law, New Wave Compass – Sara Crombie, Ampersand Graphics, JoAnna Oster, RE/MAX of Stuart, Pinder’s Nursery, All Jetting Technologies, Elegant Entries, Lesser Landy Smith Siegel PLLC, SwissMango and Sal’s Air. “Every adopted classroom, funded project and donated resource sends a powerful message to our teachers and students that this community believes in them,” said Lisa Rhodes, executive director of the Education Foundation of Martin County. “When local residents and businesses step forward, they help turn classroom ideas into learning experiences that can inspire achievement all year long.” Steven C. Simon, managing shareholder at Rosenthal, Levy, Simon Sosa Injury Lawyers, said his firm was pleased to support the foundation’s Your Classroom Connection program. “Educators make a lasting difference in the lives of students, and we are grateful for the opportunity to help strengthen classrooms across Martin County. It is a privilege to stand with many leading community businesses and join the Education Foundation in investing in educational excellence and student success,” he said. The Education Foundation of Martin County is the Martin County School District’s nonprofit partner. It raises and distributes private and corporate donations through classroom enrichment grants, literacy and STEAM programs, teacher professional development, scholarships and other educational initiatives. To adopt a classroom, fund a project, respond to a classroom need or learn more about the Education Foundation of Martin County, visit www.EducationFoundationMC.org or call 772-600-8062. A petition with nearly 800 signatures is mounting against a proposal that could transform Fort Pierce's Museum Pointe — a public waterfront park along the Indian River Lagoon — into a mega-yacht marina.WATCH BELOW: 'We have been talking for years about better locations for that history center,' Erick Gill tells WPTV's Kate HusseyThe proposal is part of the Port of Fort Pierce's updated 2026 Master Plan. It calls for redeveloping Museum Pointe, which is currently home to a history center, public waterfront access, fishing piers, and green space, into a facility featuring floating docks, a multi-story marina, an event center, a waterfront restaurant, and a clubhouse.Opponents fear the plan could privatize one of the city's most treasured public spaces."Giving public land to private folks," said Terry Howard, a volunteer at the History Center at Museum Pointe Park. Howard contacted WPTV's Kate Hussey after learning about the master plan. "Development is just rampant in Florida, and at least we can fight for this one particular area and keep it green," Howard said.He said the loss of public waterfront access is a concern — but his biggest worry is the fate of the museum itself."This is the place where this museum should be, right here on this Museum Pointe," said Howard. For more than 50 years, the museum has preserved artifacts from Florida's Native American tribes, Spanish shipwrecks, and more. The master plan's renderings place the proposed marina clubhouse exactly where the museum stands today."Basically taking away a gem — a public gem that belongs to the people and replacing it with a facility for mega yachts," Howard said. "We're trying to keep this area as it is." St. Lucie County spokesperson Erick Gill said the museum's future is not in jeopardy if the project moves forward."Staff's intent was never to close the museum," Gill said. "We have been talking for years about better locations for that history center; it is on a barrier island, in a flood zone, so it may not be the best place to store artifacts."Gill said the museum and its collection would be preserved and relocated if the project proceeds. He added that the master plan is designed to expand economic development, create jobs, and generate county revenue."I think all local governments are looking for a way to generate revenue, so we can continue to lower the taxes for St. Lucie County residents and generate revenue from economic development, and we already have dock space there," Gill said."Anything that's going to be a positive economic driver for the City of Fort Pierce, I'm going to embrace completely," Fort Pierce City Commissioner Michael Broderick added. Broderick said the city will have the final say on whether the project moves forward, and that commissioners will have to weigh economic benefits against preserving waterfront access.When asked which priority — economic development or waterfront access — would take precedence, Broderick said the answer is not simple."That's the challenging question right there. I believe that we can strike a balance," Broderick said. "We always have to be careful not to eliminate public access to the waterway. Period." For Howard, the stakes go beyond the present."This is a gem that once we develop around it, it'll never be replaced again," Howard said. "The museum has been here since the 1970s. If they want to boat docks for mega yachts, they can do it someplace else." St. Lucie County leaders are scheduled to discuss the proposal and its current status at a 9 a.m. Lucie County Commission Chambers.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. A man awaiting a possible retrial in the fatal shooting of his former girlfriend is accused of attacking convicted murderer Otto Lenke inside the St. According to an arrest affidavit, Robert Castro approached Lenke in a jail dorm on July 6 and struck him in the face, knocking off his glasses. Lenke approached an intercom and reported the attack to corrections staff, the affidavit says. A deputy noticed a cut on the upper part of Lenke’s nose, and a nurse treated the injury. A jail sergeant witnessed Castro strike Lenke, according to investigators. Surveillance video also showed Castro approaching Lenke and hitting him in the face, the affidavit says. Lenke later told a detective he had been using a jail-issued tablet to watch a chess game when Castro attacked him. Investigators attempted to interview Castro on July 16. The affidavit says Castro repeatedly stated that he did not understand his Miranda rights and did not want to speak with the detective, ending the interview. Castro, 30, is charged with battery by a person detained in a prison or jail facility, a felony. The new charge was filed July 20. Lenke, a former Melbourne police officer and Indian River County firefighter, was convicted in May of first-degree murder and first-degree arson in the 2021 death of Richard Benson. Prosecutors said Lenke shot Benson three times inside Benson’s Fort Pierce motorcycle shop, poured an accelerant on him and set him on fire while he was still alive. A jury later voted 11-1 to recommend that Lenke be sentenced to death. Castro’s murder conviction reversed Castro was convicted in 2024 of first-degree murder with a firearm in the death of his former girlfriend, Taylor Ann Sato, and sentenced to life in prison. However, the Fourth District Court of Appeal reversed the conviction in February after finding that the trial court failed to properly complete the process for determining whether Castro was competent to stand trial. A psychologist found Castro competent in November 2022. Five days later, his attorneys raised concerns about his condition, and the original judge said Castro had definitely decompensated before ordering another evaluation. The appeals court said the record contained no additional evaluation, report or competency hearing after that order. Nearly two years later, a different judge declared Castro competent based on the original 2022 evaluation. Castro then went to trial and was convicted. The appellate court ruled that a two-year-old evaluation was not sufficient because competency must be assessed close to the time of trial. The case was sent back to the trial court to determine whether Castro’s competency during the 2024 trial can now be reliably evaluated. Castro would receive a new trial if a retrospective evaluation cannot be conducted or if the court determines he was not competent during the original trial. 2022 killing Fort Pierce police accused Castro of killing Sato outside her Timber Ridge Lane home during the early morning hours of July 23, 2022. According to the original arrest affidavit, a man called 911 and said he had shot and killed his girlfriend and was considering killing himself. Officers arrived and found Sato outside the home with multiple gunshot wounds. Investigators reported finding six gunshot wounds and several 9 mm shell casings near her body. Sato’s stepfather told detectives that she and Castro had recently ended a long-term relationship. He said Sato had blocked Castro’s phone number, but Castro continued trying to contact her by sending repeated $1 transactions through Cash App with messages attached. The stepfather also told police Castro had previously threatened to kill Sato. After listening to part of the 911 call, he identified the caller’s voice as Castro’s, according to the affidavit. Castro later surrendered to deputies in St. Investigators said several rounds of 9 mm ammunition were found in his pocket. His police interview ended after an attorney arrived and directed detectives not to question him further.
