A new dance festival is set to debut in West Palm Beach this summer, bringing together nationally recognized choreographers, aspiring dancers and community arts programming across Palm Beach County.The inaugural Banyan Dance Festival will take place Aug. 3-8 throughout West Palm Beach, according to organizers Natural Movers Foundation and Grounded WPB. The weeklong event will feature performances, professional dance training, public classes, artist talkbacks and community experiences designed to strengthen South Florida’s dance community.Festival founders Ericka Squire of Natural Movers Foundation and Branndi Lewis of Grounded WPB said the event was created to expand opportunities for dancers and choreographers while positioning Palm Beach County as a destination for dance.“At its core, Banyan is about creating opportunities for artists,” Squire said in a statement. “Palm Beach County is Florida’s Cultural Capital®, and we wanted to create an opportunity for audiences to experience high-quality dance performances while also creating real pathways for dancers and choreographers to train, work, create, and be seen right here in Palm Beach County.”Festival organizers said the event will bring together professional artists, students and community members through performances, creative development and educational programming hosted at venues throughout the city.Featured artists include internationally recognized choreographers and educators Sean Aaron Carmon, Babatunji and Loni Landon, along with local, national and international performers participating throughout the week.Carmon, a former dancer with Alvin Ailey American Dance Theater, will create an original work for the Banyan Dance Company. Babatunji, a former member of Alonzo King LINES Ballet, will choreograph a new piece for the Banyan Dance Ensemble.Landon, a Princess Grace Choreography Fellowship Award winner and Guggenheim fellow, will teach during the festival and create a featured solo work for a dancer participating in the Banyan Dance Intensive.The festival’s inaugural Banyan Choreography Fellowship was awarded to Betty Garcia Diaz, a Cuban-born dancer and choreographer who has performed with companies including Northwest Dance Project, Malpaso Dance Company and Boston Dance Theater. Organizers said Garcia Diaz will create a newly commissioned work during the festival.Programming throughout the week includes:Youth Artist Program classes for dancers ages 9-15A pre-professional dance intensive for dancers ages 16-25Community dance classes sponsored by the Downtown Development AuthorityA Banyan Silent Disco at Nora DistrictRehearsal observations and artist talkbacks at Ballet FloridaThe Banyan Gala at the Community Foundation for Palm Beach and Martin CountiesThe Banyan Dance Festival Concert at the Norton Museum of ArtLewis said the festival is designed to create opportunities for dancers who previously may have needed to leave South Florida to pursue professional growth.“Banyan Dance Festival is building something that doesn’t currently exist in South Florida,” Lewis said in a statement. “Together, Grounded WPB and Natural Movers Foundation have created a platform that expands the local dance ecosystem while investing in artists through paid opportunities, professional training, and a full creative pipeline.”More information and a full schedule can be found at banyandancefestival.com or on Instagram at @banyandancefestival.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. It's a conversation many families avoid because it's uncomfortable, but legal experts say putting off estate planning could leave loved ones facing expensive legal challenges and even put generations of family property at risk.WATCH BELOW: 'They can't sell it. They can't leverage the equity in it,' Tequisha Myles tells WPTV's Vannia JosephThe Legal Aid Society of Palm Beach County is encouraging homeowners to take advantage of a free estate planning and probate assistance program designed to help families protect one of their biggest investments — their home.According to Tequisha Myles with the Legal Aid Society, many families continue paying the mortgage, property taxes and maintaining a home after a loved one dies, but never complete the legal process to transfer ownership."When a homeowner dies without a will, or probate is never completed, the property remains legally in the name of the deceased," Myles said. "People are caring for the property, they're paying the mortgage, they're maybe keeping up with the taxes, but they don't have the title in their name. They can't leverage the equity in it."Without clear ownership, families can face significant financial consequences. Myles said homeowners may not be able to access the equity in the home during emergencies or qualify for disaster assistance after a hurricane."FEMA is not going to do payouts to people that don't have clear title to the property," she said. "You may have been keeping it in the family, but now to really keep it for generational wealth, you've got to actually put it in your name."The Legal Aid Society said its Heirs' Property Project helps eligible Palm Beach County homeowners resolve tangled property titles and complete estate planning documents at no cost.The program, funded through a $1 million grant from the Federal Home Loan Bank of Atlanta and Palm Beach County, includes:A Last Will and TestamentPower of AttorneyDesignation of Health Care SurrogateLiving WillLady Bird DeedProbate and heirs' property assistance, when neededMyles said those services typically cost between $3,000 and $5,000 through a private attorney."We do the drafting, you come in for a signing, it takes an hour and you have peace of mind," Myles said. "It's just a matter of planning, and I think planning helps you prepare for whatever happens."Unlike many legal assistance programs, eligibility is not based on income. Applicants must own a home in Palm Beach County and meet the program requirements.Legal Aid estimates it can still help approximately 150 more families, but applications should be submitted by Sept. 1 so attorneys have enough time to complete the work before grant funding expires at the end of September.Homeowners interested in applying or learning more about the Heirs' Property Project can visit legalaidpbc.org/heirsintake.

With fewer than three weeks remaining before Florida's primary, the Republican race for governor is producing new ads, dueling polls and increasingly pointed attacks — but little evidence that the contest has tightened at the top.U.S. Byron Donalds remains the clear frontrunner, bolstered by President Donald Trump's early endorsement, superior name recognition and a significant financial advantage over his Republican rivals.This week, a political committee supporting Donalds released a statewide television and digital ad centered on affordability. The spot shows Donalds playing basketball with his sons while promising to cut property taxes, lower insurance rates and reduce housing costs."My boys deserve the same shot I got—but Florida’s pricing out our future," Donalds says.WATCH: Donalds focuses on affordability as Republican rivals scramble for momentumThe ad reflects a campaign increasingly focused on pocketbook issues—and one largely looking past former House Speaker Paul Renner, Lt. Jay Collins and investor James Fishback.University of South Florida political scientist Susan MacManus said the basic shape of the race has changed little. Donalds' three leading challengers remain divided, making it more difficult for any one of them to consolidate the opposition."Name ID, credibility, Trump endorsement—it's made it really hard for the other three candidates to gain any traction, no matter how hard they try," MacManus said.A public Cygnal survey conducted July 12-13 found Donalds leading with 43%, followed by Fishback at 12%, Collins at 11% and Renner at 2%. Another 31% remained undecided. The survey included 500 likely Republican primary voters and had a margin of error of 4.38 percentage points. View the Cygnal poll.Collins' campaign, however, released an internal poll this week showing a significantly closer contest. That survey put Donalds at 46%, Collins at 30%, Fishback at 9.8% and Renner at 5.9%.The Collins campaign argued the results show the race consolidating into a two-candidate contest. Public polling has generally shown Collins much farther behind, with Donalds leading his nearest rivals by roughly 30 points or more.MacManus said Donalds’ support has remained particularly durable among the highly partisan voters most likely to participate in a Republican primary."The three people who are running against Donalds are going to split the vote, which makes Donalds' likelihood of gaining the nomination very, very strong," she said.Fishback is trying to use a courtroom victory to generate momentum after Leon County Circuit Judge David Frank rejected Collins’ attempt to remove him from the ballot.Florida's Constitution requires a candidate for governor to have lived in the state for the seven years preceding the election. Collins pointed to Fishback’s 2020 vote in Washington, D.C., his purchase of a condominium there and tax, mortgage and homestead records as evidence that Fishback had established residency outside Florida.Fishback maintained that he never intended to abandon his Florida residency. Frank ruled that Collins failed to overcome Florida’s legal presumptions favoring continued residency and candidate access to the ballot. Read more about the ruling.Fishback responded by calling on Collins to resign as lieutenant governor.“This was not about election integrity,” Fishback said. "This was about rigging an election."Collins dismissed the demand and criticized the ruling on Thursday."I think that his decision has basically put us in a position where, if you identify as a Floridian, you are a Floridian," Collins said. "I guess we can be trans-Floridian now."Asked whether he would appeal, Collins said his team had not yet made a final decision.Renner is using his closing campaign ads to emphasize his record as House speaker, including the expansion of school-choice programs and conservative legislation passed while he led the chamber.He is casting himself as the most experienced candidate to continue Gov. Ron DeSantis' policies."If you want to have something as close to Ron DeSantis as possible, I am that person by far," Renner said.Renner also escalated his criticism of Dr. Anthony Fauci, alleging the former federal infectious-disease official helped direct taxpayer money to coronavirus research in China that Renner believes led to the pandemic."The one that to me is potentially traitorous is his support in directing taxpayer money…for gain-of-function research," Renner said.Federal audits confirm that National Institutes of Health grants to the nonprofit EcoHealth Alliance included subawards involving the Wuhan Institute of Virology. The Department of Health and Human Services' inspector general found significant failures in NIH and EcoHealth’s oversight of the grants, but its audit did not conclude that the research created SARS-CoV-2 or caused the pandemic. Read the HHS inspector general's findings.The origin of the virus remains unresolved. The World Health Organization said the weight of available scientific evidence favors an animal-to-human spillover, either directly from bats or through another animal. The organization has not ruled out a laboratory incident, saying China has not provided information needed to fully evaluate that possibility. Read the WHO assessment.On the Democratic side, David Jolly is already focusing his attacks on Donalds.Jolly this week promised to halt new AI data-center construction until Florida develops stronger protections for its water supply, electric grid, communities and consumer privacy. His campaign also accused Donalds of being too closely aligned with the industry, pointing to millions of dollars in support it says came from interests connected to data-center development."Byron Donalds wants to hand ‘pristine’ Florida land over to the data center industry that’s funding his campaign," Jolly said. "Florida is not for sale."Donalds has argued Florida should embrace data centers while imposing protections for residents. He recently introduced federal legislation that would require the facilities to secure electricity and water from private sources instead of relying on public utility systems. The proposal is intended to prevent data centers from raising residential utility costs.Vote-by-mail ballots have already been distributed for the Aug. Florida's mandatory early-voting period begins Aug. 8 and continues through Aug. 15, though counties may offer additional days. See Florida's election calendar.

An 86-year-old woman died Thursday afternoon following a two-vehicle crash at a Port St. Lucie intersection, police said.Marie Martin was driving a 2006 Hyundai Elantra westbound on SW Lawndale Avenue around 2:30 p.m. when she entered the intersection at SW Savona Boulevard and failed to yield the right-of-way to oncoming traffic, according to the Port St. Lucie Police Department.A 17-year-old male driving a 2026 Honda HR-V northbound on SW Savona Boulevard struck the driver's side of Martin's vehicle, causing a T-bone collision.Emergency responders had to extricate Martin from her vehicle before transporting her to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital with critical injuries. The Big Brothers Big Sisters Florida specialty license plate raises money to support youth mentoring programs in Palm Beach and Martin counties. MARTIN COUNTY — A daily drive can help put a child on the road to a brighter future through the Big Brothers Big Sisters Florida specialty license plate. Proceeds from the plate support mentoring programs in Martin County and across Florida, including those offered by Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin counties. Available through the Florida Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles, the specialty tag costs $25 annually in addition to the standard vehicle registration fee. The full amount supports youth mentoring. Proceeds go to the Big Brothers Big Sisters Association of Florida and its network of 11 local agencies, including Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties. The funding supports one-to-one mentoring relationships, training and support for volunteer mentors and resources for children in the program. Money from the plates helps recruit and train mentors in Palm Beach and Martin counties, expand access to mentoring services and support workplace readiness programs. Residents can request the Big Brothers Big Sisters specialty plate at a Martin County Tax Collector’s Office. Appointments are available at the main office, 3485 S.E. Willoughby Blvd., Stuart; 11734 S.E. Federal Highway, Hobe Sound; 16550 S.W. Warfield Blvd., Indiantown; and 3001 S.W. Martin Downs Blvd., Palm City. Drivers do not have to wait until their vehicle registration renewal to change their license plate. Because the Palm Beach and Martin County tax collector offices do not offer online specialty plate ordering, residents who prefer to order online may use a neighboring county’s tax collector website that offers the service or a licensed Florida courier tag agency. Tag agencies may charge convenience, service and shipping fees. Customers will need their current license plate number, insurance company and policy number and a copy of a valid Florida driver’s license. New Martin County residents can select the Big Brothers Big Sisters specialty plate when registering a vehicle through the Florida Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles. Drivers seeking a personalized plate can check availability through the department’s Personalized Plate Inquiry tool, complete an Application for Personalized License Plate and submit it at a tax collector’s office. VERO BEACH — The cheers have quieted and another Little League season has come to a close, but the impact of Vero Beach Little League’s 12U All-Stars is only beginning. While their postseason journey ended at the Florida Little League State Tournament in Sarasota, the example this team set continues to resonate throughout the league and the community that proudly supported them. For Chris McIntosh, Vero Beach Little League’s vice president of sponsorships and partnerships, the greatest reward wasn’t measured on a scoreboard. It was watching a group of young athletes grow together. “What makes me smile the most is seeing how much these kids grew—not just as baseball players, but as teammates and young men,” McIntosh said. “They learned how to compete, handle adversity, support one another and represent Vero Beach the right way.” McIntosh said competing against some of Florida’s top Little League teams taught the players lessons that extended well beyond baseball. Learning to respond to pressure, overcome disappointment and celebrate success together are experiences he believes will benefit them for years to come. Among his favorite memories was watching the team capture the Section 2 Championship on its home field, earning the opportunity to represent Vero Beach in Sarasota. The celebration ended with players surprising Manager George with a Gatorade shower after the shutout victory—a moment McIntosh said perfectly reflected the joy and camaraderie the team shared. While this group added another impressive chapter to a history that includes multiple district and sectional championships, along with a 10U state title, McIntosh believes their greatest accomplishment is the example they leave behind. “I think this team’s legacy will be that they showed the next generation of VBLL players what is possible,” he said. “They helped raise the expectations for Vero Beach Little League and showed younger players what can happen when you work hard, believe in your teammates and represent your community with pride.” McIntosh also credited the volunteer coaches, families and community supporters whose dedication made the season possible. He noted that the work often happened long before game day, pointing to one coach who even mowed Michael Field every other day during his lunch break to ensure it was ready for the players. As one memorable season comes to a close, another is about to begin. Registration is now open for Vero Beach Little League s fall season, which begins Sept. A student receives a back-to-school haircut at Fort Pierce Beauty Academy. A client receives a fresh look at Fort Pierce Beauty Academy. FORT PIERCE — A fresh haircut can help students walk into a new school year with a little more confidence. The Academies of Cosmetology is offering free back-to-school haircuts for school-age children at its three Treasure Coast campuses through Aug. Families do not need appointments or advance registration. Students and parents may walk in, sign in and wait for the next available barbering or cosmetology student, much as they would at a traditional barbershop or salon. Kris Evangelista said the schools have long offered discounted back-to-school haircuts, but began offering them for free only within the past few years. “It’s always been discounts for the kids for back to school, but I believe this is the second or third year we’re doing the free cuts,” Evangelista said. All students at the three campuses are expected to participate, with instructors supervising the work to ensure children receive quality haircuts. Families may request a specific student stylist if they choose. Evangelista said the service is especially meaningful because a haircut can make a difference in how children feel when they return to school. “It’s a fresh year, fresh haircut,” Evangelista said. “It boosts their confidence, their self-esteem.” The promotion has become popular with families, including regular clients who return each year and bring relatives and friends. Evangelista said the academies do not plan to turn anyone away. Michael Prevette owns the Academies of Cosmetology, where Evangelista assists. Evangelista said the academies also plan to continue their community outreach beyond the back-to-school season by hosting free spring and fall festivals. The free back-to-school haircuts are at Beauty and Massage Institute, 1375 U.S. 1, Suite 2, Vero Beach, 772-978-7178; Port St. Lucie Beauty Academy, 10036 South U.S. Lucie, 772-337-4747; and Fort Pierce Beauty Academy, 3028 South U.S. 1, Fort Pierce, 772-464-4885. Martin County is weighing changes to its local shark fishing ordinance after the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission directed the county to align its rules with state regulations. It's a move that has drawn significant public concern.The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission asked the county to bring its ordinance in line with state law, which preempts counties from regulating saltwater fishing.WATCH WPTV'S COVERAGE BELOW:"There is a state statute that has essentially preempted the powers from the county to regulate salt water fishing that includes shark fishing. Preemption meaning the state says, 'county you can't control this anymore,'" Assistant County Attorney Melissa Petrick said.State law requires a saltwater fishing license and a special permit for shark fishing. It also allows shark fishing within 1,000 feet of a guarded beach at all hours.Among those opposing the changes is Jessica Veatch, whose then-3-year-old daughter Violet was attacked by a bull shark on Bathtub Beach in Martin County 9 years ago."I hear a scream that goes Mommy," Veatch said. "I come up out of the water and all I can see is the blood filling the water and I lifted her up out of the water and saw what was left of her leg."Veatch said she believes nearby fishing activity may have lead to the attack.."We noticed some young men that were spearfishing on the reef," Veatch said. "That is what provoked the attack on my daughter."Veatch said she was alarmed to learn the county may now be forced to eliminate its local shark fishing regulations."They're currently treating our shoreline like a Pavlov's dog experiment with an apex predator and I don't think that's going to work out in anybody's best interest," Veatch said.Indian River Keeper Jim Moir raised concerns about the potential impact of the changes at the Tuesday commission meeting."These animals are incredibly important to our ecosystems. The angler offshore are complaining bitterly daily about how many of their caught fish are being depraved by sharks. Attracting more sharks to the coast is not only bad for human safety, but it's bad for angling, its bad for our public awareness, it's bad for the sharks," Moir said.County attorneys suggested the ordinance does not need to be eliminated entirely."We can rework the ordinance and then instead of eliminating everything we can just reference the illegality of things under state law," Petrick said.County commissioners voted to table the discussion, directing staff to review concerns raised by the community and commissioners and draft new ordinance language.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. A joint investigation by the Florida Lottery Division of Security and the United States Postal Service Office of Inspector General (USPS OIG) has led to the arrest of a letter carrier accused of stealing a winning lottery ticket from the mail and fraudulently claiming the prize.USPS letter carrier Lekaysha Lockhart was arrested July 23 after a Florida Lottery player reported that a winning Pick 4 ticket she mailed never reached its intended destination, the Florida Lottery's Office of Communications said in a news release.A Florida Lottery Inspector determined the ticket had been redeemed by Lockhart on June 19 at the Florida Lottery's Miami District Office. Following her arrest, Florida Lottery Special Agents and USPS OIG investigators said Lockhart admitted to stealing the winning lottery ticket and redeeming it.Florida Lottery Secretary Reginald D. Dixon said the case reflects the agency's commitment to player protection."Our players deserve confidence that every Lottery prize is protected through strong security measures and diligent oversight," Dixon said in the news release. "I commend our Division of Security for their outstanding investigative work and thank our partners at the United States Postal Service Office of Inspector General and the Broward County Sheriff's Office for their collaboration in protecting the integrity of Florida Lottery games and bringing this case to a successful resolution."Lockhart was arrested on charges of grand theft, dealing in stolen property, filing a false claim for payment, two counts of unlawful use of a two-way communications device and mail theft. Because the alleged offenses occurred in multiple judicial circuits, the cases will be prosecuted separately, the Florida Lottery Division of Security said.

Two senior FIFA officials criticized Gianni Infantino's World Cup sell-off plan Friday with one resigning as a presidential adviser and a second saying staff were deceived by project that must not go ahead.Carlos Cordeiro, who represented the soccer body on the White House Task Force for the World Cup, resigned in protest at the private equity plan."I cannot stand by while FIFA considers selling a stake in the World Cup," Cordeiro, a former Goldman Sachs banker, said in a statement resigning as adviser to FIFA President Gianni Infantino that urged other senior FIFA staff to speak out.RELATED STORY | UEFA members threaten FIFA boycott, Concacaf rejects World Cup investor planFIFA's chief operating officer Kevin Lamour said in a statement to The Associated Press staff were "deceived" by Infantino's lack of openness planning the private investor scheme and "deserve better than contempt and intimidation.""It is the project of one person," Lamour, a long-time colleague of Infantino at both FIFA and UEFA, wrote. "Not only must this project not go ahead … but the time has now come for football political leaders to ask themselves the right questions and make the right decisions."Lamour did not resign the post he held since 2024 but said he had a duty to his colleagues."And if that means I lose my job, then so be it" the French official said. "I will understand and respect that decision. At least I'll sleep well tonight."Cordeiro often joined Infantino on working visits to meet U.S. President Donald Trump at the White House in recent years."Let me be clear. I had no involvement in this proposal, and I oppose it unequivocally," Cordeiro, the former U.S. Soccer Federation president said, calling the $20 billion commercial subsidiary "a bad deal for football.""Football has been central to my life, and after more than 35 years in banking, I understand both the value of this asset and the consequences of giving part of it away" he said. "That is why this proposal should be rejected."RELATED STORY | FIFA's Infantino sets deadline to members in Kushner-backed World Cup planInfantino has proposed spinning off FIFA's commercial businesses — including World Cups and Club World Cups for men and women — into a $20 billion subsidiary with 20% owned by private investors.The "anchor investor," described by FIFA, is a New York-based investment firm created by Joshua Kushner, the younger brother of Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner."FIFA already has access to extraordinary financial resources. The organization sits on billions of dollars in reserves and no debt," Cordeiro said, noting FIFA's revenue of $15 billion over the last four years tied to the men's Wold Cup just ended."Against that backdrop, selling a permanent stake in football's most valuable asset to raise $4.2 billion makes little sense. It is mortgaging football's future without any compelling justification," he said.Cordeiro said he shared five years working for FIFA alongside Infantino with "dedicated, principled people who care deeply about the game.""I hope they, too, will speak up," he wrote, "because decisions of this magnitude should be made in the interests of football, not those who stand to profit from it."Infantino has been president of FIFA for more than 10 years and had seemed sure to be reelected unopposed next March. 18 deadline for challengers to come forward.

The King's Landing development project in downtown Fort Pierce is advancing, with construction milestones bringing excitement to the community and local business owners. The project features ten luxury villas, condos, retail spaces, restaurants, a parking garage, and a hotel. A petition with nearly 800 signatures is mounting against a proposal that could transform Fort Pierce's Museum Pointe — a public waterfront park along the Indian River Lagoon — into a mega-yacht marina.WATCH BELOW: 'We have been talking for years about better locations for that history center,' Erick Gill tells WPTV's Kate HusseyThe proposal is part of the Port of Fort Pierce's updated 2026 Master Plan. It calls for redeveloping Museum Pointe, which is currently home to a history center, public waterfront access, fishing piers, and green space, into a facility featuring floating docks, a multi-story marina, an event center, a waterfront restaurant, and a clubhouse.Opponents fear the plan could privatize one of the city's most treasured public spaces."Giving public land to private folks," said Terry Howard, a volunteer at the History Center at Museum Pointe Park. For more than 50 years, the museum has preserved artifacts from Florida's Native American tribes, Spanish shipwrecks, and more. The master plan's renderings place the proposed marina clubhouse exactly where the museum stands today."Basically taking away a gem — a public gem that belongs to the people and replacing it with a facility for mega yachts," Howard said. "We're trying to keep this area as it is." St. Lucie County spokesperson Erick Gill said the museum's future is not in jeopardy if the project moves forward."Staff's intent was never to close the museum," Gill said. "We have been talking for years about better locations for that history center; it is on a barrier island, in a flood zone, so it may not be the best place to store artifacts."Gill said the museum and its collection would be preserved and relocated if the project proceeds. He added that the master plan is designed to expand economic development, create jobs, and generate county revenue."I think all local governments are looking for a way to generate revenue, so we can continue to lower the taxes for St. Lucie County residents and generate revenue from economic development, and we already have dock space there," Gill said."Anything that's going to be a positive economic driver for the City of Fort Pierce, I'm going to embrace completely," Fort Pierce City Commissioner Michael Broderick added. A prosecutor says they have dropped charges against Gregory Allen Davis, 49, of Port St. Lucie in an incident June 24 in Port St. Lucie when Davis ordered three juveniles out of their car at gunpoint and told them to get on the ground at the intersection of SW Morelia Lane and SW Acapulco Terrace. Minutes earlier, one of the teens had fired an Orbeez toy gun at the car that Davis and his fiancee were in. An Orbeez toy gun shoots soft water-absorbing beads. According to a prosecutor, the reason they dropped the charges against Davis is because in Florida, citizens have the right to make a citizen's arrest if they see that a felony has been committed in their presence. The felony that Davis saw was the teen firing a gun at his vehicle. "Basically, under Florida law, a citizen has a right to make a citizen's arrest if they observe a felony, occur in their presence. So that's basically what happened here. When someone effects a citizen's arrest, basically, they have the same powers as a police officer would, at least temporarily," said Jason Bruin, Assistant State Attorney, 19th Judicial Circuit. Bruin says if the case had gone to a jury, they would've returned a verdict of not guilty. Davis, in this case, gets out of the vehicle and holds the the people that were in that car at gunpoint. No, we don't recommend that people take the law into their own hands like that. Let the police do their job. Call the police, let the police do their job," Bruin said. Davis was charged with three counts of false imprisonment and three counts of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon. Those six charges carry a maximum sentence of 30 years in prison if convicted. "I am very grateful as I am a father of three and everything I do is for my kids. The thought of being away from them is horrifying. Martin County commissioners faced a wave of public pushback during Tuesday morning's meeting as residents, local surfers, and marine experts urged local leaders to keep strict limits on beachside shark fishing. The debate centers on potential language changes to local ordinances regarding land-based shark fishing, a practice where anglers deploy lines from the shore using heavy gear, kayaks, or drones to drop bait and chum into deeper waters. Under current Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC) rules, shore anglers are required to hold a specialized permit, keep sharks in the water, and use non-offset circle hooks to prevent injury to the animals. However, local ordinances in coastal counties can set stricter safety boundaries near public swimming areas. During public comments, speakers warned that chumming , releasing fish parts and blood into the surf to attract sharks, endangers swimmers, surfers, and families. "I myself have been caught in shark fishing lines, and it is not fun," said local surfer Jay Noyes, speaking in support of beachgoers and surfers. Dottie Lanci, a member of the Hutchinson Island Preservation Initiative, strongly opposed any effort to loosen existing restrictions that ban shark baiting on lifeguard-protected beaches. Lansing called on commissioners to prioritize safety and extend the ban across all county beaches, citing an incident she witnessed outside her home where anglers used drones to drop chum in the water. "The next morning a family of four put up their umbrellas. Two young children were playing in the water there, completely unaware of what took place the day before and that some hungry sharks might still be there," Lanci said. She also noted that other Florida municipalities, such as Miami Beach, passed local bans on land-based shark fishing earlier this year. Safety concerns over shark activity on local beaches are far from theoretical for many residents . In August 2017, a 3-year-old girl named Violet Veatch was bitten on the leg by a suspected bull shark while wading in shallow water at Bathtub Reef Beach in Martin County. The toddler's mother, Jessica Veatch, later pushed for stricter local beach safety regulations , believing the shark was drawn to the crowded swimming area by spearfishermen carrying bloody fish through the water. Jessica Veatch, Violet's mother, says these new regulations would be great, but enforcement of them has been a problem. Enforcement is a big issue. You can put anything down on paper, but if you're not enforcing it, people are going to do what they want to do. We basically have our beaches turning into a cowboy sport, and if you don't like it, then you can go somewhere else. That is basically the mentality that a lot of these fishermen have, said Veatch. Justin Grubich, a marine conservation expert and local surfer who moved to the area from Fort Lauderdale, urged the commission to maintain strong local restrictions. Pointing to recent research presented at statewide conservation forums, Grubich warned that regular baiting near popular beaches conditions wildlife. "There's new scientific evidence or more accumulated scientific evidence that you can create problem sharks like problem bears," Grubich cautioned commissioners, advocating for rules that limit chumming and keep blood out of coastal waters. Commissioners did not take immediate action on the ordinance during the meeting, but requested further review of local public safety boundaries alongside state FWC regulations. County staff confirmed the current ordinance banning chumming is still in place. Current county rules ban fishing on guarded beaches when lifeguards are present. A new ordinance referring residents to FWC for state laws and tightening restrictions on county beaches is currently in the works. There is no timeline for when this new ordinance will come to a vote or exactly what new restrictions will go into place. One of the items discussed was increased drone restrictions on beaches amid concerns that they may be used to bait sharks. Other proposals included extended beach fishing hours and county shark fishing permits.

A Fort Pierce resort says an abandoned sailboat that washed ashore three weeks ago is damaging property, slamming into other boats, and costing them thousands in business, but state law prevents them from moving it. "This is a danger to people and personal property," said Joe Zebrowski, general manager of Dockside Marina and Resort. The sailboat washed ashore near On The Edge Bar and Grill, and Zabrowski and his team quickly secured it. However, Zabrowski said the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC) informed him that the boat cannot be moved. The agency is giving the owners 60 days to claim the vessel, and the resort is also prohibited from moving it. "I did a good deed, but no deed goes unpunished," Zebrowski said. The FWC used a chain to secure the sailboat, but Zebrowski said it hasn’t stopped the vessel from causing problems. "It kept it from floating away but didn’t keep it from whipping back and forth," he said. Zebrowski explained that the sailboat has slammed into a docked boat, destroyed a piling, and forced the restaurant to block off several tables near the vessel, which has significantly impacted their revenue. "These are our prime tables. They probably cost us about 25 percent of our overall business for the past month," Zebrowski said. According to state law, moving a boat that has washed ashore onto private property without proper permission can expose individuals to legal liabilities or even charges of theft. "There needs to be a carveout in however the law takes care of situations like this that takes care of people who are innocent and stop protecting an owner who has abandoned his boat that I don’t think is registered or has insurance," Zebrowski said. The FWC confirmed to WPBF that no one can touch the boat except its owners. WPBF is working to contact the owners of the boat for comment. The FWC is working on providing a more detailed statement. Lucie County Sheriff's Office are investigating the death of a 3-month-old baby in Fort Pierce, which occurred in August of last year, and say further charges could be pending. Additional details about the case reveal the environment in which the infant was living. "I can tell you the facts of this case. Doesn't even paint a picture clear to what we saw at the hospital," Detective Corporal Jennifer Diaz said. Investigators identified the three caregivers as the baby's mother, Nicole Maxwell, the baby's grandfather, Robert Maxwell, and his girlfriend, Vikki Koon. "There were a lack of food and a lack of fluid intake. So therefore, the baby potentially was not properly being fed and due to the child's age, was unable to care for themselves," Diaz said. The baby and Nicole Maxwell’s 9-year-old son, who has autism, lived in the mobile home with their grandfather and his girlfriend. Nicole Maxwell lived with her boyfriend in Vero Beach but would visit occasionally. Authorities noted that the family has a history of involvement with the Department of Children and Families. Martin County commissioners faced a wave of public pushback during Tuesday morning's meeting as residents, local surfers, and marine experts urged local leaders to keep strict limits on beachside shark fishing. The debate centers on potential language changes to local ordinances regarding land-based shark fishing, a practice where anglers deploy lines from the shore using heavy gear, kayaks, or drones to drop bait and chum into deeper waters. Under current Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC) rules, shore anglers are required to hold a specialized permit, keep sharks in the water, and use non-offset circle hooks to prevent injury to the animals. However, local ordinances in coastal counties can set stricter safety boundaries near public swimming areas. During public comments, speakers warned that chumming , releasing fish parts and blood into the surf to attract sharks, endangers swimmers, surfers, and families. "I myself have been caught in shark fishing lines, and it is not fun," said local surfer Jay Noyes, speaking in support of beachgoers and surfers. Dottie Lanci, a member of the Hutchinson Island Preservation Initiative, strongly opposed any effort to loosen existing restrictions that ban shark baiting on lifeguard-protected beaches. Lansing called on commissioners to prioritize safety and extend the ban across all county beaches, citing an incident she witnessed outside her home where anglers used drones to drop chum in the water. "The next morning a family of four put up their umbrellas. Two young children were playing in the water there, completely unaware of what took place the day before and that some hungry sharks might still be there," Lanci said. She also noted that other Florida municipalities, such as Miami Beach, passed local bans on land-based shark fishing earlier this year. Safety concerns over shark activity on local beaches are far from theoretical for many residents . In August 2017, a 3-year-old girl named Violet Veatch was bitten on the leg by a suspected bull shark while wading in shallow water at Bathtub Reef Beach in Martin County. The toddler's mother, Jessica Veatch, later pushed for stricter local beach safety regulations , believing the shark was drawn to the crowded swimming area by spearfishermen carrying bloody fish through the water. Jessica Veatch, Violet's mother, says these new regulations would be great, but enforcement of them has been a problem. Enforcement is a big issue. You can put anything down on paper, but if you're not enforcing it, people are going to do what they want to do. We basically have our beaches turning into a cowboy sport, and if you don't like it, then you can go somewhere else. That is basically the mentality that a lot of these fishermen have, said Veatch. Justin Grubich, a marine conservation expert and local surfer who moved to the area from Fort Lauderdale, urged the commission to maintain strong local restrictions. Pointing to recent research presented at statewide conservation forums, Grubich warned that regular baiting near popular beaches conditions wildlife. "There's new scientific evidence or more accumulated scientific evidence that you can create problem sharks like problem bears," Grubich cautioned commissioners, advocating for rules that limit chumming and keep blood out of coastal waters. Commissioners did not take immediate action on the ordinance during the meeting, but requested further review of local public safety boundaries alongside state FWC regulations. County staff confirmed the current ordinance banning chumming is still in place. Current county rules ban fishing on guarded beaches when lifeguards are present. A new ordinance referring residents to FWC for state laws and tightening restrictions on county beaches is currently in the works. There is no timeline for when this new ordinance will come to a vote or exactly what new restrictions will go into place. One of the items discussed was increased drone restrictions on beaches amid concerns that they may be used to bait sharks. Other proposals included extended beach fishing hours and county shark fishing permits.

Federal prosecutors said a Los Angeles man was sentenced to life in federal prison for selling fentanyl that caused the death of a Treasure Coast man, then continuing to traffic the deadly drug just two days later. District Judge Aileen Cannon imposed the sentence on Alfonso Guerrero, 39, of Los Angeles, after a federal jury convicted him in May 2026 of conspiracy to possess with intent to distribute fentanyl resulting in death and distribution of fentanyl resulting in death. “A tenth of a gram of fentanyl, about the size of a small pinch of salt, was enough to kill David Eller,” U.S. Reding Quiñones for the Southern District of Florida said in a statement. “This was not a small drug deal. Guerrero sold the fentanyl that killed his friend and, just two days later, was caught carrying more fentanyl for distribution. Today’s life sentence is the consequence of that deadly conduct and his long record of violence and crime. Together with the DEA and our local law enforcement partners, we will trace fatal doses back to the dealers who sold them and hold those dealers fully accountable.” According to court records and evidence presented at trial, the U.S. Attorney’s Office said Guerrero sold fentanyl in Indian River County. On May 16, 2023, prosecutors said he exchanged 0.1 gram of fentanyl — commonly known as “a point” — for another controlled substance known as “molly.” Officials said the drug transaction was captured on a doorbell camera. Hours later, Eller was found dead inside his Vero Beach home. Investigators recovered drug paraphernalia, including a small piece of burnt aluminum foil that the victim used to receive the fentanyl from Guerrero on the victim’s front porch, near his body. Two days later, on May 18, 2023, prosecutors said Guerrero was arrested and found in possession of additional quantities of fentanyl intended for distribution. Officials said Guerrero’s extensive criminal history included documented gang membership and prior convictions for attempted robbery with a firearm in California, aggravated assault in Georgia, and cocaine and fentanyl possession offenses in Florida.

Newly released 911 calls capture desperate attempts to save two men after gunfire erupted outside a Port St. Lucie home , leaving one caller pleading for help as a wounded man faded in front of her. Multiple callers contacted dispatchers shortly before 3:30 a.m. July 19 after hearing repeated gunshots near Southeast Rivergreen Circle. The calls show residents trying to direct officers toward the shooting while remaining inside their homes as police rushed to the neighborhood. Please, please, the caller told a dispatcher shortly after 3:28 a.m. When asked whether anyone had been hit, she answered, Yes. The caller repeatedly urged one of the wounded men to remain conscious. Breathe, baby, please, she said. Officers responding to Southeast Rivergreen Circle found 24-year-old Carl Loubeau and 22-year-old Juliun Stokes suffering from multiple gunshot wounds. Both were taken to hospitals, where they later died. The calls show how quickly the shooting unfolded. The first caller apparently mistook the gunfire for fireworks and asked police to check the area near the dog park because the noise had awakened his young daughter. Within seconds, other residents began reporting gunshots, screaming and people lying outside. One neighbor said about eight shots woke him but told the dispatcher he was too frightened to look outside. No, I don’t even want to look, he said. Another caller estimated hearing 10 shots, followed by a brief pause and another burst. It got quiet for less than a minute, and then a couple more rounds went off, the caller said. A resident watching through a home security camera reported seeing someone lying in a driveway. I’m looking through my camera because I didn’t want to go outside, the caller said. I woke up from the gunshots and the screaming, and I just see someone laying in the driveway. Man who returned fire calls 911 The most significant call appears to have come from 20-year-old Dwayne Walker, whom investigators identified as the man who returned fire after Loubeau allegedly shot Stokes . Somebody shot my cousin, and I shot back, Walker told a dispatcher. Walker pleaded for police and paramedics to hurry, saying his cousin was not responding. See also: PBSO seeks more victims after barber arrested in alleged trafficking of 17-year-old He shot my cousin, sir, Walker said as officers arrived. Walker also repeatedly told officers that the guns had been dropped and said he did not want any trouble. The guns are dropped, he said. I haven’t done anything at all, sir. Later in the call, Walker described what he said happened before the shooting. We were just coming to a house, and her boyfriend shot my cousin, Walker said. Because my cousin said, Hey,’ to him, and he laughed, and he said, Do I know you?’ And he shot my cousin. Police initially said an argument over a house key had escalated into a shootout between the two victims. Investigators later revised that account, saying jealousy involving a woman apparently triggered the violence and that Stokes did not fire a weapon. Lucie Police Chief Leo Niemczyk, Stokes and several friends had gone bowling with Loubeau’s girlfriend earlier that night. When the group returned to the home and realized they were locked out, the woman called Loubeau and asked him to bring a spare key. Police believe Loubeau became jealous when he arrived and saw his girlfriend with Stokes and Walker. Investigators said Loubeau approached Stokes as he stood beside the open driver’s door of a Ford Mustang and opened fire. Police believe Loubeau may have mistaken Stokes for Walker, who authorities said had some type of relationship with Loubeau’s girlfriend. Walker, who was near the rear of the Mustang, drew a lawfully carried handgun and returned fire, striking Loubeau, police said. Investigators determined Walker acted in self-defense and said he will not face criminal charges. Police said Loubeau fired eight rounds from a 9 mm handgun and one round from a .380-caliber weapon. Walker fired eight rounds from a .40-caliber handgun, according to the department’s preliminary findings. See also: PBSO seeks more victims after barber arrested in alleged trafficking of 17-year-old Stokes was armed, but investigators said there was no evidence that he fired his weapon. The 911 recordings also capture the chaotic arrival of officers, who can be heard ordering people to the ground and demanding that they keep their hands visible while callers continued begging for medical aid. He needs an ambulance, someone shouted as police secured the scene. No arrests have been made. Detectives are continuing to review forensic evidence, phone records, toxicology findings and autopsy reports before formally closing the investigation. Anyone with additional information is asked to contact the Port St. Lucie Police Department at 772-871-5000 .

A suspected burglar dressed for happy hour instead of a police lineup is now known across St. Lucie County as the Flamingo Bandit. The nickname comes courtesy of the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office , which is searching for a man photographed wearing a tropical shirt dominated by a giant pink flamingo. Some criminals try to blend in, the agency wrote. This one apparently took fashion advice from a Jimmy Buffett concert. But deputies said the man’s alleged itinerary involved burglary, not boats, beaches or frozen drinks. Investigators said the suspect entered a residence on July 28 and stole a laptop, miscellaneous food and a key to the home. The sheriff’s office shared an image of the flamboyantly dressed suspect, hoping his difficult-to-miss wardrobe will help someone identify him. A man awaiting a possible retrial in the fatal shooting of his former girlfriend is accused of attacking convicted murderer Otto Lenke inside the St. According to an arrest affidavit, Robert Castro approached Lenke in a jail dorm on July 6 and struck him in the face, knocking off his glasses. Lenke approached an intercom and reported the attack to corrections staff, the affidavit says. A deputy noticed a cut on the upper part of Lenke’s nose, and a nurse treated the injury. A jail sergeant witnessed Castro strike Lenke, according to investigators. Surveillance video also showed Castro approaching Lenke and hitting him in the face, the affidavit says. Lenke later told a detective he had been using a jail-issued tablet to watch a chess game when Castro attacked him. Investigators attempted to interview Castro on July 16. The affidavit says Castro repeatedly stated that he did not understand his Miranda rights and did not want to speak with the detective, ending the interview. Castro, 30, is charged with battery by a person detained in a prison or jail facility, a felony. The new charge was filed July 20. Lenke, a former Melbourne police officer and Indian River County firefighter, was convicted in May of first-degree murder and first-degree arson in the 2021 death of Richard Benson. Prosecutors said Lenke shot Benson three times inside Benson’s Fort Pierce motorcycle shop, poured an accelerant on him and set him on fire while he was still alive. A jury later voted 11-1 to recommend that Lenke be sentenced to death. Castro’s murder conviction reversed Castro was convicted in 2024 of first-degree murder with a firearm in the death of his former girlfriend, Taylor Ann Sato, and sentenced to life in prison. However, the Fourth District Court of Appeal reversed the conviction in February after finding that the trial court failed to properly complete the process for determining whether Castro was competent to stand trial. A psychologist found Castro competent in November 2022. Five days later, his attorneys raised concerns about his condition, and the original judge said Castro had definitely decompensated before ordering another evaluation. The appeals court said the record contained no additional evaluation, report or competency hearing after that order. Nearly two years later, a different judge declared Castro competent based on the original 2022 evaluation. Castro then went to trial and was convicted. The appellate court ruled that a two-year-old evaluation was not sufficient because competency must be assessed close to the time of trial. The case was sent back to the trial court to determine whether Castro’s competency during the 2024 trial can now be reliably evaluated. Castro would receive a new trial if a retrospective evaluation cannot be conducted or if the court determines he was not competent during the original trial. 2022 killing Fort Pierce police accused Castro of killing Sato outside her Timber Ridge Lane home during the early morning hours of July 23, 2022. According to the original arrest affidavit, a man called 911 and said he had shot and killed his girlfriend and was considering killing himself. Officers arrived and found Sato outside the home with multiple gunshot wounds. Investigators reported finding six gunshot wounds and several 9 mm shell casings near her body. Sato’s stepfather told detectives that she and Castro had recently ended a long-term relationship. He said Sato had blocked Castro’s phone number, but Castro continued trying to contact her by sending repeated $1 transactions through Cash App with messages attached. The stepfather also told police Castro had previously threatened to kill Sato. After listening to part of the 911 call, he identified the caller’s voice as Castro’s, according to the affidavit. Castro later surrendered to deputies in St. Investigators said several rounds of 9 mm ammunition were found in his pocket. His police interview ended after an attorney arrived and directed detectives not to question him further.

The Martin County School District has approved a consolidation of bus routes that officials say will save $255,000 without affecting students or eliminating any driver positions. The school board voted Tuesday unanimously to reduce the number of bus routes by 3, bringing the total from 58 to 55 ahead of the upcoming school year. District officials say all bus stops will remain the same and students will not be impacted by the change. WATCH WPTV'S COVERAGE BELOW: "Right now, we have 55 routes and roughly 56 drivers. So we have all of our routes covered," Superintendent Michael Maine said. The $255,000 in savings reflects a reduced transportation budget and will not be redirected to a specific expense, according to the school district. Parents have mixed reactions. Marino Reyes and Tiffany Gugumuck expressed support for the financial decision. "I think that's a great thing. A quarter million dollars that's a lot of money just for that one situation there. So many other needs that we can put the money towards," Reyes and Gugumuck said. Parent Ken Winstanley wondered what the change means for the budget. "Where's the money gonna go to?" Winstanley said. Michael Skinner, the President of the local AFSCME labor union chapter, voiced concerns during public comment on behalf of the bus drivers. "As what my feedback from the bus drivers were is that their routes or their buses are always full and cutting routes are not actually a good idea," Skinner said. Transportation Director Ruth Spires pushed back on that concern, noting that the buses hold a maximum of 77 passengers and are not operating at capacity. Spires also confirmed that no drivers were let go as part of the consolidation. "We were already challenged with a shortage last year. So the routes that were merged—consolidated—yes, the drivers were already covering. So no one was cut at all," Spires said. Drivers will be paid for any additional hours they work as a result of the consolidation, Spires explained. The district said it is confident it will maintain the same level of service with fewer buses on the road. Newly released 911 calls capture desperate attempts to save two men after gunfire erupted outside a Port St. Lucie home , leaving one caller pleading for help as a wounded man faded in front of her. Multiple callers contacted dispatchers shortly before 3:30 a.m. July 19 after hearing repeated gunshots near Southeast Rivergreen Circle. The calls show residents trying to direct officers toward the shooting while remaining inside their homes as police rushed to the neighborhood. Please, please, the caller told a dispatcher shortly after 3:28 a.m. When asked whether anyone had been hit, she answered, Yes. The caller repeatedly urged one of the wounded men to remain conscious. Breathe, baby, please, she said. Officers responding to Southeast Rivergreen Circle found 24-year-old Carl Loubeau and 22-year-old Juliun Stokes suffering from multiple gunshot wounds. Both were taken to hospitals, where they later died. The calls show how quickly the shooting unfolded. The first caller apparently mistook the gunfire for fireworks and asked police to check the area near the dog park because the noise had awakened his young daughter. Within seconds, other residents began reporting gunshots, screaming and people lying outside. One neighbor said about eight shots woke him but told the dispatcher he was too frightened to look outside. No, I don’t even want to look, he said. Another caller estimated hearing 10 shots, followed by a brief pause and another burst. It got quiet for less than a minute, and then a couple more rounds went off, the caller said. A resident watching through a home security camera reported seeing someone lying in a driveway. I’m looking through my camera because I didn’t want to go outside, the caller said. I woke up from the gunshots and the screaming, and I just see someone laying in the driveway. Man who returned fire calls 911 The most significant call appears to have come from 20-year-old Dwayne Walker, whom investigators identified as the man who returned fire after Loubeau allegedly shot Stokes . Somebody shot my cousin, and I shot back, Walker told a dispatcher. Walker pleaded for police and paramedics to hurry, saying his cousin was not responding. See also: PBSO seeks more victims after barber arrested in alleged trafficking of 17-year-old He shot my cousin, sir, Walker said as officers arrived. Walker also repeatedly told officers that the guns had been dropped and said he did not want any trouble. The guns are dropped, he said. I haven’t done anything at all, sir. Later in the call, Walker described what he said happened before the shooting. We were just coming to a house, and her boyfriend shot my cousin, Walker said. Because my cousin said, Hey,’ to him, and he laughed, and he said, Do I know you?’ And he shot my cousin. Police initially said an argument over a house key had escalated into a shootout between the two victims. Investigators later revised that account, saying jealousy involving a woman apparently triggered the violence and that Stokes did not fire a weapon. Lucie Police Chief Leo Niemczyk, Stokes and several friends had gone bowling with Loubeau’s girlfriend earlier that night. When the group returned to the home and realized they were locked out, the woman called Loubeau and asked him to bring a spare key. Police believe Loubeau became jealous when he arrived and saw his girlfriend with Stokes and Walker. Investigators said Loubeau approached Stokes as he stood beside the open driver’s door of a Ford Mustang and opened fire. Police believe Loubeau may have mistaken Stokes for Walker, who authorities said had some type of relationship with Loubeau’s girlfriend. Walker, who was near the rear of the Mustang, drew a lawfully carried handgun and returned fire, striking Loubeau, police said. Investigators determined Walker acted in self-defense and said he will not face criminal charges. Police said Loubeau fired eight rounds from a 9 mm handgun and one round from a .380-caliber weapon. Walker fired eight rounds from a .40-caliber handgun, according to the department’s preliminary findings. See also: PBSO seeks more victims after barber arrested in alleged trafficking of 17-year-old Stokes was armed, but investigators said there was no evidence that he fired his weapon. The 911 recordings also capture the chaotic arrival of officers, who can be heard ordering people to the ground and demanding that they keep their hands visible while callers continued begging for medical aid. He needs an ambulance, someone shouted as police secured the scene. No arrests have been made. Detectives are continuing to review forensic evidence, phone records, toxicology findings and autopsy reports before formally closing the investigation. Anyone with additional information is asked to contact the Port St. Lucie Police Department at 772-871-5000 .

Computers, laptops, printers and certain accessories may also qualify for the temporary tax exemption.Some items are excluded from the tax break, including cellphones, video game consoles, jewelry and purchases made inside airports, theme parks and hotels.BACK-TO-SCHOOL SHOE DRIVEJulie Schalm, marketing manager for The Mall at Wellington Green, said the annual shopping season also creates opportunities to support local students and teachers before classes begin in August.The mall is partnering with the Wellington Community Foundation for the second annual Back-to-School Shoe Drive benefiting students in need throughout the Wellington area.Community members can participate by visiting the display in the Grand Court near the glass elevators, selecting a donation tag and purchasing a new pair of shoes matching the requested size listed for a student.Organizers said donations will be accepted through Monday, July 27.A TOAST TO TEACHERSThe mall is also partnering with the Education Foundation of Palm Beach County and the Wellington Community Foundation for “A Toast to Teachers,” an annual private celebration honoring more than 150 local educators ahead of the new school year.The event includes brunch, entertainment, classroom giveaways and support from local retailers and sponsors.Community leaders said teacher appreciation efforts and student donation drives have become increasingly important as many families and educators continue navigating rising back-to-school costs.Across Palm Beach County, organizations and businesses are expanding local partnerships to help students head into the classroom with the supplies they need while recognizing teachers preparing for another academic year.Additional information about the shoe drive and mall events is available at shopwellingtongreen.com.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Federal prosecutors said a Los Angeles man was sentenced to life in federal prison for selling fentanyl that caused the death of a Treasure Coast man, then continuing to traffic the deadly drug just two days later.U.S. District Judge Aileen Cannon imposed the sentence on Alfonso Guerrero, 39, of Los Angeles, after a federal jury convicted him in May 2026 of conspiracy to possess with intent to distribute fentanyl resulting in death and distribution of fentanyl resulting in death."A tenth of a gram of fentanyl, about the size of a small pinch of salt, was enough to kill David Eller," U.S. Reding Quiñones for the Southern District of Florida said in a statement. "This was not a small drug deal. Guerrero sold the fentanyl that killed his friend and, just two days later, was caught carrying more fentanyl for distribution. Today’s life sentence is the consequence of that deadly conduct and his long record of violence and crime. Together with the DEA and our local law enforcement partners, we will trace fatal doses back to the dealers who sold them and hold those dealers fully accountable."According to court records and evidence presented at trial, the U.S. Attorney's Office said Guerrero sold fentanyl in Indian River County. On May 16, 2023, prosecutors said he exchanged 0.1 gram of fentanyl — commonly known as "a point" — for another controlled substance known as "molly." Officials said the drug transaction was captured on a doorbell camera. Hours later, Eller was found dead inside his Vero Beach home. Investigators recovered drug paraphernalia, including a small piece of burnt aluminum foil that the victim used to receive the fentanyl from Guerrero on the victim's front porch, near his body.Two days later, on May 18, 2023, prosecutors said Guerrero was arrested and found in possession of additional quantities of fentanyl intended for distribution.Officials said Guerrero's extensive criminal history included documented gang membership and prior convictions for attempted robbery with a firearm in California, aggravated assault in Georgia, and cocaine and fentanyl possession offenses in Florida.

A man awaiting a possible retrial in the fatal shooting of his former girlfriend is accused of attacking convicted murderer Otto Lenke inside the St. According to an arrest affidavit, Robert Castro approached Lenke in a jail dorm on July 6 and struck him in the face, knocking off his glasses. Lenke approached an intercom and reported the attack to corrections staff, the affidavit says. A deputy noticed a cut on the upper part of Lenke’s nose, and a nurse treated the injury. A jail sergeant witnessed Castro strike Lenke, according to investigators. Surveillance video also showed Castro approaching Lenke and hitting him in the face, the affidavit says. Lenke later told a detective he had been using a jail-issued tablet to watch a chess game when Castro attacked him. Investigators attempted to interview Castro on July 16. The affidavit says Castro repeatedly stated that he did not understand his Miranda rights and did not want to speak with the detective, ending the interview. Castro, 30, is charged with battery by a person detained in a prison or jail facility, a felony. The new charge was filed July 20. Lenke, a former Melbourne police officer and Indian River County firefighter, was convicted in May of first-degree murder and first-degree arson in the 2021 death of Richard Benson. Prosecutors said Lenke shot Benson three times inside Benson’s Fort Pierce motorcycle shop, poured an accelerant on him and set him on fire while he was still alive. A jury later voted 11-1 to recommend that Lenke be sentenced to death. Castro’s murder conviction reversed Castro was convicted in 2024 of first-degree murder with a firearm in the death of his former girlfriend, Taylor Ann Sato, and sentenced to life in prison. However, the Fourth District Court of Appeal reversed the conviction in February after finding that the trial court failed to properly complete the process for determining whether Castro was competent to stand trial. A psychologist found Castro competent in November 2022. Five days later, his attorneys raised concerns about his condition, and the original judge said Castro had definitely decompensated before ordering another evaluation. The appeals court said the record contained no additional evaluation, report or competency hearing after that order. Nearly two years later, a different judge declared Castro competent based on the original 2022 evaluation. Castro then went to trial and was convicted. The appellate court ruled that a two-year-old evaluation was not sufficient because competency must be assessed close to the time of trial. The case was sent back to the trial court to determine whether Castro’s competency during the 2024 trial can now be reliably evaluated. Castro would receive a new trial if a retrospective evaluation cannot be conducted or if the court determines he was not competent during the original trial. 2022 killing Fort Pierce police accused Castro of killing Sato outside her Timber Ridge Lane home during the early morning hours of July 23, 2022. According to the original arrest affidavit, a man called 911 and said he had shot and killed his girlfriend and was considering killing himself. Officers arrived and found Sato outside the home with multiple gunshot wounds. Investigators reported finding six gunshot wounds and several 9 mm shell casings near her body. Sato’s stepfather told detectives that she and Castro had recently ended a long-term relationship. He said Sato had blocked Castro’s phone number, but Castro continued trying to contact her by sending repeated $1 transactions through Cash App with messages attached. The stepfather also told police Castro had previously threatened to kill Sato. After listening to part of the 911 call, he identified the caller’s voice as Castro’s, according to the affidavit. Castro later surrendered to deputies in St. Investigators said several rounds of 9 mm ammunition were found in his pocket. His police interview ended after an attorney arrived and directed detectives not to question him further.

A Fort Pierce pizza shop known for giving back is creating an even bigger space to inspire young readers. Big Apple Pizza owner Scott Van Duzer is expanding the restaurant’s free book program by transforming its outdoor patio into a dedicated reading room where children can pick up a book any time they visit. For years, Van Duzer has kept shelves of free books inside the restaurant, inviting children to take one home at no cost. He said seeing kids light up when they discover a new book has been one of the most rewarding parts of the program. “The books are there so when the kids come in the store they’re easily available,” Van Duzer said. “They’ll come in and they’re excited they can take whatever they want home.” As more children have stopped by to pick up books, the collection has continued to grow. Van Duzer said the restaurant has simply run out of space inside, prompting the decision to turn the outdoor patio into a permanent reading room. “We have so many books and we are trying to keep ahead of the game that we have turned our porch into what’s going to be the reading room,” Van Duzer said. “So now anytime a child stops by they can get a book free of charge no questions asked.” The goal, he said, is to make books easy to access and help encourage a lifelong love of reading. Whether a family comes in for pizza or simply stops by for a book, every child is welcome to take one home. For Van Duzer, giving back has always been part of the restaurant’s mission. He said that commitment comes from the example his mother set while he was growing up. “I didn’t have a lot,” Van Duzer said. “My mom was pretty instrumental in my life so she just said if you can give back, give back. We live that every day.” Construction on the new reading room is underway and is expected to be completed later this fall. Until then, children can continue picking up free books inside Big Apple Pizza, where the message remains the same: every child is welcome to take a book home, no questions asked. Big Apple Pizza is located at 2311 S 35th St, Fort Pierce FL 34981.

Lucie County sheriff's deputy was fired after an Internal Affairs investigation found she created a social media post that mocked Sheriff Richard Del Toro's "Standards of Performance." According to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office Internal Affairs report, on Oct. 10, 2025, Sheriff Richard Del Toro was made aware of a Facebook post on Deputy Tina Speicker's personal social media account featuring an image titled "Standards of Power." The report says the image closely resembled Del Toro's "Standards of Performance," which was introduced after he was sworn into office. The Standards of Performance outlined eight performance expectations for employees, agency divisions and the Sheriff's Office's core values. See also: PSL police seek missing 14-year-old girl last seen Tuesday night The report says Speicker's Facebook post mirrored the "Standards of Performance" but replaced the original language with phrases depicting domination, manipulation and exploitation. Investigators alleged the post was intended to disparage the Sheriff's Office and Sheriff Del Toro and violated agency rules and regulations. According to the Internal Affairs report, Speicker's "Standards of Power" graphic stated: Top-down domination. Keep everyone beneath you guessing who's next to take the blame. Set confusion for others to follow. The less they know, the more control you have. Display a ruthless work ethic with a focus on self-preservation. Take credit for wins, redirect the failures. Demonstrate selective respect. Favor those who serve your goals; silence those who don't. Being unfair-strategically. Tip the scales to your advantage. Remain obsessive and paranoid. Control every detail, question every motive. Be committed to manipulation and influence. Knowledge is leverage trade it like currency. You own what you exploit and sign off to survive. The Internal Affairs investigator identified several similarities between the "Standards of Power" graphic and Del Toro's "Standards of Performance," including that both contained eight principles, used similar wording and sentence structure, began each bullet point with the same first word and featured a similar two-tone outline. Investigators concluded the graphic was intended to parody the Sheriff's official standards. During the investigation, the Sheriff's Office interviewed Sheriff Del Toro, agency supervisors, other deputies and Speicker. The IA report states Speicker acknowledged posting the graphic to her Facebook page but said it was intended as commentary on Congress and the federal government shutdown. The report also found Speicker gave inconsistent statements during multiple interviews, leading investigators to sustain allegations of criticism of orders or policies, conduct unbecoming, violating the code of ethics for public officers and employees, and false testimony. As a result of the investigation, Speicker was terminated on June 12, 2026. The investigation concluded that Speicker violated Sheriff's Office policies regarding criticism of orders or policies, conduct unbecoming, the code of ethics for public officers and employees, and false testimony.

Lucie police officer resigned while under investigation after walking away from a vehicle containing a man who had shot and killed himself, only to return minutes later as backup. According to an internal affairs report, 23-year-old Officer Mathew Brown resigned on April 17, 2026, facing sustained findings for neglect of duty and inefficiency. Surveillance video from the Treasure Coast Church of God Worship Center showed Brown pulling behind a dark blue Porsche at 1:47 a.m. Brown shined his lights on the car, ran a license plate check, and walked up to the passenger side. However, after looking through the window, Brown turned right around and drove off without calling dispatch or checking on the person inside. At 2:02 a.m., a second officer stopped to check on the suspicious car and found a man dead inside from a gunshot wound, with a handgun sitting on his lap. Paramedics confirmed he was dead, and investigators ruled the death a suicide. Lucie Police Chief Leo Niemczyk recounts his first reaction to the investigation. Very frustrated and just seeking for some understanding because I can't fathom how a police officer would respond to a situation the way he did, said Niemczyk. As he was sent back to the scene as backup, Brown told the responding officer he had driven by earlier but "didn't see anyone in it." Related: Sergeant demoted, officer suspended after Boynton Beach traffic stop investigation Body camera footage captured Brown telling the officer to "go blue," muting both of their cameras for 32 seconds. When a supervisor later pointed out fresh tire tracks in the muddy grass right next to the Porsche, Brown stayed silent, failing to admit they were from his patrol SUV. Investigators concluded Brown failed to do a basic welfare check, offer help, or properly report what he saw. Brown submitted his resignation on April 2 while under investigation, which Niemczyk accepted. Internal Affairs formally sustained the violations on June 24th, marking his file as "resigned under investigation." Two other responding officers were cleared of any wrongdoing. He opted to resign and, you know, prior to the investigation being completed. So, we never had the opportunity to interview him on the record and get his explanation for his behavior. So, it's kind of unsolved in my mind, said Niemczyk. The chief says the public shouldn't expect this out of law enforcement, noting that Brown was the exception, not the expectation.
