Martin County commissioners faced a wave of public pushback during Tuesday morning's meeting as residents, local surfers, and marine experts urged local leaders to keep strict limits on beachside shark fishing. The debate centers on potential language changes to local ordinances regarding land-based shark fishing, a practice where anglers deploy lines from the shore using heavy gear, kayaks, or drones to drop bait and chum into deeper waters. Under current Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC) rules, shore anglers are required to hold a specialized permit, keep sharks in the water, and use non-offset circle hooks to prevent injury to the animals. However, local ordinances in coastal counties can set stricter safety boundaries near public swimming areas. During public comments, speakers warned that chumming , releasing fish parts and blood into the surf to attract sharks, endangers swimmers, surfers, and families. "I myself have been caught in shark fishing lines, and it is not fun," said local surfer Jay Noyes, speaking in support of beachgoers and surfers. Dottie Lanci, a member of the Hutchinson Island Preservation Initiative, strongly opposed any effort to loosen existing restrictions that ban shark baiting on lifeguard-protected beaches. Lansing called on commissioners to prioritize safety and extend the ban across all county beaches, citing an incident she witnessed outside her home where anglers used drones to drop chum in the water. "The next morning a family of four put up their umbrellas. Two young children were playing in the water there, completely unaware of what took place the day before and that some hungry sharks might still be there," Lanci said. She also noted that other Florida municipalities, such as Miami Beach, passed local bans on land-based shark fishing earlier this year. Safety concerns over shark activity on local beaches are far from theoretical for many residents . In August 2017, a 3-year-old girl named Violet Veatch was bitten on the leg by a suspected bull shark while wading in shallow water at Bathtub Reef Beach in Martin County. The toddler's mother, Jessica Veatch, later pushed for stricter local beach safety regulations , believing the shark was drawn to the crowded swimming area by spearfishermen carrying bloody fish through the water. Jessica Veatch, Violet's mother, says these new regulations would be great, but enforcement of them has been a problem. Enforcement is a big issue. You can put anything down on paper, but if you're not enforcing it, people are going to do what they want to do. We basically have our beaches turning into a cowboy sport, and if you don't like it, then you can go somewhere else. That is basically the mentality that a lot of these fishermen have, said Veatch. Justin Grubich, a marine conservation expert and local surfer who moved to the area from Fort Lauderdale, urged the commission to maintain strong local restrictions. Pointing to recent research presented at statewide conservation forums, Grubich warned that regular baiting near popular beaches conditions wildlife. "There's new scientific evidence or more accumulated scientific evidence that you can create problem sharks like problem bears," Grubich cautioned commissioners, advocating for rules that limit chumming and keep blood out of coastal waters. Commissioners did not take immediate action on the ordinance during the meeting, but requested further review of local public safety boundaries alongside state FWC regulations. County staff confirmed the current ordinance banning chumming is still in place. Current county rules ban fishing on guarded beaches when lifeguards are present. A new ordinance referring residents to FWC for state laws and tightening restrictions on county beaches is currently in the works. There is no timeline for when this new ordinance will come to a vote or exactly what new restrictions will go into place. One of the items discussed was increased drone restrictions on beaches amid concerns that they may be used to bait sharks. Other proposals included extended beach fishing hours and county shark fishing permits.

West Palm Beach Police Chief Tony Araujo announced Friday the termination of five command-level officers following a nearly two-year administrative investigation into overtime misconduct, marking the latest development in what has rocked the department since 2020.WATCH WPTV'S MOST RECENT REPORT:"Yesterday, following a thorough, nearly two-year administrative investigation, and after careful review of the findings, I made the difficult decision to terminate five command-level officers," Araujo said during a Friday morning press conference.The firings come as the culmination of an investigation that began after a 2020 audit commissioned by the city uncovered nearly $20,000 worth of "double dipping" on timecards and thousands of hours of questionable overtime payments within the police department.WATCH THE FULL PRESS CONFERENCE BELOW:The controversy dates back to 2020 when a third-party audit examined the finances of multiple city departments. The audit revealed what officials called "pretty egregious" overtime spending patterns within the police department that had gone undetected for years.The investigation eventually led to the firing of former Police Chief Frank Adderley and placed seven officers on administrative leave related to financial misconduct. The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office was brought in to handle the administrative investigation to ensure impartiality.The press conference Friday morning comes after the union pushed back against the terminations, claiming a "different standard" was applied to the fired captains compared to other officers involved in the overtime scheme. The union had previously filed a lawsuit alleging violations of the Police Officers' Bill of Rights, though that lawsuit was subsequently withdrawn."I respect the union. They have their own opinion. They have their own interpretation. I'm going to respectfully disagree," Araujo said. "But again, we're going to leave that to the continued due process that will take place, and I don't begrudge the union for advocating for their membership."Araujo emphasized that the terminations were part of a broader effort to rebuild trust and accountability within the department. He said the department has strengthened training, reviewed overtime practices, and implemented better supervision of extra duty assignments."Public trust is not something we inherit; it's something we earn every day through our actions," Araujo said. The chief acknowledged the department had been on accreditation probation when he arrived, a status that city leadership was unaware of at the time. He said those issues have since been corrected.Araujo indicated the department may need to conduct promotions to fill the vacant leadership positions.The chief stressed that despite the misconduct by some officers, the majority of the department's personnel continue to provide professional service to the community."We have good people at the West Palm Beach Police Department. Be certain of that, we have good leadership" Araujo said. "We can't look at the department as a whole and make a decision of the whole just based on the few."

A Fort Pierce pizza shop known for giving back is creating an even bigger space to inspire young readers. Big Apple Pizza owner Scott Van Duzer is expanding the restaurant’s free book program by transforming its outdoor patio into a dedicated reading room where children can pick up a book any time they visit. For years, Van Duzer has kept shelves of free books inside the restaurant, inviting children to take one home at no cost. He said seeing kids light up when they discover a new book has been one of the most rewarding parts of the program. “The books are there so when the kids come in the store they’re easily available,” Van Duzer said. “They’ll come in and they’re excited they can take whatever they want home.” As more children have stopped by to pick up books, the collection has continued to grow. Van Duzer said the restaurant has simply run out of space inside, prompting the decision to turn the outdoor patio into a permanent reading room. “We have so many books and we are trying to keep ahead of the game that we have turned our porch into what’s going to be the reading room,” Van Duzer said. “So now anytime a child stops by they can get a book free of charge no questions asked.” The goal, he said, is to make books easy to access and help encourage a lifelong love of reading. Whether a family comes in for pizza or simply stops by for a book, every child is welcome to take one home. For Van Duzer, giving back has always been part of the restaurant’s mission. He said that commitment comes from the example his mother set while he was growing up. “I didn’t have a lot,” Van Duzer said. “My mom was pretty instrumental in my life so she just said if you can give back, give back. We live that every day.” Construction on the new reading room is underway and is expected to be completed later this fall. Until then, children can continue picking up free books inside Big Apple Pizza, where the message remains the same: every child is welcome to take a book home, no questions asked. Lucie police officer resigned while under investigation after walking away from a vehicle containing a man who had shot and killed himself, only to return minutes later as backup. According to an internal affairs report, 23-year-old Officer Mathew Brown resigned on April 17, 2026, facing sustained findings for neglect of duty and inefficiency. Surveillance video from the Treasure Coast Church of God Worship Center showed Brown pulling behind a dark blue Porsche at 1:47 a.m. Brown shined his lights on the car, ran a license plate check, and walked up to the passenger side. However, after looking through the window, Brown turned right around and drove off without calling dispatch or checking on the person inside. At 2:02 a.m., a second officer stopped to check on the suspicious car and found a man dead inside from a gunshot wound, with a handgun sitting on his lap. Paramedics confirmed he was dead, and investigators ruled the death a suicide. Lucie Police Chief Leo Niemczyk recounts his first reaction to the investigation. Very frustrated and just seeking for some understanding because I can't fathom how a police officer would respond to a situation the way he did, said Niemczyk. As he was sent back to the scene as backup, Brown told the responding officer he had driven by earlier but "didn't see anyone in it." Related: Sergeant demoted, officer suspended after Boynton Beach traffic stop investigation Body camera footage captured Brown telling the officer to "go blue," muting both of their cameras for 32 seconds. When a supervisor later pointed out fresh tire tracks in the muddy grass right next to the Porsche, Brown stayed silent, failing to admit they were from his patrol SUV. Investigators concluded Brown failed to do a basic welfare check, offer help, or properly report what he saw. Brown submitted his resignation on April 2 while under investigation, which Niemczyk accepted. Internal Affairs formally sustained the violations on June 24th, marking his file as "resigned under investigation." Two other responding officers were cleared of any wrongdoing. He opted to resign and, you know, prior to the investigation being completed. So, we never had the opportunity to interview him on the record and get his explanation for his behavior. So, it's kind of unsolved in my mind, said Niemczyk. The chief says the public shouldn't expect this out of law enforcement, noting that Brown was the exception, not the expectation. This is not normal common behavior by a police officer. They have a right to expect police officers to provide all due care for human life and dignity. And that did not happen in this case. We're very disappointed, Niemczyk said.

A Fort Pierce resort says an abandoned sailboat that washed ashore three weeks ago is damaging property, slamming into other boats, and costing them thousands in business, but state law prevents them from moving it. "This is a danger to people and personal property," said Joe Zebrowski, general manager of Dockside Marina and Resort. The sailboat washed ashore near On The Edge Bar and Grill, and Zabrowski and his team quickly secured it. However, Zabrowski said the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC) informed him that the boat cannot be moved. The agency is giving the owners 60 days to claim the vessel, and the resort is also prohibited from moving it. "I did a good deed, but no deed goes unpunished," Zebrowski said. The FWC used a chain to secure the sailboat, but Zebrowski said it hasn’t stopped the vessel from causing problems. "It kept it from floating away but didn’t keep it from whipping back and forth," he said. Zebrowski explained that the sailboat has slammed into a docked boat, destroyed a piling, and forced the restaurant to block off several tables near the vessel, which has significantly impacted their revenue. "These are our prime tables. They probably cost us about 25 percent of our overall business for the past month," Zebrowski said. According to state law, moving a boat that has washed ashore onto private property without proper permission can expose individuals to legal liabilities or even charges of theft. "There needs to be a carveout in however the law takes care of situations like this that takes care of people who are innocent and stop protecting an owner who has abandoned his boat that I don’t think is registered or has insurance," Zebrowski said. The FWC confirmed to WPBF that no one can touch the boat except its owners. WPBF is working to contact the owners of the boat for comment. The FWC is working on providing a more detailed statement. Martin County’s fire chief is warning that a proposed expansion of Florida’s homestead exemption could significantly reduce funding for Fire Rescue, potentially leading to station closures, firefighter layoffs and longer emergency response times. The measure, which will go before Florida voters in November, could lower property tax bills for homeowners. However, local governments have warned that it could also reduce revenue used to pay for public services. During Tuesday’s Martin County Commission meeting, Fire Chief Chad Cianciulli presented a planning exercise outlining how his department could respond to the projected revenue loss. This is real," Cianciulli said. Martin County Fire Rescue projects its annual budget would decline by $9.5 million in the first year. By the second year, the annual loss would reach $16.5 million, a 22% reduction from the department’s current budget. Under the scenario, Fire Rescue could close Station 18 on Britt Road, Station 33 in Hobe Sound, and Station 23 on Kanner Highway. Cianciulli added the department could be forced to lay off as many as 116 firefighters by the second year. That is equivalent to one of the department’s three shifts. The chief also warned that the funding loss could force Martin County to eliminate specialized teams responsible for hazardous materials incidents, technical rescues and dive operations. The department could then have to request assistance from neighboring agencies in Palm Beach or St. Lucie counties, potentially increasing response times. In an interview after the meeting, Cianciulli pointed to the deadly Camp Mystic flooding in Texas as an example of the delays that can occur when a community must rely on outside resources. "They had to call for outside assets, a 14-hour response to start mitigating that scene," Cianciulli said. "We’re in a position in the county, if we have any incident here, we are able to do an immediate mitigation. We’re not wasting any second." Your neighborhood: Local coverage from WPBF 25 News During public comment, one resident and a commissioner questioned whether reducing employee salaries could help address the potential shortfall. Cianciulli responded, saying Martin County already has difficulty recruiting trained firefighter-paramedics because departments farther south offer better compensation. Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app. "When we did our last class that we had, we had roughly 22 open positions; I only had about three paramedics that actually graduated that class," Cianciulli said. "The rest were firefighter EMTs. It’s because the compensation package for a firefighter medic that is already trained is much higher down south." Cianciulli advised residents to learn as much as possible about the proposal and its potential effects before casting their ballots in November.

It calls for redeveloping Museum Pointe, which is currently home to a history center, public waterfront access, fishing piers, and green space, into a facility featuring floating docks, a multi-story marina, an event center, a waterfront restaurant, and a clubhouse.Opponents fear the plan could privatize one of the city's most treasured public spaces."Giving public land to private folks," said Terry Howard, a volunteer at the History Center at Museum Pointe Park. Gabby Rothman, MPA Florida voters will soon make an important decision about property taxes. Amendment 3 would substantially increase the homestead exemption from non-school property taxes and require the Legislature to establish a schedule for eventually eliminating those taxes on qualifying homesteaded property. The amendment needs approval from at least 60 percent of voters to pass. Local government officials are warning that the loss of property tax revenue could lead to hiring freezes, reduced services, higher fees, and employee layoffs. Those concerns should be taken seriously. State economists have projected that the amendment could reduce local government property tax revenue across Florida by nearly $5 billion during its first fiscal year of implementation, with the impact increasing substantially in later years. But before government leaders begin frightening employees and residents with immediate predictions of layoffs, they should answer a fundamental question: Are we making full use of the people, skills, and opportunities already available in our community? I ask that question because I have personally watched an innovative government workforce solution succeed. For many years, I worked with Diamond Litty, the elected Public Defender for Florida’s 19th Judicial Circuit. Diamond did not believe that every staffing challenge automatically required another permanent government position with a salary, insurance, retirement benefits, and continuing costs. She looked for opportunities. One of the best examples was the Investigator Intern Program she created. The program gave participants structured training and practical experience while providing meaningful investigative assistance to the Public Defender’s Office. These were not volunteers simply answering telephones or stuffing envelopes. Participants learned how to interview clients and witnesses, review case information, assist with investigations, and understand the real responsibilities of the criminal justice system. The office received additional workforce capacity. Participants received extensive training and experience that could open the door to a new career. I watched Diamond create that program. I watched it grow and earn recognition far beyond our circuit. More importantly, I learned from it. Diamond demonstrated that innovation in government does not always begin with additional tax revenue. Sometimes it begins with a leader who recognizes two separate needs and finds a responsible way to connect them. That lesson stayed with me throughout my own public service career. Years later, while earning my Master of Public Administration degree, I began researching whether a similar philosophy could address two different challenges. Local governments have workforce needs. At the same time, many senior homeowners living on limited incomes struggle to keep up with property taxes and the increasing costs of remaining in their homes. My research “Is a ‘Work Off’ Program a Property Tax Solution for Florida Fixed Income Seniors?” examined programs in three states that allowed qualifying senior homeowners to perform approved public service in exchange for a limited property tax benefit. I developed a proposed model that would allow an eligible senior to contribute documented and supervised service to a participating government agency. The value of that service, up to an annual limit of $1,500, could then be applied toward a portion of the homeowner’s property tax obligation. Eligibility would be based on financial need. Work assignments would be clearly defined. Hours would be recorded and verified. Participants would be supervised and would not make legal decisions, determine taxes, handle public money, or perform work beyond their training and authority. A senior with experience in accounting might assist with an appropriate records project. A retired teacher might help prepare public education materials. Someone with administrative experience might assist with customer navigation, appointment scheduling, telephone support, outreach, or document organization. Let me be clear: the proposal was not intended to replace essential employees. It was designed to recognize that retirement does not erase a person’s knowledge, experience, or desire to contribute. This research also became personal to me during my campaign for St. Lucie County Tax Collector. I thought about the senior homeowner who might eventually stand at the counter and say, “I have lived in my home for decades, but I can no longer afford this tax bill.” The Tax Collector does not determine property values, establish tax rates, or create exemptions. The office must collect the amount placed on the tax roll and follow Florida law when taxes become delinquent. Without an authorized alternative, the Tax Collector may have little more to offer than an explanation of the law and the consequences of nonpayment. I believed we could at least study whether a better option was possible. A Tax Collector could not create this program independently. It would require legislative authority, legal review, funding, and cooperation among the taxing authorities, Property Appraiser, Tax Collector, senior service organizations, risk management professionals, and participating government agencies. Questions involving liability, confidentiality, insurance, workers’ compensation, public records, and the possible displacement of employees would have to be resolved. Those are legitimate concerns. They are also the kind of questions serious public administrators should be willing to examine rather than using them as reasons to reject innovation. No volunteer or service exchange program could absorb the entire financial impact of Amendment 3. It would be dishonest to suggest otherwise. Some government positions require professional training, legal authority, institutional knowledge, and permanent public accountability. Volunteers cannot simply replace essential employees. But it is equally unreasonable to act as though government has only two choices: collect the same amount of money or begin laying off employees. Other questions should be asked first. Can vacancies remain open? Can processes be simplified? Can technology reduce repetitive work? Can colleges provide supervised interns? Can retirees contribute their professional skills? Can government partner with community organizations? Can administrative layers be reduced before frontline positions are threatened? Perhaps the amendment will pass. Either way, the debate has exposed a larger problem. Too often, government waits for a financial crisis before discussing efficiency and innovation. That work should already be happening. I watched Diamond Litty identify an opportunity that others might have overlooked. She connected people seeking experience with an office that needed help, then built a structured program that benefited both. That same philosophy inspired my own thesis research defense. Look at the people already around us. Respect the value of their experience. Establish appropriate safeguards. Before government tells residents which services must disappear or tells employees which jobs may be lost, in my professional opinion, leaders should first demonstrate that they have explored every responsible opportunity available. A Fort Pierce pizza shop known for giving back is creating an even bigger space to inspire young readers.Big Apple Pizza owner Scott Van Duzer is expanding the restaurant's free book program by transforming its outdoor patio into a dedicated reading room where children can pick up a book any time they visit.WATCH: For years, Van Duzer has kept shelves of free books inside the restaurant, inviting children to take one home at no cost. He said seeing kids light up when they discover a new book has been one of the most rewarding parts of the program."The books are there so when the kids come in the store they're easily available," Van Duzer said. "They'll come in and they're excited they can take whatever they want home."As more children have stopped by to pick up books, the collection has continued to grow. Van Duzer said the restaurant has simply run out of space inside, prompting the decision to turn the outdoor patio into a permanent reading room."We have so many books and we are trying to keep ahead of the game that we have turned our porch into what's going to be the reading room," Van Duzer said. "So now anytime a child stops by they can get a book free of charge no questions asked."The goal, he said, is to make books easy to access and help encourage a lifelong love of reading. Whether a family comes in for pizza or simply stops by for a book, every child is welcome to take one home.For Van Duzer, giving back has always been part of the restaurant's mission. He said that commitment comes from the example his mother set while he was growing up."I didn't have a lot," Van Duzer said. "My mom was pretty instrumental in my life so she just said if you can give back, give back. We live that every day."Construction on the new reading room is underway and is expected to be completed later this fall. Until then, children can continue picking up free books inside Big Apple Pizza, where the message remains the same: every child is welcome to take a book home, no questions asked.Big Apple Pizza is located at 2311 S 35th St, Fort Pierce FL 34981.

Martin County commissioners faced a wave of public pushback during Tuesday morning's meeting as residents, local surfers, and marine experts urged local leaders to keep strict limits on beachside shark fishing. The debate centers on potential language changes to local ordinances regarding land-based shark fishing, a practice where anglers deploy lines from the shore using heavy gear, kayaks, or drones to drop bait and chum into deeper waters. Under current Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC) rules, shore anglers are required to hold a specialized permit, keep sharks in the water, and use non-offset circle hooks to prevent injury to the animals. However, local ordinances in coastal counties can set stricter safety boundaries near public swimming areas. During public comments, speakers warned that chumming , releasing fish parts and blood into the surf to attract sharks, endangers swimmers, surfers, and families. "I myself have been caught in shark fishing lines, and it is not fun," said local surfer Jay Noyes, speaking in support of beachgoers and surfers. Dottie Lanci, a member of the Hutchinson Island Preservation Initiative, strongly opposed any effort to loosen existing restrictions that ban shark baiting on lifeguard-protected beaches. Lansing called on commissioners to prioritize safety and extend the ban across all county beaches, citing an incident she witnessed outside her home where anglers used drones to drop chum in the water. "The next morning a family of four put up their umbrellas. Two young children were playing in the water there, completely unaware of what took place the day before and that some hungry sharks might still be there," Lanci said. She also noted that other Florida municipalities, such as Miami Beach, passed local bans on land-based shark fishing earlier this year. Safety concerns over shark activity on local beaches are far from theoretical for many residents . In August 2017, a 3-year-old girl named Violet Veatch was bitten on the leg by a suspected bull shark while wading in shallow water at Bathtub Reef Beach in Martin County. The toddler's mother, Jessica Veatch, later pushed for stricter local beach safety regulations , believing the shark was drawn to the crowded swimming area by spearfishermen carrying bloody fish through the water. Justin Grubich, a marine conservation expert and local surfer who moved to the area from Fort Lauderdale, urged the commission to maintain strong local restrictions. Pointing to recent research presented at statewide conservation forums, Grubich warned that regular baiting near popular beaches conditions wildlife. "There's new scientific evidence or more accumulated scientific evidence that you can create problem sharks like problem bears," Grubich cautioned commissioners, advocating for rules that limit chumming and keep blood out of coastal waters. Commissioners did not take immediate action on the ordinance during the meeting, but requested further review of local public safety boundaries alongside state FWC regulations.

Lucie review the upcoming city budget as some city council members worry about lost revenue if property taxes go away. Lucie hosted the summer budget workshop at the Port St. Lucie Community Center Thursday morning. During the workshop, City Manager Jesus Merejo told the City Council the city would lose over $48 million in property taxes over the next two years if the item passes in November. To prepare for the potential hit, the city isn't just deferring projects it's also holding the line on hiring. Lucie says it won't fund 184 requested positions, worth $28.3 million, including 25 new police officers and parks staff the city had already planned to add this year to keep up with growth at Torino Regional Park and the new BMX facility at Tradition Regional Park. Well, our costs continually rise just like everybody else. So, the only place that we can take that from is personnel. So, we'll have to reduce the size of the place, said Police Chief Leo Niemczyk when asked how this budget will impact the department. See also: Funeral held for Belle Glade father, two sons killed when pickup overturned into canal City employees also won't get a cost-of-living raise in the coming budget. On the capital side, the $7.8 million in canceled projects includes a study for a new interchange connecting Marshall Parkway to I-95, an inclusive playground at McChesney Park, and parking improvements at Riverland Paseo Park, along with construction on a new City Hall and parking garage Despite parks and recreation receiving an extra $1.34 million, most of that money is tied to new developments, such as the Torino Regional Park and the BMX facility at Tradition Regional Park. Parks and recreation officials told city councilors what a lack of new staff to keep these parks going will look like. I dare say the dirty words of deferred maintenance. But that's the reality when you don't have the people in the parks to maintain them at the level that we've been accustomed to doing, said Brad Keen, the director of the parks and recreation department. Not everything is being cut, though. The police department's budget is actually going up nearly 10%, to just under $104 million, driven mostly by a 5% contractual raise for sworn officers along with new equipment, training and technology upgrades. But the number of officers isn't growing; staffing stays flat at just over 468 positions, meaning the department is spending more to keep the officers it already has, not to add more. City leaders have flagged public safety, police, code enforcement, and emergency management as the areas most exposed if deeper cuts are eventually needed, since they already eat up 56% of the city's general fund. This is the reality of what the future is for, not just our city, but all this needs for safety if we're not able to be competitive and keep our officers, said Vice Mayor Jolien Caraballo. The proposal, known as Amendment 3, is headed to Florida voters on the November 3, 2026 ballot after the Legislature passed it during a June special session. If approved, it would raise the state's homestead exemption from $50,000 to $150,000 starting in January 2027, and to $250,000 in January 2028, while also directing lawmakers to come up with a plan to eliminate non-school property taxes on homesteaded properties eventually. Because it's a constitutional amendment, it needs at least 60% approval from voters to pass. Economists have estimated the change could cut local government revenue statewide by billions of dollars a year, which is why cities and counties across Florida, including Port St. Lucie, are already building the potential loss into their budget planning. Lucie County homeowners currently pay the highest property tax in the state, according to Florida tax data. Scott Samples with the city said the council will reconvene shortly after the November 3rd election to determine next steps, whether the proposal is passed or fails.

FIFA President Gianni Infantino set a Sept. 19 deadline on Wednesday for the 211 member federations to accept one-off $20 million offers as part of a project to sell stakes in the World Cup to private investors.The $20 billion FIFA subsidiary, bankrolled by the brother of Jared Kushner, was blasted by international soccer organizations. European soccer body UEFA aims to call its 55 member federations to an emergency online meeting, likely on Thursday."But having held discussions with many stakeholders across the game, UEFA knows there is significant and growing opposition to FIFA's scheme," the organization said in a statement.The effort also marks Infantino's latest effort to align with those in the orbit of U.S. President Donald Trump: by creating the FIFA peace prize, letting Trump intervene in a process that led to United States forward Folarin Balogun playing at the World Cup, and now trying to lock in Joshua Kushner's investment firm to a 12-year ownership deal with the Switzerland-based not-for-profit soccer body.RELATED STORY | A behind the scenes look at the digital brains of the World CupInfantino set out the "singular and unique funding opportunity" in a letter detailing why he wants to create the $20 billion FIFA subsidiary — 20% owned by private investors — that would run the soccer body's competitions and events like World Cups and Club World Cups."It is my duty and responsibility as FIFA president to present such game-changing opportunities to you, our members," Infantino wrote in the letter seen by The Associated Press.The proposal revealed Tuesday and backed by Joshua Kushner's investment firm Thrive Capital was met with immediate fury from Infantino's former colleagues at UEFA, which said the World Cup "is not FIFA's to sell."One option open to European soccer is threaten a boycott of FIFA competitions — a tactic used in 2021 when UEFA-led opposition helped stop Infantino's plan to play the World Cup every two years instead of four.FIFA's private equity plan is the latest ambitious project proposed during Infantino's 11-year presidency in which he has increasingly seemed to be an executive leader acting without consulting with soccer's major stakeholders.Previous plans include creating a FIFA Peace Prize — awarded to Trump in December at the World Cup draw — and trying to push through a secretive $25 billion private equity plan in 2018 to create new and bigger men's competitions. That was resisted by UEFA.Concerns about the latest and previously secret plan were aired Wednesday by the continental soccer bodies for Asia and the North American region known as CONCACAF.RELATED STORY | The 2026 World Cup is officially the most attended ever, according to FIFA"We are deeply concerned by the lack of due process," CONCACAF said in a statement.The Kuala Lumpur-based Asian Football Confederation said it was "disappointed that a matter of such significance entered the public domain before the AFC family had been afforded the opportunity to examine and discuss it."Continental bodies that organize their own international club and national-team competitions — such as the Champions League, European Championship and Copa America — likely will see threats to those events from FIFA wanting to increase revenue and value for investors by playing World Cups and Club World Cups for men and women more often, along with adding more teams.The influential, 850-member European Football Clubs group — which has a joint venture with UEFA to manage the Champions League — said it "learned about this proposal in the same way as most global football stakeholders — without warning and through the media."Inviting in private investors could also, sports governance academic Antoine Duval suggested Wednesday "incentivize FIFA to further commodify the World Cup (think more hydration breaks and dynamic pricing ) in a drive to increase its revenue."If the FIFA Forward Enterprise subsidiary is approved by a majority of the 211 members, they also each are promised $20 million in funding from the four-year commercial cycle tied to the men's 2030 World Cup.That would lead, Infantinto wrote, to "a pool of diverse international investors" joining Joshua Kushner's Thrive as the anchor investor: "This process will be led by J.P. Morgan."If Infantino's plan is rejected, those members will get their previously promised $10 million over the next four years, his letter stated.The cash difference on offer Wednesday to FIFA members appears to be $86 million over 12 years compared to about $36 million in existing promised funding for rejecting the private equity deal.The rushed deadline to claim an initial $20 million "says everything you need to know about this plan," UEFA said. "FIFA cannot continue to use our sport to enrich themselves and their friends."Dozens of member federations typically rely on FIFA for funding, have national teams with little realistic chance of qualifying for World Cups, and whose best players rarely, if ever, join clubs playing at the highest level of international competitions.FIFA's one-member, one-vote democratic system means the most powerful soccer nations on the field easily can be outvoted by those who rarely play top-level games.FIFA's plan met quick opposition from British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, whose government is preparing to support hosting the 2035 Women's World Cup in England, Scotland, Wales and Ireland. FIFA is set to confirm that lone bid for 2035 at an online meeting in November."Football does not belong to investors," Burnham, a longtime soccer fan, said in a video message on Instagram. "Once you have sold a piece of (the World Cup), you have sold out. Football belongs to the fans. It always has, and it always will."Resistance by British lawmakers — including threats of legislation by then-Prime Minister Boris Johnson in 2021 — previously helped stop the divisive European Super League project that was an existential threat to UEFA's Champions League, and which Infantino had discreetly supported. MorganInfantino has seemed to be cruising toward being reelected unopposed as FIFA president for a fourth and final term through 2031.Promising more FIFA funds to member federations was a decisive part of his initial election-day speech in February 2016, and at his unopposed reelections in 2019 and 2023.Some observers have long suspected Infantino wants a longer-term role running the sport. A CEO or commissioner role at a FIFA subsidiary FFE would fit that bill.This week, Infantino has ignited frustration with his leadership beyond the usual circles in Europe, which have almost four months to commit to an election challenge.The candidate entry deadline is Nov. 18 for an election scheduled next March 18 at Rabat in Morocco, which has been a key Infantino ally in recent years and will co-host the 2030 World Cup.

A prosecutor says they have dropped charges against Gregory Allen Davis, 49, of Port St. Lucie in an incident June 24 in Port St. Lucie when Davis ordered three juveniles out of their car at gunpoint and told them to get on the ground. Minutes earlier, one of the teens had fired an Orbeez toy gun at the car that Davis and his fiancee were in. An Orbeez toy gun shoots soft water-absorbing beads. According to a prosecutor, the reason they dropped the charges against Davis is because in Florida, citizens have the right to make a citizen's arrest if they see that a felony has been committed in their presence. The felony that Davis saw was the teen firing a gun at his vehicle. "Basically, under Florida law, a citizen has a right to make a citizen's arrest if they observe a felony, occur in their presence, um, so that's basically what happened here," said Jason Bruin, Assistant State Attorney, 19th Judicial Circuit. Bruin says if the case had gone to a jury, they would've returned a verdict of not guilty. Davis, in this case, gets out of the vehicle and holds the the people that were in that car at gunpoint. No, we don't recommend that people take the law into their own hands like that. Let the police do their job. Call the police, let the police do their job," Bruin said. Davis was charged with three counts of false imprisonment and three counts of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon. Those six charges carry a maximum sentence of 30 years in prison if convicted. "I am very grateful as I am a father of three, and everything I do is for my kids. The thought of being away from them is horrifying. I have a daughter that is the same age as the person who did the shooting, and I spend my time teaching my children not to do dumb things like that. Obviously I would never want anyone to ever get hurt. Especially over what they consider to be a prank. I believe behavior like this starts with the parents. It is our job to teach our kids right from wrong and be their parent first and their friend second," Davis said in a text message to CBS12 News, reacting to the fact that the charges against him were dropped. A new study released this month reveals the high hourly wage needed to afford rent in Florida.According to a report from the National Low Income Housing Coalition, Florida ranks 10th highest in the nation for the hourly wage renters need to afford a two-bedroom apartment at $37.93."In order to afford this level of rent and utilities — without paying more than 30% of income on housing — a household must earn $6,575 monthly or $78,905 annually," the report said.In West Palm Beach-Boca Raton, that figure is even higher, with renters needing $43.35 an hour."Even workers with the nation's most common occupations struggle to afford modestly priced housing," the report stated.According to Apartments.com, the average rent for a two-bedroom apartment in West Palm Beach is $2,426 – $2,606 per month, and overall rents in the area run about 29% higher than the national average.The National Low Income Housing Coalition study said the most expensive area for Florida renters is in Monroe County (Florida Keys), which costs an hourly wage of $48.15, with Miami coming in second most expensive at $46.85.Are you feeling the squeeze? A new dance festival is set to debut in West Palm Beach this summer, bringing together nationally recognized choreographers, aspiring dancers and community arts programming across Palm Beach County.The inaugural Banyan Dance Festival will take place Aug. 3-8 throughout West Palm Beach, according to organizers Natural Movers Foundation and Grounded WPB. The weeklong event will feature performances, professional dance training, public classes, artist talkbacks and community experiences designed to strengthen South Florida’s dance community.Festival founders Ericka Squire of Natural Movers Foundation and Branndi Lewis of Grounded WPB said the event was created to expand opportunities for dancers and choreographers while positioning Palm Beach County as a destination for dance.“At its core, Banyan is about creating opportunities for artists,” Squire said in a statement. “Palm Beach County is Florida’s Cultural Capital®, and we wanted to create an opportunity for audiences to experience high-quality dance performances while also creating real pathways for dancers and choreographers to train, work, create, and be seen right here in Palm Beach County.”Festival organizers said the event will bring together professional artists, students and community members through performances, creative development and educational programming hosted at venues throughout the city.Featured artists include internationally recognized choreographers and educators Sean Aaron Carmon, Babatunji and Loni Landon, along with local, national and international performers participating throughout the week.Carmon, a former dancer with Alvin Ailey American Dance Theater, will create an original work for the Banyan Dance Company. Babatunji, a former member of Alonzo King LINES Ballet, will choreograph a new piece for the Banyan Dance Ensemble.Landon, a Princess Grace Choreography Fellowship Award winner and Guggenheim fellow, will teach during the festival and create a featured solo work for a dancer participating in the Banyan Dance Intensive.The festival’s inaugural Banyan Choreography Fellowship was awarded to Betty Garcia Diaz, a Cuban-born dancer and choreographer who has performed with companies including Northwest Dance Project, Malpaso Dance Company and Boston Dance Theater. Organizers said Garcia Diaz will create a newly commissioned work during the festival.Programming throughout the week includes:Youth Artist Program classes for dancers ages 9-15A pre-professional dance intensive for dancers ages 16-25Community dance classes sponsored by the Downtown Development AuthorityA Banyan Silent Disco at Nora DistrictRehearsal observations and artist talkbacks at Ballet FloridaThe Banyan Gala at the Community Foundation for Palm Beach and Martin CountiesThe Banyan Dance Festival Concert at the Norton Museum of ArtLewis said the festival is designed to create opportunities for dancers who previously may have needed to leave South Florida to pursue professional growth.“Banyan Dance Festival is building something that doesn’t currently exist in South Florida,” Lewis said in a statement. “Together, Grounded WPB and Natural Movers Foundation have created a platform that expands the local dance ecosystem while investing in artists through paid opportunities, professional training, and a full creative pipeline.”More information and a full schedule can be found at banyandancefestival.com or on Instagram at @banyandancefestival.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. It is time to find out where I've been exploring this week. This week's clue placed me near a tree that saves lives!I found myself pedaling across the Flagler Memorial Bridge with Visit Palm Beach, and let me tell you, I was excited about what we were going to discover. My guide told me we were heading to see some very pretty things when we got over to the Lake Trail and Ocean Boulevard, and boy, was that an understatement.WATCH: What struck me immediately was how the Lake Trail hugs the water for most of its length. And there's the Breakers – that absolutely stunning hotel – and what looked like a golf course stretching out beside it. I learned that it's one of the oldest golf courses in Florida! Then I noticed it – this magnificent, towering tree that seemed to command the entire area. And that's when I learned something absolutely fascinating. "That's a kapok tree," my guide explained. "Its seeds create this cotton-like substance that was used in bedding and linens. But here's the really amazing part – it has a buoyancy effect, so they used kapok in life vests and life preservers. That tree has witnessed so much history on Palm Beach Island. They say it's over 200 years old."I was blown away. Here I was, standing next to a tree that literally helped save lives! The kapok was first used by the U.S. Navy starting in 1915 for life preservers. During World War II, they stopped using it for that purpose, but you know what? They still use kapok today – in those alternative pillows we love, the ones with bamboo and kapok filling that are so comfortable.Standing there in its shade, looking out over the water where countless boats have passed by over the decades, I felt connected to all the history this tree has witnessed.The whole experience reminded me why I love these adventures so much. You never know what amazing stories you're going to uncover when you start exploring. A simple bike ride can lead you to a 200-year-old tree with a life-saving legacy that most people just walk right past without knowing its incredible story.That's the beauty of getting out there and asking questions – you discover that even the most ordinary-looking places have extraordinary tales to tell.

A petition with nearly 800 signatures is mounting against a proposal that could transform Fort Pierce's Museum Pointe — a public waterfront park along the Indian River Lagoon — into a mega-yacht marina. WATCH BELOW: 'We have been talking for years about better locations for that history center,' Erick Gill tells WPTV's Kate Hussey The proposal is part of the Port of Fort Pierce's updated 2026 Master Plan. It calls for redeveloping Museum Pointe, which is currently home to a history center, public waterfront access, fishing piers, and green space, into a facility featuring floating docks, a multi-story marina, an event center, a waterfront restaurant, and a clubhouse. Opponents fear the plan could privatize one of the city's most treasured public spaces. "Giving public land to private folks," said Terry Howard, a volunteer at the History Center at Museum Pointe Park. Howard contacted WPTV's Kate Hussey after learning about the master plan. "Development is just rampant in Florida, and at least we can fight for this one particular area and keep it green," Howard said. He said the loss of public waterfront access is a concern — but his biggest worry is the fate of the museum itself. "This is the place where this museum should be, right here on this Museum Pointe," said Howard. For more than 50 years, the museum has preserved artifacts from Florida's Native American tribes, Spanish shipwrecks, and more. The master plan's renderings place the proposed marina clubhouse exactly where the museum stands today. "Basically taking away a gem — a public gem that belongs to the people and replacing it with a facility for mega yachts," Howard said. "We're trying to keep this area as it is." St. Lucie County spokesperson Erick Gill said the museum's future is not in jeopardy if the project moves forward. "Staff's intent was never to close the museum," Gill said. "We have been talking for years about better locations for that history center; it is on a barrier island, in a flood zone, so it may not be the best place to store artifacts." Gill said the museum and its collection would be preserved and relocated if the project proceeds. He added that the master plan is designed to expand economic development, create jobs, and generate county revenue. "I think all local governments are looking for a way to generate revenue, so we can continue to lower the taxes for St. Lucie County residents and generate revenue from economic development, and we already have dock space there," Gill said. "Anything that's going to be a positive economic driver for the City of Fort Pierce, I'm going to embrace completely," Fort Pierce City Commissioner Michael Broderick added. Broderick said the city will have the final say on whether the project moves forward, and that commissioners will have to weigh economic benefits against preserving waterfront access. When asked which priority — economic development or waterfront access — would take precedence, Broderick said the answer is not simple. "That's the challenging question right there. I believe that we can strike a balance," Broderick said. "We always have to be careful not to eliminate public access to the waterway. Period." For Howard, the stakes go beyond the present. "This is a gem that once we develop around it, it'll never be replaced again," Howard said. "The museum has been here since the 1970s. If they want to boat docks for mega yachts, they can do it someplace else." St. Lucie County leaders are scheduled to discuss the proposal and its current status at a 9 a.m. Lucie County Commission Chambers. The Martin County School District has approved changes to its bus routes for the upcoming school year, aiming to improve efficiency and reduce costs. The new routes, which will begin on August 10, will consolidate existing routes while keeping bus stops and buses unchanged from last year. According to the district’s director of transportation, the changes address a decline in ridership and will save the district the cost of operating three bus routes. “Let’s say there’s a route that only has two tiers. Now picked up an extra tier like they had an elementary and a high school, now they’re picking up a middle school. They will get paid for what they work,” said Ruth, the district’s director of transportation. The district also cited a shortage of bus drivers as part of the reason for the decision. However, no jobs were lost as a result of the changes. Parents can track their child’s bus route in real time using the MyReaxium app. The route changes also include activity buses for after-school programs. The school district said the changes will save $255,000. To find information about the new school bus routes, click here.

A Fort Pierce pizza shop known for giving back is creating an even bigger space to inspire young readers.Big Apple Pizza owner Scott Van Duzer is expanding the restaurant's free book program by transforming its outdoor patio into a dedicated reading room where children can pick up a book any time they visit.WATCH: For years, Van Duzer has kept shelves of free books inside the restaurant, inviting children to take one home at no cost. He said seeing kids light up when they discover a new book has been one of the most rewarding parts of the program."The books are there so when the kids come in the store they're easily available," Van Duzer said. "They'll come in and they're excited they can take whatever they want home."As more children have stopped by to pick up books, the collection has continued to grow. Van Duzer said the restaurant has simply run out of space inside, prompting the decision to turn the outdoor patio into a permanent reading room."We have so many books and we are trying to keep ahead of the game that we have turned our porch into what's going to be the reading room," Van Duzer said. "So now anytime a child stops by they can get a book free of charge no questions asked."The goal, he said, is to make books easy to access and help encourage a lifelong love of reading. Whether a family comes in for pizza or simply stops by for a book, every child is welcome to take one home.For Van Duzer, giving back has always been part of the restaurant's mission. He said that commitment comes from the example his mother set while he was growing up."I didn't have a lot," Van Duzer said. "My mom was pretty instrumental in my life so she just said if you can give back, give back. We live that every day."Construction on the new reading room is underway and is expected to be completed later this fall. Until then, children can continue picking up free books inside Big Apple Pizza, where the message remains the same: every child is welcome to take a book home, no questions asked.Big Apple Pizza is located at 2311 S 35th St, Fort Pierce FL 34981.

A flashing traffic light installed at the intersection of Glades Cut Off Road and Commerce Center Drive more than six months ago is still not fully operational, and neighbors say the confusion it's creating is becoming a safety concern. More than six months after installation, Lorsten said nothing appears to have changed. "We just haven't seen any work being done on that at all," Lorsten said. Lorsten said the flashing light can add major backups and worries that confused, aggressive driving could put her family at risk. "My son, who's a new driver, not knowing what to do when everybody's confused and something really happening bad to him," Lorsten said. WPTV reached out to the Wylder community, FEC Railways and St. Lucie County to find out who is responsible for making the light fully operational, but the answer remains unclear. "It's just not clear whose responsibility it is, and what time frame that would fit into," Packard said. We're still working to hear back from all parties. A Fort Pierce pizza shop known for giving back is creating an even bigger space to inspire young readers. Big Apple Pizza owner Scott Van Duzer is expanding the restaurant’s free book program by transforming its outdoor patio into a dedicated reading room where children can pick up a book any time they visit. For years, Van Duzer has kept shelves of free books inside the restaurant, inviting children to take one home at no cost. He said seeing kids light up when they discover a new book has been one of the most rewarding parts of the program. “The books are there so when the kids come in the store they’re easily available,” Van Duzer said. “They’ll come in and they’re excited they can take whatever they want home.” As more children have stopped by to pick up books, the collection has continued to grow. Van Duzer said the restaurant has simply run out of space inside, prompting the decision to turn the outdoor patio into a permanent reading room. “We have so many books and we are trying to keep ahead of the game that we have turned our porch into what’s going to be the reading room,” Van Duzer said. “So now anytime a child stops by they can get a book free of charge no questions asked.” The goal, he said, is to make books easy to access and help encourage a lifelong love of reading. Whether a family comes in for pizza or simply stops by for a book, every child is welcome to take one home. For Van Duzer, giving back has always been part of the restaurant’s mission. He said that commitment comes from the example his mother set while he was growing up. “I didn’t have a lot,” Van Duzer said. “My mom was pretty instrumental in my life so she just said if you can give back, give back. We live that every day.” Construction on the new reading room is underway and is expected to be completed later this fall. Until then, children can continue picking up free books inside Big Apple Pizza, where the message remains the same: every child is welcome to take a book home, no questions asked. Big Apple Pizza is located at 2311 S 35th St, Fort Pierce FL 34981.

Martin County commissioners are expected to hear a presentation Tuesday outlining how a proposed expansion of Florida’s homestead exemption could affect Martin County Fire Rescue if voters approve the constitutional amendment on the November ballot. The presentation is expected to focus on the projected financial impact of the proposed tax changes and what they could mean for the department’s budget, staffing, operations and emergency response. See the presentation in the gallery above. "As a public servant, I will be glad to honor the will of the voters, whatever they decide regarding the proposed constitutional amendment. But, we do have some concerns about the depth of the cuts that would be needed as they relate to a number of areas of government operations, particularly fire rescue," said Martin County Commissioner James Blake Capps, District 3. According to county documents, Martin County Fire Rescue projects it could lose 116 firefighters over the next two years about one-third of its workforce because of reduced property tax revenue tied to the proposed amendment. "We in Martin County have been used to the very best in fire rescue services, and I would hate to see our level of service suffer greatly. It seems to me that we would be in for that if this constitutional amendment were to pass," said Capps. Fire Rescue leaders are also expected to discuss potential operational changes if those revenue reductions occur. Previous county projections have outlined possible station closures, reductions to specialized teams including HAZMAT, Technical Rescue, the dive team and LifeStar, and delays in replacing equipment. County leaders have previously said the department has few options to absorb the projected revenue loss because about 93% of the Fire Rescue budget is dedicated to personnel. Officials have also warned the proposed cuts could lead to longer emergency response times and affect specialized emergency services provided throughout Martin County. "There would also have to be a no-overtime policy for all of our fire rescue personnel. That doesn't sound so bad initially, but when you think about the consequences, it means no backfilling of stations with personnel, which would result in randomized brownouts of stations," said Capps. Tuesday’s discussion comes as commissioners consider several other agenda items, including final solid waste assessment rates, proposed changes to fishing rules on county-owned property, development proposals, and conservation land purchases. "Another serious consequence for Martin County residents would be higher insurance premiums. If you're within five miles of a fire station, you receive a break on your homeowner's insurance. But if you're farther than five miles away, you pay higher premiums. If we shut down three fire stations, a lot of people would end up paying more for homeowner's insurance. There would also be consequences for our level of service and our comprehensive plan," said Capps. No vote on firefighter layoffs or fire station closures is expected during Tuesday’s meeting. Instead, commissioners will receive the presentation as they continue evaluating the potential local impacts of the proposed homestead exemption expansion. "I think it could be rather severe. When you think about three fire stations disappearing, response times for the people living near those stations would increase, which could have very serious consequences for residents," said Capps. Voters will have the final say on the constitutional amendment during the November general election. The meeting starts at 9 a.m. CBS12 News will have a team inside. A Leon County circuit judge heard arguments Wednesday over whether the ballot title and summary for Florida's Amendment 3 property-tax proposal give voters a fair explanation of the measure — or amount to a political sales pitch.Leon County Circuit Judge David Frank heard arguments in three consolidated lawsuits challenging the title and summary scheduled to appear on November ballots. Frank did not immediately rule, instead ordering attorneys to submit proposed decisions by 5 p.m. Monday.WATCH WPTV'S COVERAGE BELOW:The challengers include the nonprofit Save Our Voters From Misleading Ballot Language, several former mayors, former Republican state Sen. Jeff Brandes and former Democratic U.S. Al Lawson Jr.They argue the amendment's title — "Save Our Homes From Excessive Property Taxes" — and phrases promising to benefit taxpayers, protect small businesses, preserve core services and ensure fairness are biased, inaccurate and designed to persuade voters.Plaintiffs' attorney Jamie Cole told the court the language crosses a line."This is probably the worst example of a biased ballot question and an inaccurate ballot question that we've seen," Cole said. "This is really just a political campaign flyer."Cole argued that "save" is an emotionally loaded word suggesting homeowners face an immediate threat. He pointed to a previous Florida Supreme Court decision rejecting a proposed amendment titled "Save Our Everglades" and noted that the state's existing Save Our Homes assessment cap was originally presented to voters in 1992 under the more neutral title "Homestead Valuation Limitation."The current Amendment 3 proposal would not change that 3% Save Our Homes assessment cap for homesteaded properties.Brandes, speaking outside the courtroom, said the language gives voters the benefits without fully explaining the potential costs or consequences."They've rolled a live grenade into the Constitution here with this amendment, and people need to be very cognizant of what's going on," Brandes said.The official ballot summary says the amendment would ensure funding for core services by requiring local governments to spend remaining property-tax revenue on public needs such as public safety, schools, infrastructure and natural resources.Plaintiffs argued that restricting how remaining revenue may be spent does not guarantee that enough money will remain to fund those services.They also challenged the promise of protecting small businesses. The amendment would reduce the annual assessment-growth cap on non-homestead property from 10% to 5%, but that change would apply broadly to commercial property, rental homes and second homes — not specifically to small businesses.Another dispute centers on language promising a "schedule for full elimination" of non-school homestead property taxes. The amendment's full text instead directs lawmakers to create a uniform procedure allowing counties and municipalities to increase the exemption up to a home's remaining assessed value. A state fiscal analysis notes that the proposal sets no timeline for those future increases.Plaintiffs also argue the summary fails to explain a potentially significant shift in control over local property-tax revenue. The amendment would add categories describing how cities and counties may spend those dollars while allowing the Legislature to prohibit some expenditures through state law.At one point, Frank questioned whether disagreement among the plaintiffs about the effect of that provision supported their broader argument that the measure is unclear."If the lawyers for both these groups can't figure out what it is, doesn't that sort of support that argument?" Frank said.Attorneys representing the attorney general, secretary of state and Department of State urged Frank to uphold the language.State attorney Ben Gibson argued the title and summary must be read together and that Florida law requires them to explain only the amendment's chief purpose — not every possible consequence or implementation detail."The summary is supposed to be written for voters, not for lawyers," Gibson said.Gibson argued the title identifies what homes would supposedly be saved from — excessive property taxes — and therefore does not leave voters to imagine an undefined threat. He also said the summary makes clear that only "remaining" property-tax revenue would be reserved for core services, rather than guaranteeing a particular amount of funding.The state further argued that small businesses would benefit from the lower non-homestead assessment cap even if other property owners receive the same protection.Ultimately, Gibson said, the challengers must prove the title and summary are "clearly and conclusively defective," not merely that different wording could have been better.The Legislature approved the proposal during a June special session, passing it 75-26 in the House and 30-9 in the Senate. Because it is a proposed constitutional amendment, it was not subject to the governor's signature or veto. It needs support from at least 60% of voters in November.For people who establish permanent Florida residency by Dec. 31, the proposal would increase the non-school homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. It would be adjusted for inflation beginning in 2029.People establishing residency after that cutoff would receive a smaller exemption for 4 years before becoming eligible for the larger amount in the fifth year. School district property taxes would remain unaffected.The amendment would also reduce the assessment-growth cap on non-homestead property from 10% to 5%.A July analysis by Florida's Revenue Estimating Conference projected the quantifiable portions of the amendment would reduce local property-tax collections by nearly $4.93 billion in the 2027-28 fiscal year. The modeled recurring impact is approximately $11.83 billion annually, although the estimate does not account for future policy changes by local governments or referendums authorized by the amendment.Election officials told the court that county supervisors may begin printing ballots Aug. 27, adding urgency to the case and any appeal.If Frank upholds the current language, it would remain on the ballot unless an appellate court intervenes. If he finds all of the ballot statements defective and appeals are declined or exhausted, Florida law gives Attorney General James Uthmeier 10 days to submit corrected wording.Any rewritten title or summary could also face another expedited challenge before the same court.

Lucie City Council has permanently banned construction of a gas station on a 9.4-acre commercial parcel at the southwest corner of Crosstown Parkway and Fairgreen Drive in Tradition. The council unanimously approved the restriction on July 13 as part of the 16th amendment to the Tradition Master Planned Unit Development, ending nearly three months of debate over the future of land originally planned as Phase 3 of the Heritage Oaks at Tradition residential development. Winding River Crosstown LLC requested permission in May to convert the parcel from residential to commercial use. While council members supported commercial development, several raised concerns that a convenience store with gas pumps would worsen traffic along Crosstown Parkway west of Interstate 95. Vice Mayor Jolien Caraballo and other council members asked staff to determine whether gas stations could be eliminated as a permitted use, leading the council to table the request on May 26. Heritage Oaks residents urged the council in June to reject the land-use change, citing traffic, noise and neighborhood impacts. The council voted 4-0 on June 22 to approve the commercial designation after the developer agreed to permanently give up the right to build a gas station. The July 13 ordinance codified that restriction into the Tradition MPUD documents, ensuring the prohibition remains with the property regardless of future ownership. City planner Bridget Kean said service stations remain permitted elsewhere in the Tradition mixed-use area but are now prohibited on Parcel 11A. The updated plan also requires the developer to install a fence along the southern property line before mass grading and to complete an architectural wall and landscape buffering along the southeastern and southern boundaries before the first building permit is issued. Councilman Anthony Bonna defended the public process and the decision, saying Port St. Lucie has long lacked commercial development, placing a burden on homeowners. Councilman David Pickett said the city has consistently heard residents oppose additional housing and called the shift to commercial the best outcome for the corner. Councilwoman Stephanie Morgan, who initially questioned whether prohibiting a specific business type amounted to government interference, ultimately voted with the council. Mayor Shannon Martin confirmed the restriction would remain with the property in perpetuity before the final unanimous vote. Sandra Owens says the Delray Beach Memorial Gardens Municipal Cemetery triggers a wave of emotions."It took me some time to get my head, because I was all emotional," Owens said.WATCH WPTV'S COVERAGE BELOW:Owens says a year after her parents died and were buried in 2005, she bought her own burial plot next to them. The city confirmed she purchased the plot in 2006.Fast forward to 2024 — Owens made a startling discovery during a visit."I went to visit my parents' burial site, and lo and behold, there's some guy buried with the whole plot and everything," Owens said.Owens was shocked to find out her burial plot had been resold."I've lost sleep; I wake up at night because it's just not right," Owens said.The city says the issue stems from a cemetery management software error that listed the already-sold plot as available.The city's attorney's office has been involved in the resolution process, offering Owens a full refund, adjacent burial plots so she can be laid to rest, or the option to relocate her mother's remains at no cost to an adjacent available space.But those are resolutions Owens does not want. Since her only son is in the military, she says she wants to be next to her parents."I'm like, I don't want to be buried in the back of the cemetery; I want to be buried where I paid for," Owens said."They offered me, well, we can give you your money back. I didn't worry about dying because now, I knew where I was going to be buried. Now they're sending out memos: there are no more plots in the Delray cemetery," Owens said.The city says its software has been replaced and, at this time, it does not know of any other impacted plots.WPTV reporter Zitlali Solache reached out to city commissioners about alternative solutions and is still waiting to hear back.Meanwhile, Owens says she has been in touch with attorneys and is exploring legal options. “At the end of the day, Zitlali, all I want to do is be buried next to my mother," Owens said. "It's just a mess.”Statement from the City of Delray Beach:"This is an unfortunate situation, and the City recognizes the significance of the circumstances for everyone involved. We regret that this occurred and remain committed to working with the resident to identify a respectful resolution while honoring the rights of all families affected. The City has confirmed that the resident purchased the burial plot in 2006. Our review determined that the issue resulted from an error associated with the cemetery management software that was in use at the time, which incorrectly identified a previously sold plot as available. That software has since been replaced, and additional safeguards and procedures have been implemented to prevent this situation from occurring again. Since learning of the issue, City staff has worked directly with the resident over an extended period to identify a resolution. Throughout those discussions, we have remained committed to treating all families with dignity and compassion. Because another individual has since been laid to rest in the plot, this matter now involves the wishes and legal rights of two families. The City cannot unilaterally authorize the disinterment of a loved one without the consent of that family and all applicable legal requirements being met. To resolve the matter, the City has offered several options, including a full refund of the original purchase price, providing adjacent burial plots so the resident can be laid to rest next to her brother, or relocating her mother's remains at no cost to an adjacent available space so the resident may ultimately be buried beside her mother. While we understand these options may not be the resident's preferred outcome, they reflect our effort to find a compassionate solution while respecting the rights and dignity of everyone affected. We remain willing to continue working with the resident should she wish to discuss any available options."

A 3-month-old died from dehydration and malnutrition after living in a home with boarded windows, exposed electrical wiring and cockroaches, according to court documents and investigators with the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office. The infant’s mother, Nicole Maxwell, grandfather, Robert Maxwell and the grandfather’s girlfriend, Vikki Koon, now face charges of aggravated manslaughter of a child and aggravated child abuse. “In my 20 years of law enforcement, this is one of the worst cases I’ve ever worked,” St Lucie County Sheriff’s Office Detective Jennifer Diaz said. The investigation began in August 2025 when investigators responded to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital after the 3-month-old was brought in deceased by Robert Maxwell and Koon. The medical examiner determined the child died from dehydration and malnutrition. Court documents describe the infant’s “ribs more prominent than its stomach.” “I can tell you the facts of this case don’t even paint a picture clear to what we saw at the hospital,” Diaz said. Diaz said the child lived primarily with Maxwell and Koon while the child’s mother, Nicole Maxwell, lived at her boyfriend’s home. Investigators said the child’s father lived in Virginia. According to court documents, Koon primarily fed the infant only twice a day and admitted to investigators that when she ran out of formula, she fed the child “watered-down milk with bay cereal mixed in.” Other children of Nicole Maxwell were also living in the home, which court documents describe as having windows boarded shut, exposed electrical wiring and live and dead cockroaches throughout. “The living conditions at this time were environmental hazards,” Diaz said. A neighbor named Suzan, said she witnessed the conditions firsthand. “It just looked unlivable,” Suzan said. Suzan said she would often see one of the other children walking around the neighborhood. “They would come and ask for water, you know. I see the child be thirsty. I mean, not bathe, same clothes every day,” Suzan said. Suzan said she is heartbroken thinking about the infant who lived only a few feet away. “Nobody should suffer or go hungry, and especially for a child that didn’t ask to come here,” Suzan said. Diaz said the Department of Children and Families had been involved with the family before. Nicole Maxwell’s other children who were living inside the mobile home are now in foster care. All three suspects faces charges of aggravated manslaughter of a child and aggravated child abuse. “The baby finally got justice,” Suzan said. Diaz said emphasized the importance of reporting suspicious activity to protect children. “These tips are so instrumental to keeping our children safe,” Diaz said.
