hero.headline: Los Angeles man sentenced to life in prison for fentanyl sale that killed Vero Beach resident
hero.body:
Alfonso Guerrero, 39, of Los Angeles was sentenced to life in federal prison for selling fentanyl that caused the death of David Eller of Vero Beach in May 2023. Guerrero was convicted in May 2026 of distributing fentanyl resulting in death.

Evidence shown in court proved that Guerrero sold a tenth of a gram of fentanyl to Eller on May 16, 2023. The transaction was captured on doorbell camera. Hours later, Eller was found dead in his Vero Beach home.

The Indian River County Sheriff's Office arrested Guerrero days after Eller's death. At the time of his arrest, Guerrero had additional fentanyl ready to distribute. The case was investigated by the Indian River County Sheriff's Office and the DEA Miami Field Division.

Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers said the department will not tolerate drugs being sold in the community. The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Florida prosecuted the case.

hero.headline: Prosecutors drop charges against Port St. Lucie man who held teens at gunpoint after Orbeez shooting
hero.teaser: Charges against Gregory Allen Davis, 49, were dropped after prosecutors cited Florida's citizen's arrest law following a June incident where Davis held three teens at gunpoint.
hero.body:
Prosecutors dropped charges against Gregory Allen Davis, 49, of Port St. Lucie in an incident on June 24 when Davis ordered three juveniles out of their car at gunpoint and told them to get on the ground at the intersection of SW Morelia Lane and SW Acapulco Terrace. Minutes earlier, one of the teens had fired an Orbeez toy gun at the car that Davis and his fiancee were in. An Orbeez toy gun shoots soft water-absorbing beads.

According to Jason Bruin, Assistant State Attorney for the 19th Judicial Circuit, the charges were dropped because in Florida, citizens have the right to make a citizen's arrest if they see that a felony has been committed in their presence. Bruin said if the case had gone to a jury, they would have returned a verdict of not guilty. Davis was charged with three counts of false imprisonment and three counts of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon, which carried a maximum sentence of 30 years in prison if convicted.

According to Port St. Lucie Police, Jordan Gomez, 15, was charged with shooting or throwing a missile at or into an occupied vehicle. In the aftermath of the shooting, the popular St. Lucie County scanner page on Facebook that Davis ran distanced itself from the founder after his arrest.

When someone effects a citizen's arrest, basically, they have the same powers as a police officer would, at least temporarily," said Jason Bruin, Assistant State Attorney, 19th Judicial Circuit. cards.headline: Woman, 86, dies in Port St. Lucie crash after failing to yield at intersection
cards.body:
Marie Martin, 86, died Thursday afternoon following a two-vehicle crash at the intersection of SW Savona Boulevard and SW Lawndale Avenue in Port St. Lucie. Martin was driving a 2006 Hyundai Elantra westbound on SW Lawndale Avenue around 2:30 p.m. when she entered the intersection and failed to yield the right-of-way to oncoming traffic, according to the Port St. Lucie Police Department.

A 17-year-old male driving a 2026 Honda HR-V northbound on SW Savona Boulevard struck the driver's side of Martin's vehicle, causing a T-bone collision. Emergency responders had to extricate Martin from her vehicle before transporting her to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital with critical injuries.

Despite lifesaving efforts by medical staff, Martin later died from her injuries. The teenage driver was not injured in the crash.

The Port St. Lucie Police Department's Traffic Homicide Unit is continuing to investigate the circumstances surrounding the fatal collision.

cards.teaser: Michael Ruiz, 31, was caught on surveillance video stuffing bottles of tequila into a backpack and walking out with three cases of tequila without paying.
cards.body:
The Martin County Sheriff's Office released surveillance video that investigators say shows a Port St. Lucie man stealing thousands of dollars' worth of tequila from a local liquor store. According to deputies, Michael Ruiz, 31, was caught on camera stuffing bottles of tequila into a backpack while inside the store. The video also allegedly shows Ruiz entering a storage room, grabbing three cases of tequila and walking out without paying.

Authorities say the stolen alcohol was worth thousands of dollars. Ruiz was later arrested in neighboring St. Lucie County on unrelated charges after police said he was driving under the influence. Investigators believe Ruiz may be connected to several other recent tequila thefts reported across the area and are continuing to look into those cases.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County deputy fired for Facebook post mocking sheriff's performance standards
cards.teaser: Deputy Tina Speicker was terminated after an Internal Affairs investigation found she created a social media post that mocked Sheriff Richard Del Toro's Standards of Performance.
cards.body:
Deputy Tina Speicker was fired after an Internal Affairs investigation found she created a social media post that mocked Sheriff Richard Del Toro's Standards of Performance. According to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office Internal Affairs report, on Oct. 10, 2025, Sheriff Richard Del Toro was made aware of a Facebook post on Speicker's personal social media account featuring an image titled Standards of Power. The image closely resembled Del Toro's Standards of Performance, which was introduced after he was sworn into office.

The report says Speicker's Facebook post mirrored the Standards of Performance but replaced the original language with phrases depicting domination, manipulation and exploitation. Investigators alleged the post was intended to disparage the Sheriff's Office and Sheriff Del Toro and violated agency rules and regulations. During the investigation, Speicker acknowledged posting the graphic to her Facebook page but said it was intended as commentary on Congress and the federal government shutdown.

The report also found Speicker gave inconsistent statements during multiple interviews, leading investigators to sustain allegations of criticism of orders or policies, conduct unbecoming, violating the code of ethics for public officers and employees, and false testimony. As a result of the investigation, Speicker was terminated on June 12, 2026.

According to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office Internal Affairs report, on Oct. 10, 2025, Sheriff Richard Del Toro was made aware of a Facebook post on Deputy Tina Speicker's personal social media account featuring an image titled "Standards of Power." The report says the image closely resembled Del Toro's "Standards of Performance," which was introduced after he was sworn into office. The Standards of Performance outlined eight performance expectations for employees, agency divisions and the Sheriff's Office's core values. See also: PSL police seek missing 14-year-old girl last seen Tuesday night The report says Speicker's Facebook post mirrored the "Standards of Performance" but replaced the original language with phrases depicting domination, manipulation and exploitation. Investigators alleged the post was intended to disparage the Sheriff's Office and Sheriff Del Toro and violated agency rules and regulations. According to the Internal Affairs report, Speicker's "Standards of Power" graphic stated: Top-down domination. Keep everyone beneath you guessing who's next to take the blame. Set confusion for others to follow. The less they know, the more control you have. Display a ruthless work ethic with a focus on self-preservation. Take credit for wins, redirect the failures. Demonstrate selective respect. Favor those who serve your goals; silence those who don't. Being unfair-strategically. Tip the scales to your advantage. Remain obsessive and paranoid. Control every detail, question every motive. Be committed to manipulation and influence. Knowledge is leverage trade it like currency. You own what you exploit and sign off to survive. The Internal Affairs investigator identified several similarities between the "Standards of Power" graphic and Del Toro's "Standards of Performance," including that both contained eight principles, used similar wording and sentence structure, began each bullet point with the same first word and featured a similar two-tone outline. Investigators concluded the graphic was intended to parody the Sheriff's official standards. During the investigation, the Sheriff's Office interviewed Sheriff Del Toro, agency supervisors, other deputies and Speicker. The IA report states Speicker acknowledged posting the graphic to her Facebook page but said it was intended as commentary on Congress and the federal government shutdown. The report also found Speicker gave inconsistent statements during multiple interviews, leading investigators to sustain allegations of criticism of orders or policies, conduct unbecoming, violating the code of ethics for public officers and employees, and false testimony. As a result of the investigation, Speicker was terminated on June 12, 2026. The investigation concluded that Speicker violated Sheriff's Office policies regarding criticism of orders or policies, conduct unbecoming, the code of ethics for public officers and employees, and false testimony.

hero.headline: Postal worker arrested for stealing winning Florida Lottery ticket from mail in Miami
hero.body:
A United States Postal Service letter carrier was arrested July 23 on charges of stealing a winning Pick 4 lottery ticket from the mail and fraudulently claiming the prize. Lekaysha Lockhart, who worked as a USPS letter carrier, faces charges including grand theft, dealing in stolen property, filing a false claim for payment, two counts of unlawful use of a two-way communications device and mail theft.

The arrest followed a joint investigation by the Florida Lottery Division of Security and the United States Postal Service Office of Inspector General. A Florida Lottery player reported that a winning Pick 4 ticket she mailed never reached its intended destination. A Florida Lottery Inspector determined the ticket had been redeemed by Lockhart on June 19 at the Florida Lottery's Miami District Office.

Following her arrest, Florida Lottery Special Agents and USPS OIG investigators said Lockhart admitted to stealing the winning lottery ticket and redeeming it. Florida Lottery Secretary Reginald D. Dixon said the case reflects the agency's commitment to player protection. Dixon commended the Division of Security for their investigative work and thanked partners at the United States Postal Service Office of Inspector General and the Broward County Sheriff's Office for their collaboration.

Because the alleged offenses occurred in multiple judicial circuits, the cases will be prosecuted separately, the Florida Lottery Division of Security said. The Florida Lottery's Office of Communications released details of the arrest in a news release.

Following her arrest, Florida Lottery Special Agents and USPS OIG investigators said Lockhart admitted to stealing the winning lottery ticket and redeeming it. Florida Lottery Secretary Reginald D. Dixon said the case reflects the agency's commitment to player protection. 'Our players deserve confidence that every Lottery prize is protected through strong security measures and diligent oversight,' Dixon said in the news release. 'I commend our Division of Security for their outstanding investigative work and thank our partners at the United States Postal Service Office of Inspector General and the Broward County Sheriff's Office for their collaboration in protecting the integrity of Florida Lottery games and bringing this case to a successful resolution.' Lockhart was arrested on charges of grand theft, dealing in stolen property, filing a false claim for payment, two counts of unlawful use of a two-way communications device and mail theft. Because the alleged offenses occurred in multiple judicial circuits, the cases will be prosecuted separately, the Florida Lottery Division of Security said.

cards.headline: Woman, 86, killed in crash after failing to yield at Port St. Lucie intersection
cards.body:
An 86-year-old woman died Thursday afternoon following a two-vehicle crash at the intersection of SW Lawndale Avenue and SW Savona Boulevard in Port St. Lucie. Marie Martin was driving a 2006 Hyundai Elantra westbound on SW Lawndale Avenue around 2:30 p.m. when she entered the intersection and failed to yield the right-of-way to oncoming traffic, according to the Port St. Lucie Police Department.

A 17-year-old male driving a 2026 Honda HR-V northbound on SW Savona Boulevard struck the driver's side of Martin's vehicle, causing a T-bone collision. Emergency responders had to extricate Martin from her vehicle before transporting her to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital with critical injuries.

Despite lifesaving efforts by medical staff, Martin later died from her injuries. The teenage driver was not injured in the crash.

The Port St. Lucie Police Department's Traffic Homicide Unit is continuing to investigate the circumstances surrounding the fatal collision. Additional information will be released as the investigation progresses.

cards.headline: Charges dropped against Port St. Lucie man who held teens at gunpoint after Orbeez shooting
cards.teaser: Prosecutors dropped six felony charges against Gregory Allen Davis, 49, citing Florida's citizen's arrest law after he held three juveniles at gunpoint following an Orbeez toy gun incident.
cards.body:
Prosecutors have dropped charges against Gregory Allen Davis, 49, of Port St. Lucie in an incident June 24 when Davis ordered three juveniles out of their car at gunpoint and told them to get on the ground at the intersection of SW Morelia Lane and SW Acapulco Terrace. Minutes earlier, one of the teens had fired an Orbeez toy gun at the car that Davis and his fiancee were in.

According to Assistant State Attorney Jason Bruin of the 19th Judicial Circuit, the charges were dropped because in Florida, citizens have the right to make a citizen's arrest if they see that a felony has been committed in their presence. Bruin said that under Florida law, when someone effects a citizen's arrest, they have the same powers as a police officer would, at least temporarily. Davis was charged with three counts of false imprisonment and three counts of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon, which carry a maximum sentence of 30 years in prison if convicted.

Bruin said the prosecutor's office does not recommend that people take the law into their own hands and should call the police instead. According to Port St. Lucie Police, Jordan Gomez, 15, was charged with shooting or throwing a missile at or into an occupied vehicle. In the aftermath, the popular St. Lucie County scanner page on Facebook that Davis ran distanced itself from the founder after his arrest.

hero.headline: Martin County fire chief warns homestead exemption expansion could close stations, cut 116 firefighters
hero.body:
Martin County Fire Rescue could lose $9.5 million in its first year and $16.5 million annually by the second year if Florida voters approve a proposed homestead exemption expansion in November, Fire Chief Chad Cianciulli told county commissioners Tuesday. The revenue loss would amount to a 22% reduction from the department's current budget.

Under the scenario presented by Cianciulli, Fire Rescue could close Station 18 on Britt Road, Station 33 in Hobe Sound, and Station 23 on Kanner Highway. The department could be forced to lay off as many as 116 firefighters by the second year, equivalent to one of the department's three shifts.

The funding loss could force Martin County to eliminate specialized teams responsible for hazardous materials incidents, technical rescues and dive operations. The department could then have to request assistance from neighboring agencies in Palm Beach or St. Lucie counties, potentially increasing response times. Cianciulli pointed to the deadly Camp Mystic flooding in Texas as an example of delays that can occur when a community must rely on outside resources, noting they had to call for outside assets with a 14-hour response to start mitigating that scene.

Cianciulli responded to suggestions about reducing employee salaries by saying Martin County already has difficulty recruiting trained firefighter-paramedics because departments farther south offer better compensation. When the department did its last class with roughly 22 open positions, only about three paramedics graduated that class, with the rest being firefighter EMTs, because the compensation package for a firefighter medic that is already trained is much higher down south. Cianciulli advised residents to learn as much as possible about the proposal and its potential effects before casting their ballots in November.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County firefighter says anonymity promise broken after sharing hazing videos that led to five disciplinary actions
hero.body:
A St. Lucie County firefighter who provided videos of alleged hazing at Station 1A told an independent investigator his promised anonymity was not upheld after three firefighters were terminated and two were suspended. In a deposition conducted by investigator J.K. Keller, the firefighter said he was told sharing the videos would be anonymous and he would stay out of it. WPBF is not identifying the firefighter because he was not fired.

The videos show firefighters at Station 1A using a modified bug zapper to administer electric shocks to newer employees. The firefighter said he was shocked once while walking when someone got him in the back. He cited two reasons for sharing the videos: that the hazing sometimes went too far and that the guys were in a jam. He also mentioned a stigma that discourages firefighters from speaking up.

Despite assurances of confidentiality, the firefighter expressed frustration during the deposition. He said if it was not anonymous, he would not have done this and that he felt back-doored. He also voiced concerns about retaliation. When asked by Keller whose idea it was to engage in the hazing, the firefighter responded that he did not know and was just there. During the deposition, the firefighter identified many of the individuals in the videos as those who were disciplined.

Two of the terminated firefighters, Jordon Hutchinson and Doug Boudrias, defended their actions to WPBF on Wednesday, calling the videos comradery-building. The union president said Wednesday he has been communicating with the district chief and is working to ultimately get the terminated firefighters their jobs again while avoiding a long-term court battle.

However, local governments have warned that it could also reduce revenue used to pay for public services. During Tuesday’s Martin County Commission meeting, Fire Chief Chad Cianciulli presented a planning exercise outlining how his department could respond to the projected revenue loss. This is real," Cianciulli said. Martin County Fire Rescue projects its annual budget would decline by $9.5 million in the first year. By the second year, the annual loss would reach $16.5 million, a 22% reduction from the department’s current budget. Under the scenario, Fire Rescue could close Station 18 on Britt Road, Station 33 in Hobe Sound, and Station 23 on Kanner Highway. Cianciulli added the department could be forced to lay off as many as 116 firefighters by the second year. That is equivalent to one of the department’s three shifts. The chief also warned that the funding loss could force Martin County to eliminate specialized teams responsible for hazardous materials incidents, technical rescues and dive operations. The department could then have to request assistance from neighboring agencies in Palm Beach or St. Lucie counties, potentially increasing response times. In an interview after the meeting, Cianciulli pointed to the deadly Camp Mystic flooding in Texas as an example of the delays that can occur when a community must rely on outside resources. "They had to call for outside assets, a 14-hour response to start mitigating that scene," Cianciulli said. "We’re in a position in the county, if we have any incident here, we are able to do an immediate mitigation. We’re not wasting any second." Your neighborhood: Local coverage from WPBF 25 News During public comment, one resident and a commissioner questioned whether reducing employee salaries could help address the potential shortfall. Cianciulli responded, saying Martin County already has difficulty recruiting trained firefighter-paramedics because departments farther south offer better compensation. Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app. "When we did our last class that we had, we had roughly 22 open positions; I only had about three paramedics that actually graduated that class," Cianciulli said. "The rest were firefighter EMTs. It’s because the compensation package for a firefighter medic that is already trained is much higher down south." Cianciulli advised residents to learn as much as possible about the proposal and its potential effects before casting their ballots in November.

hero.headline: Los Angeles man sentenced to life in prison for selling fentanyl that killed Vero Beach man
hero.body:
Alfonso Guerrero, 39, of Los Angeles was sentenced to life in federal prison for selling fentanyl that caused the death of David Eller of Vero Beach. Guerrero was convicted by a federal jury in May 2026 of distributing fentanyl resulting in death.

Court evidence showed Guerrero sold a tenth of a gram of fentanyl to Eller on May 16, 2023, in a transaction captured on a doorbell camera. Eller was found dead in his Vero Beach home hours later. Two days after Eller's death, Guerrero was arrested with additional fentanyl intended for distribution.

Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers said the case demonstrates the commitment to holding drug dealers accountable. Flowers said the department will not tolerate drugs being sold in the community and praised detectives and federal partners for their investigative work.

The case was investigated by the Indian River County Sheriff's Office and the DEA Miami Field Division. The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Florida prosecuted the case.

hero.headline: 911 calls reveal desperate pleas after Port St. Lucie shooting left two dead
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie police released 911 calls from a July 19 shooting on Southeast Rivergreen Circle that killed 24-year-old Carl Loubeau and 22-year-old Juliun Stokes. Multiple callers contacted dispatchers shortly before 3:30 a.m. after hearing repeated gunshots, with one caller pleading with a wounded man to stay conscious. Breathe, baby, please, the caller said as officers rushed to the scene. Both men were found suffering from multiple gunshot wounds and later died at hospitals.

The calls show residents woke to what one initially mistook for fireworks before the violence became clear. One neighbor reported hearing about eight shots but told the dispatcher he was too frightened to look outside. Another caller estimated hearing 10 shots, followed by a brief pause and another burst. A resident watching through a home security camera reported seeing someone lying in a driveway after waking to gunshots and screaming.

The most significant call came from 20-year-old Dwayne Walker, whom investigators identified as the man who returned fire after Loubeau allegedly shot Stokes. Somebody shot my cousin, and I shot back, Walker told a dispatcher. Police Chief Leo Niemczyk said Stokes and several friends had gone bowling with Loubeau's girlfriend earlier that night. When the group returned to the home and realized they were locked out, the woman called Loubeau and asked him to bring a spare key. Police believe Loubeau became jealous when he arrived and saw his girlfriend with Stokes and Walker.

Investigators determined Walker, who was near the rear of a Ford Mustang, drew a lawfully carried handgun and acted in self-defense after Loubeau approached Stokes beside the open driver's door and opened fire. Police believe Loubeau may have mistaken Stokes for Walker, who authorities said had some type of relationship with Loubeau's girlfriend. Police said Loubeau fired eight rounds from a 9 mm handgun and one round from a .380-caliber weapon. Walker fired eight rounds from a .40-caliber handgun and will not face criminal charges. Detectives are continuing to review forensic evidence, phone records, toxicology findings and autopsy reports before formally closing the investigation. Anyone with additional information is asked to contact the Port St. Lucie Police Department at 772-871-5000.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce man jailed on child sexual battery charges spanning six years
cards.body:
Fort Pierce Police arrested James Ronald Owens, 58, of the 1600 block of Linwood Avenue on July 24 on charges of sexual battery on a child under 12, sexual battery on a victim ages 12 to 18, lewd or lascivious molestation on a victim under 12, and lewd or lascivious molestation of a victim ages 12 to 16. Owens remained in the St. Lucie County Jail on no bond as of Thursday.

The victim, now in a mental health facility, told investigators that Owens, a family friend and tutor, started touching her inappropriately as early as June 2019 and had sexual encounters with her in various locations over the years. The victim said the last contact with Owens occurred in January 2005. She told investigators Owens had pictures of her on hard drives and that she had not reported the incidents because Owens was blackmailing her and had threatened to rape and kill her. She stated Owens had nude photographs of her on his computer, on a black hard drive he usually kept inside a shed, and on a white cell phone.

Other individuals, many of them juveniles, who investigators interviewed made similar allegations against Owens from various periods of time. Owens told investigators that the girl told him she was being molested by several men but he denied being one of the men and said he never thought the girl would make accusations against him.

Owens is a registered sexual offender following a 2009 sex-related case in St. Lucie County, according to the Florida Department of Law Enforcement. Fort Pierce Police and the U.S. Marshals Service made the arrest.

hero.headline: Sanctuary at Winterlakes residents in Port St. Lucie report unanswered maintenance requests
hero.body:
Residents at Sanctuary at Winterlakes Apartments in Port St. Lucie said they have been living with unresolved maintenance issues and that their requests for help are being ignored. Alison Malio said she and her neighbors submit maintenance requests through an online portal, but she claims those requests go unanswered or get deleted and are sometimes marked complete even when no work has been done.

Malio walked through her apartment, pointing out what she believes is structural damage in her bedroom and damage she described as rot near the foundation. She also said her freezer seal was damaged and has cost her thousands of dollars in lost food. Malio said she has had to throw away over $1,500 in the last year and a half worth of meat or frozen food. Malio also showed a cockroach problem inside her apartment and building. She said pest control only comes once every 13 weeks and that she replaces adhesive traps about three times a week because they get so full. Malio said it has been six or seven years of the property management doing nothing to help and that she has cameras and a ring doorbell so she knows if maintenance comes in to look at issues.

Across the parking lot, neighbor Cheryl Jones said her air conditioning was out for nine weeks. Jones said it was too hot in her apartment to cook and that she could make breakfast with her coffee maker and the toaster but could not cook a meal. Jones said maintenance eventually fixed the air conditioning, but mold had grown inside her apartment. Jones sent a report from a company that tested her unit and found evidence of mold, recommending that drywall, insulation and other materials be removed. Jones said she sent that report to property management but has not heard anything back.

Property management sent a statement saying they are looking into the issues and that they prioritize the safety and well-being of their tenants. When asked why she does not move, Malio said she cannot afford to. Jones said the same, stating she has nowhere to go and cannot afford to go anywhere else.

cards.headline: Charges dropped against Port St. Lucie man who held teens at gunpoint after Orbeez shooting
cards.teaser: Prosecutors dropped charges against Gregory Allen Davis, 49, of Port St. Lucie who held three juveniles at gunpoint on June 24 after one of them fired an Orbeez toy gun at his vehicle.
cards.body:
A prosecutor said they dropped charges against Gregory Allen Davis, 49, of Port St. Lucie in an incident June 24 when Davis ordered three juveniles out of their car at gunpoint and told them to get on the ground at the intersection of SW Morelia Lane and SW Acapulco Terrace. Minutes earlier, one of the teens had fired an Orbeez toy gun at the car that Davis and his fiancee were in. An Orbeez toy gun shoots soft water-absorbing beads.

According to a prosecutor, the reason they dropped the charges against Davis is because in Florida, citizens have the right to make a citizen's arrest if they see that a felony has been committed in their presence. The felony that Davis saw was the teen firing a gun at his vehicle. Jason Bruin, Assistant State Attorney for the 19th Judicial Circuit, said that under Florida law, a citizen has a right to make a citizen's arrest if they observe a felony occur in their presence. Bruin said when someone effects a citizen's arrest, they have the same powers as a police officer would, at least temporarily. Bruin said if the case had gone to a jury, they would have returned a verdict of not guilty.

Davis was charged with three counts of false imprisonment and three counts of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon. Those six charges carry a maximum sentence of 30 years in prison if convicted. According to Port St. Lucie Police, Jordan Gomez, 15, was charged with shooting or throwing a missile at or into an occupied vehicle. In the aftermath of the incident, the popular St. Lucie County scanner page on Facebook that Davis ran distanced itself from the founder after his arrest.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce resort says abandoned sailboat is damaging property and costing thousands in revenue
cards.teaser: A Fort Pierce resort says an abandoned sailboat that washed ashore three weeks ago is damaging property and costing them thousands in business, but state law prevents them from moving it.
cards.body:
Dockside Marina and Resort in Fort Pierce says an abandoned sailboat that washed ashore three weeks ago near On The Edge Bar and Grill is damaging property, slamming into other boats, and costing them thousands in business. Joe Zebrowski, general manager of Dockside Marina and Resort, said the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission informed him that the boat cannot be moved. The agency is giving the owners 60 days to claim the vessel, and the resort is also prohibited from moving it.

Zebrowski and his team quickly secured the boat when it washed ashore. The FWC used a chain to secure the sailboat, but Zebrowski said it has not stopped the vessel from causing problems. Zebrowski said the sailboat has slammed into a docked boat, destroyed a piling, and forced the restaurant to block off several tables near the vessel, which has significantly impacted their revenue. Zebrowski said the blocked tables are the restaurant's prime tables and have probably cost them about 25 percent of their overall business for the past month.

According to state law, moving a boat that has washed ashore onto private property without proper permission can expose individuals to legal liabilities or even charges of theft. The FWC confirmed that no one can touch the boat except its owners.

"This is a danger to people and personal property," said Joe Zebrowski, general manager of Dockside Marina and Resort. The sailboat washed ashore near On The Edge Bar and Grill, and Zabrowski and his team quickly secured it. However, Zabrowski said the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC) informed him that the boat cannot be moved. The agency is giving the owners 60 days to claim the vessel, and the resort is also prohibited from moving it. "I did a good deed, but no deed goes unpunished," Zebrowski said. The FWC used a chain to secure the sailboat, but Zebrowski said it hasn’t stopped the vessel from causing problems. "It kept it from floating away but didn’t keep it from whipping back and forth," he said. Zebrowski explained that the sailboat has slammed into a docked boat, destroyed a piling, and forced the restaurant to block off several tables near the vessel, which has significantly impacted their revenue. "These are our prime tables. They probably cost us about 25 percent of our overall business for the past month," Zebrowski said. According to state law, moving a boat that has washed ashore onto private property without proper permission can expose individuals to legal liabilities or even charges of theft. "There needs to be a carveout in however the law takes care of situations like this that takes care of people who are innocent and stop protecting an owner who has abandoned his boat that I don’t think is registered or has insurance," Zebrowski said. The FWC confirmed to WPBF that no one can touch the boat except its owners. WPBF is working to contact the owners of the boat for comment. The FWC is working on providing a more detailed statement. cards.headline: St. Lucie County firefighter says promised anonymity was not upheld after sharing hazing videos
cards.teaser: A St. Lucie County firefighter said his promised anonymity was not upheld after he shared videos of alleged hazing that resulted in three terminations and two suspensions within the fire district.
cards.body:
A St. Lucie County firefighter said his promised anonymity was not upheld after he shared videos of alleged hazing that resulted in three terminations and two suspensions within the fire district. In a deposition conducted by independent investigator J.K. Keller, the firefighter said he was told that it would be anonymous and that he would stay out of it. The videos reportedly show firefighters at Station 1A using a modified bug zapper to administer electric shocks to newer employees.

The firefighter said he did it for two reasons. One was that the hazing goes too far sometimes, and there is a stigma so people do not want to say anything. The other thing was that the guys were in a jam. Despite assurances of confidentiality, the firefighter said if it was not anonymous, he would not have done this. He also voiced concerns about retaliation, stating he feels like he got back-doored.

During the deposition, the firefighter identified many of the individuals in the videos as those who were disciplined. Two of the terminated firefighters, Jordon Hutchinson and Doug Boudrias, defended their actions, calling the videos comradery-building. The union president said he has been communicating with the district chief and is working to ultimately get the terminated firefighters their jobs again while avoiding a long-term court battle.

hero.headline: 108 animals rescued in Martin County hoarding case, more than a dozen adopted
hero.teaser: The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast says animals continue to come in from the same hoarding case every day, with the total number of rescued dogs and cats now at 108.
hero.body:
More than a dozen animals from a Martin County hoarding case have found forever homes and the total number of rescued dogs and cats has climbed to 108. The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast says animals continue to come in from the same case. Sarah Fisher of the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast said every single day more animals are coming forth from the same case.

Fisher said the shelter needs community support to keep up with the growing number of animals in its care. Donations have been pouring in as staff perform spay and neuter surgeries, microchip animals, and clear them medically for adoption every day. The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast recommends checking their website for the most up-to-date adoption listings. Those interested in adopting can call or visit the shelter for a meet and greet.

hero.headline: Florida ranks 10th highest nationally for hourly wage needed to afford rent, study finds
hero.body:
A study released this month by the National Low Income Housing Coalition shows Florida ranks 10th highest in the nation for the hourly wage renters need to afford a two-bedroom apartment. Renters across the state must earn $37.93 per hour to afford a two-bedroom unit without spending more than 30 percent of their income on housing.

To meet this threshold, a household must earn $6,575 monthly or $78,905 annually, according to the report. In West Palm Beach-Boca Raton, the required wage is even higher at $43.35 per hour. Average rent for a two-bedroom apartment in West Palm Beach ranges from $2,426 to $2,606 per month, running about 29 percent higher than the national average.

Monroe County, which encompasses the Florida Keys, holds the highest cost for renters in the state, requiring an hourly wage of $48.15. Miami ranks second most expensive at $46.85 per hour. The study examined what workers need to earn to afford modestly priced housing across different markets.

The National Low Income Housing Coalition report stated that even workers with the nation's most common occupations struggle to afford modestly priced housing. The findings highlight the gap between typical wages and the income needed to meet basic housing costs without exceeding the 30 percent affordability standard used by housing advocates and policymakers nationwide.

hero.headline: St. Lucie Mets pitcher Conner Ware named Florida State League Pitcher of the Week
hero.body:
St. Lucie Mets pitcher Conner Ware has been named the Florida State League Pitcher of the Week for the week of July 20-26, Minor League Baseball announced. Ware made two appearances last week at Clover Park in Port St. Lucie against Fort Myers, one start on Tuesday and one relief outing on Sunday.

The southpaw combined to pitch 7.0 scoreless innings. He scattered three hits, walked two and struck out 12. The Mets won both games with Ware getting credit for the win on Sunday.

Ware, 22, was drafted by the Mets in the 15th round out of LSU in 2025. He made his professional debut with St. Lucie in April and has been with the team all season.

This is the first FSL Pitcher or Player of the Week award for the Mets this season.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie apartment residents report unanswered maintenance requests, mold at Sanctuary at Winterlakes
hero.body:
Residents at Sanctuary at Winterlakes Apartments in Port St. Lucie said they have been living with unresolved maintenance issues and that their requests for help are being ignored. Alison Malio walked through her apartment pointing out what she believes is structural damage in her bedroom and damage she described as rot near the foundation. She also said her freezer seal was damaged and has cost her over $1,500 in lost food over the last year and a half to two years. Malio also showed a cockroach problem inside her apartment and building and said pest control only comes once every 13 weeks.

Malio said she and her neighbors submit maintenance requests through an online portal, but she claims those requests go unanswered or get deleted and are sometimes marked complete even when no work has been done. Malio said she has cameras and a ring doorbell so she knows if maintenance comes to look at issues. She said it has been six or seven years of the property management doing nothing to help residents.

Across the parking lot, neighbor Cheryl Jones said her air conditioning was out for nine weeks. Jones said it was too hot in her apartment to cook and she could only make breakfast with her coffee maker and toaster. Jones said maintenance eventually fixed the air conditioning, but mold had grown inside her apartment. Jones sent a report from a company that tested her unit and found evidence of mold, recommending that drywall, insulation and other materials be removed. Jones said she sent that report to property management but has not heard anything back.

Property management sent a statement saying they are looking into the issues and that they prioritize the safety and well-being of tenants. When asked why they do not move, both Malio and Jones said they cannot afford to go anywhere else. Jones said she has nowhere to go.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce man held without bond on sexual battery charges involving child
hero.body:
Fort Pierce police arrested a 58-year-old man on charges of sexual battery and lewd or lascivious molestation involving a child over a six-year period. James Ronald Owens of the 1600 block of Linwood Avenue, Fort Pierce, was arrested July 24 and remains in the St. Lucie County Jail without bond on one count each of sexual battery on a child under 12, sexual battery on a victim ages 12 to 18, lewd or lascivious molestation on a victim under 12, and lewd or lascivious molestation of a victim ages 12 to 16.

cards.headline: Charges dropped against Port St. Lucie man who held teens at gunpoint after Orbeez shooting
cards.teaser: A prosecutor dropped six felony charges against Gregory Allen Davis, 49, citing Florida's citizen's arrest law after a teen fired an Orbeez toy gun at his vehicle.
cards.body:
Prosecutors dropped charges against a Port St. Lucie man who ordered three juveniles out of their car at gunpoint and told them to get on the ground after one of the teens fired an Orbeez toy gun at his vehicle. Gregory Allen Davis, 49, was charged with three counts of false imprisonment and three counts of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon in connection with a June 24 incident at the intersection of SW Morelia Lane and SW Acapulco Terrace. The charges carry a maximum sentence of 30 years in prison if convicted.

Assistant State Attorney Jason Bruin of the 19th Judicial Circuit said the reason prosecutors dropped the charges is because in Florida, citizens have the right to make a citizen's arrest if they see that a felony has been committed in their presence. Bruin said if the case had gone to a jury, they would have returned a verdict of not guilty. Bruin said prosecutors do not recommend that people take the law into their own hands and should instead call police. Jordan Gomez, 15, was charged with shooting or throwing a missile at or into an occupied vehicle, according to Port St. Lucie Police.

cards.headline: 911 calls reveal panic after double fatal shooting in Port St. Lucie neighborhood
cards.teaser: Newly released recordings capture residents desperately trying to save two men after gunfire erupted on Southeast Rivergreen Circle on July 19.
cards.body:
Newly released 911 calls capture desperate attempts to save two men after gunfire erupted outside a Port St. Lucie home on Southeast Rivergreen Circle, leaving one caller pleading for help as a wounded man faded in front of her. Multiple callers contacted dispatchers shortly before 3:30 a.m. July 19 after hearing repeated gunshots near Southeast Rivergreen Circle. One caller repeatedly urged one of the wounded men to remain conscious. "Breathe, baby, please," she said.

Officers responding to Southeast Rivergreen Circle found 24-year-old Carl Loubeau and 22-year-old Juliun Stokes suffering from multiple gunshot wounds. Both were taken to hospitals, where they later died. The most significant call appears to have come from 20-year-old Dwayne Walker, whom investigators identified as the man who returned fire after Loubeau allegedly shot Stokes. "Somebody shot my cousin, and I shot back," Walker told a dispatcher. Walker also repeatedly told officers that the guns had been dropped and said he did not want any trouble.

Port St. Lucie Police Chief Leo Niemczyk said Stokes and several friends had gone bowling with Loubeau's girlfriend earlier that night. When the group returned to the home and realized they were locked out, the woman called Loubeau and asked him to bring a spare key. Police believe Loubeau became jealous when he arrived and saw his girlfriend with Stokes and Walker. Investigators said Loubeau approached Stokes as he stood beside the open drivers door of a Ford Mustang and opened fire. Walker, who was near the rear of the Mustang, drew a lawfully carried handgun and returned fire, striking Loubeau. Investigators determined Walker acted in self-defense and said he will not face criminal charges. Detectives are continuing to review forensic evidence, phone records, toxicology findings and autopsy reports before formally closing the investigation.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County firefighter says promised anonymity broken after sharing hazing videos
cards.teaser: A firefighter who provided videos of alleged hazing at Station 1A says he was assured his identity would remain confidential.
cards.body:
A St. Lucie County firefighter says his promised anonymity was not upheld after he shared videos of alleged hazing that resulted in three terminations and two suspensions within the fire district. In a deposition conducted by independent investigator J.K. Keller, the firefighter explained why he decided to come forward with the videos. "I was told that it would be anonymous, and I would stay out of it," the firefighter said. The videos reportedly show firefighters at Station 1A using a modified bug zapper to administer electric shocks to newer employees.

The firefighter said he was shocked at least once. "I think it was used on me once. I was walking, and someone got me in the back," the firefighter said during the deposition. He cited two reasons for sharing the videos. "I did it for two reasons. One of them was, obviously, you watch it and goes too far sometimes. And there's a stigma here, so you dont want to say. That's pretty much what it is. And then the other thing was, the guys were in a jam." Despite assurances of confidentiality, the firefighter expressed frustration, saying, "If it wasnt anonymous, I wouldnt have done this, so you put me in a tough spot."

During the deposition, the firefighter identified many of the individuals in the videos as those who were disciplined. When asked by Keller whose idea it was to engage in the hazing, the firefighter responded, "I dont know, I was just there." Two of the terminated firefighters, Jordon Hutchinson and Doug Boudrias, defended their actions, calling the videos "comradery-building." The union president said he has been communicating with the district chief and is working to ultimately get the terminated firefighters their jobs again, while avoiding a long-term court battle.

cards.headline: Martin County commissioners face pushback on proposed changes to beach shark fishing rules
cards.body:
Martin County commissioners heard strong public opposition during Tuesday morning's meeting as residents, local surfers, and marine experts urged local leaders to keep strict limits on beachside shark fishing. The debate centers on potential language changes to local ordinances regarding land-based shark fishing, a practice where anglers deploy lines from the shore using heavy gear, kayaks, or drones to drop bait and chum into deeper waters.

During public comments, speakers warned that chumming, releasing fish parts and blood into the surf to attract sharks, endangers swimmers, surfers, and families. Local surfer Jay Noyes said he has been caught in shark fishing lines. Dottie Lanci, a member of the Hutchinson Island Preservation Initiative, strongly opposed any effort to loosen existing restrictions that ban shark baiting on lifeguard-protected beaches. Lanci called on commissioners to prioritize safety and extend the ban across all county beaches, citing an incident she witnessed outside her home where anglers used drones to drop chum in the water. She noted that other Florida municipalities, such as Miami Beach, passed local bans on land-based shark fishing earlier this year.

Safety concerns over shark activity on local beaches carry weight with many residents. In August 2017, a 3-year-old girl named Violet Veatch was bitten on the leg by a suspected bull shark while wading in shallow water at Bathtub Reef Beach in Martin County. The toddler's mother, Jessica Veatch, later pushed for stricter local beach safety regulations, believing the shark was drawn to the crowded swimming area by spearfishermen carrying bloody fish through the water.

Justin Grubich, a marine conservation expert and local surfer who moved to the area from Fort Lauderdale, urged the commission to maintain strong local restrictions. Pointing to recent research presented at statewide conservation forums, Grubich warned that regular baiting near popular beaches conditions wildlife. Commissioners did not take immediate action on the ordinance during the meeting, but requested further review of local public safety boundaries alongside state FWC regulations.

"The next morning a family of four put up their umbrellas. Two young children were playing in the water there, completely unaware of what took place the day before and that some hungry sharks might still be there," Lanci said. She also noted that other Florida municipalities, such as Miami Beach, passed local bans on land-based shark fishing earlier this year. Safety concerns over shark activity on local beaches are far from theoretical for many residents . In August 2017, a 3-year-old girl named Violet Veatch was bitten on the leg by a suspected bull shark while wading in shallow water at Bathtub Reef Beach in Martin County. The toddler's mother, Jessica Veatch, later pushed for stricter local beach safety regulations , believing the shark was drawn to the crowded swimming area by spearfishermen carrying bloody fish through the water. Justin Grubich, a marine conservation expert and local surfer who moved to the area from Fort Lauderdale, urged the commission to maintain strong local restrictions. Pointing to recent research presented at statewide conservation forums, Grubich warned that regular baiting near popular beaches conditions wildlife. "There's new scientific evidence or more accumulated scientific evidence that you can create problem sharks like problem bears," Grubich cautioned commissioners, advocating for rules that limit chumming and keep blood out of coastal waters. Commissioners did not take immediate action on the ordinance during the meeting, but requested further review of local public safety boundaries alongside state FWC regulations.

hero.headline: Florida renters need $37.93 hourly wage to afford two-bedroom apartment, study finds
hero.body:
Florida renters must earn $37.93 per hour to afford a two-bedroom apartment without spending more than 30% of their income on housing, according to a study released this month by the National Low Income Housing Coalition. The state ranks 10th highest in the nation for rental wage requirements.

The report states that households must earn $6,575 monthly or $78,905 annually to meet this threshold. In West Palm Beach-Boca Raton, the required hourly wage climbs to $43.35. Apartments.com data shows the average rent for a two-bedroom apartment in West Palm Beach ranges from $2,426 to $2,606 per month, with overall rents running about 29% higher than the national average.

Monroe County, which includes the Florida Keys, demands the highest hourly wage in the state at $48.15, followed by Miami at $46.85. The National Low Income Housing Coalition report noted that even workers in the nation's most common occupations struggle to afford modestly priced housing.

The study measures housing affordability by calculating the wage needed to keep rent and utilities at or below 30% of household income. Florida's ranking places it among states with the most expensive rental markets relative to typical wages, highlighting the financial pressure facing renters throughout the state.

hero.headline: St. Lucie Mets pitcher Conner Ware named Florida State League Pitcher of the Week
hero.body:
St. Lucie Mets pitcher Conner Ware has been named the Florida State League Pitcher of the Week for the week of July 20-26. Minor League Baseball announced the award Tuesday.

Ware made two appearances last week at Clover Park in Port St. Lucie against Fort Myers, one start on Tuesday and one relief outing on Sunday. The southpaw combined to pitch 7.0 scoreless innings. He scattered three hits, walked two and struck out 12. The Mets won both games with Ware getting credit for the win on Sunday.

Ware, 22, was drafted by the Mets in the 15th round out of LSU in 2025. He made his pro debut with St. Lucie in April and has been with the team all season.

This is the first FSL Pitcher or Player of the Week award for the Mets this season.

hero.headline: Two arrested after high-speed chase through Port St. Lucie ends with one suspect found on occupied home's roof
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie Police arrested two men on July 23 after a high-speed chase on Southwest Becker Road ended with officers finding one suspect on the roof of an occupied home. Joseph Gary Harris, 42, and Bryan Shawn Baker, 46, fled from officers who attempted to stop their white Acura after observing multiple traffic violations and signs of impaired driving.

Harris accelerated to nearly 80 mph in a 45 mph zone on Southwest Becker Road instead of pulling over. A 911 caller reported seeing the men abandon the car in a driveway on the 900 block of Southwest Idol Avenue in Port St. Lucie. Using K9 and drone teams, police located both men and took them into custody without incident.

Harris faces charges of fleeing and eluding an officer, burglary of an occupied dwelling, resisting an officer without violence, and loitering or prowling. He is being held on a $27,000 bond as of July 30. Baker was charged with resisting an officer without violence and loitering or prowling and is being held without bond as of July 30.

The burglary charge against Harris stems from his presence on the roof of the occupied home where officers found him during the search. Both men remain in the St. Lucie County Jail.

cards.headline: Charges dropped against Port St. Lucie man who held teens at gunpoint after Orbeez toy gun shooting
cards.teaser: A prosecutor dropped six charges against Gregory Allen Davis, 49, who ordered three juveniles out of their car at gunpoint in Port St. Lucie on June 24, citing Florida's citizen's arrest law.
cards.body:
The State Attorney's Office dropped charges against Gregory Allen Davis, 49, of Port St. Lucie in an incident on June 24 when Davis ordered three juveniles out of their car at gunpoint and told them to get on the ground. Minutes earlier, one of the teens had fired an Orbeez toy gun at the car Davis and his fiancee were in. An Orbeez toy gun shoots soft water-absorbing beads.

Jason Bruin, Assistant State Attorney for the 19th Judicial Circuit, said the charges were dropped because Florida law allows citizens to make arrests when they observe a felony committed in their presence. Bruin said the felony Davis observed was the teen firing a gun at his vehicle. Bruin said if the case had gone to a jury, they would have returned a verdict of not guilty.

Davis had been charged with three counts of false imprisonment and three counts of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon, carrying a maximum sentence of 30 years in prison if convicted. Port St. Lucie Police charged 15-year-old Jordan Gomez with shooting or throwing a missile at or into an occupied vehicle. In the aftermath of the shooting, the popular St. Lucie County scanner page on Facebook that Davis ran distanced itself from the founder after his arrest.

cards.headline: 911 calls capture frantic moments after Port St. Lucie shooting that killed two men
cards.teaser: Newly released 911 calls from the July 19 shooting on Southeast Rivergreen Circle in Port St. Lucie show callers pleading for help as two men lay wounded outside a home.
cards.body:
Multiple callers contacted dispatchers shortly before 3:30 a.m. on July 19 after hearing repeated gunshots near Southeast Rivergreen Circle in Port St. Lucie. The calls show residents trying to direct officers toward the shooting while remaining inside their homes as police rushed to the neighborhood. One caller repeatedly urged a wounded man to remain conscious, saying "Breathe, baby, please."

Officers responding to Southeast Rivergreen Circle found 24-year-old Carl Loubeau and 22-year-old Juliun Stokes suffering from multiple gunshot wounds. Both were taken to hospitals, where they later died. The first caller apparently mistook the gunfire for fireworks and asked police to check the area near the dog park. Within seconds, other residents began reporting gunshots, screaming and people lying outside.

Port St. Lucie Police Chief Leo Niemczyk said Stokes and several friends had gone bowling with Loubeau's girlfriend earlier that night. When the group returned to the home and realized they were locked out, the woman called Loubeau and asked him to bring a spare key. Police believe Loubeau became jealous when he arrived and saw his girlfriend with Stokes and 20-year-old Dwayne Walker. Investigators said Loubeau approached Stokes as he stood beside the open driver's door of a Ford Mustang and opened fire. Walker, who was near the rear of the Mustang, drew a lawfully carried handgun and returned fire, striking Loubeau. Investigators determined Walker acted in self-defense and said he will not face criminal charges.

Both were taken to hospitals, where they later died. The calls show how quickly the shooting unfolded. The first caller apparently mistook the gunfire for fireworks and asked police to check the area near the dog park because the noise had awakened his young daughter. One neighbor said about eight shots woke him but told the dispatcher he was too frightened to look outside. No, I don’t even want to look, he said. Police initially said an argument over a house key had escalated into a shootout between the two victims. hero.headline: Martin County fire chief warns homestead exemption expansion could close stations, cut 116 firefighters
hero.body:
Martin County Fire Chief Chad Cianciulli told county commissioners Tuesday that a proposed expansion of Florida's homestead exemption could force the closure of three fire stations and the layoff of 116 firefighters. The measure, which will go before Florida voters in November, could lower property tax bills for homeowners but also reduce revenue used to pay for public services. Martin County Fire Rescue projects its annual budget would decline by $9.5 million in the first year and $16.5 million by the second year, a 22% reduction from the department's current budget.

Under the scenario presented by Cianciulli, Fire Rescue could close Station 18 on Britt Road, Station 33 in Hobe Sound, and Station 23 on Kanner Highway. The department could be forced to lay off as many as 116 firefighters by the second year, equivalent to one of the department's three shifts. The funding loss could force Martin County to eliminate specialized teams responsible for hazardous materials incidents, technical rescues and dive operations.

The department could then have to request assistance from neighboring agencies in Palm Beach or St. Lucie counties, potentially increasing response times. Cianciulli pointed to the deadly Camp Mystic flooding in Texas as an example of the delays that can occur when a community must rely on outside resources. He said that incident required a 14-hour response to start mitigation.

During public comment, one resident and a commissioner questioned whether reducing employee salaries could help address the potential shortfall. Cianciulli responded that Martin County already has difficulty recruiting trained firefighter-paramedics because departments farther south offer better compensation. In the department's last graduating class with roughly 22 open positions, only about three paramedics graduated, with the rest being firefighter EMTs. Cianciulli advised residents to learn as much as possible about the proposal and its potential effects before casting their ballots in November.

hero.headline: Martin County fire chief warns property tax reform could force cuts to firefighters, helicopter, and fire stations
hero.body:
Martin County Fire Chief Chad Cianciulli warned commissioners Tuesday that a proposed property tax reform on the November ballot could force sweeping cuts to fire and rescue operations in Martin County. The reform would expand homestead exemptions, potentially reducing the department's budget and forcing major reductions in service.

Among the potential cuts outlined by the chief: closing firehouses, ending hazmat, dive, and technical rescue programs, grounding the department's critical care helicopter, and using firefighting tools past their operational lifetime. The department could also be forced to cut as many as 116 firefighters over the next two years. Cianciulli said the cuts would affect the department's ability to properly respond to emergencies, forcing them to call outside agencies when incidents exceed available resources.

Residents who attended the commission meeting had mixed reactions. One resident said fire service is valuable and other budget items matter less, while another questioned why cutting personnel pay was not part of the options. Commissioners also expressed differing views, with Commissioner Edward Ciampi saying the county would need to do belt tightening and slash budgets elsewhere, while Commissioner Eileen Vargas said the county only has so many dollars to go around.

No decisions were made Tuesday. The presentation was an opportunity to gather information so the county can plan accordingly ahead of the November vote.

hero.headline: Three arrested in Fort Pierce infant death from severe dehydration and malnutrition
hero.body:
St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office arrested three people in connection with the death of a 3-month-old infant in Fort Pierce, with investigators calling it one of the worst cases they have encountered in 20 years. The baby died last August while living with his grandfather Robert Maxwell and Maxwell's girlfriend Vikki Koon at a Fort Pierce home. The infant's mother, Nicole Maxwell, was residing with a boyfriend in Vero Beach at the time.

Koon told deputies she believed a newborn should have two ounces per feeding twice a day, and when she ran out of formula, she would fill the bottle with regular milk and add water. In the days before the infant's death, Koon and Robert Maxwell contacted the baby's mother and biological father via Messenger stating they needed to come to Florida because something was wrong with the baby and he had marks all over him. An autopsy revealed the infant was emaciated with a sunken abdomen and widespread lesions consistent with severe dehydration and malnutrition.

Investigators found the Fort Pierce mobile home in poor condition. The house was extremely hot with a bug infestation, lack of food, and was unsafe for walking. Deputies said there was not an entryway they could safely make entry into the home. Tasha Wright, who was with Nicole Maxwell when detectives arrived to arrest her, said Nicole Maxwell claimed she had dropped the baby off with her father and was not present during the events leading to the death.

All three suspects face aggravated manslaughter charges. St. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro urged the public to report signs of child abuse, stating that one phone call can be the difference between a child receiving help and a life being saved. Detectives said something small could potentially save children's lives and prevent tragedies like this case.

hero.headline: Martin County Fire Rescue could lose 116 firefighters, close three stations under proposed homestead exemption expansion
hero.body:
Martin County Fire Rescue projects its annual budget would decline by $9.5 million in the first year and $16.5 million in the second year, a 22% reduction from the current budget, if Florida voters approve a proposed expansion of the homestead exemption in November. Fire Chief Chad Cianciulli presented a planning exercise to county commissioners Tuesday outlining how the department could respond to the projected revenue loss, including the possible closure of Station 18 on Britt Road, Station 33 in Hobe Sound, and Station 23 on Kanner Highway.

The department could be forced to lay off as many as 116 firefighters by the second year, equivalent to one of the department's three shifts. The funding loss could force Martin County to eliminate specialized teams responsible for hazardous materials incidents, technical rescues and dive operations. The department could then have to request assistance from neighboring agencies in Palm Beach or St. Lucie counties, potentially increasing response times.

Cianciulli pointed to the deadly Camp Mystic flooding in Texas as an example of the delays that can occur when a community must rely on outside resources. They had to call for outside assets, a 14-hour response to start mitigating that scene, Cianciulli said. We are in a position in the county, if we have any incident here, we are able to do an immediate mitigation. We are not wasting any second.

During public comment, one resident and a commissioner questioned whether reducing employee salaries could help address the potential shortfall. Cianciulli responded that Martin County already has difficulty recruiting trained firefighter-paramedics because departments farther south offer better compensation. When we did our last class that we had, we had roughly 22 open positions. I only had about three paramedics that actually graduated that class, Cianciulli said. The rest were firefighter EMTs. It is because the compensation package for a firefighter medic that is already trained is much higher down south.

hero.headline: Martin County Fire Chief warns property tax reform could force closure of firehouses, cuts to 116 firefighters
hero.body:
Martin County Fire Chief Chad Cianciulli warned commissioners Tuesday that a property tax reform proposal on the November ballot could force sweeping cuts to fire and rescue operations in Martin County. The reform would expand homestead exemptions, potentially reducing the department's budget and forcing major reductions in service.

Potential cuts outlined by Cianciulli include closing firehouses, ending hazmat, dive, and technical rescue programs, grounding the department's critical care helicopter, and using firefighting tools past their operational lifetime. The department could also be forced to cut as many as 116 firefighters over the next two years. Cianciulli said the loss of firefighters would harm the organization and the community, and force the department to call outside agencies when incidents exceed their reduced capabilities.

Residents who attended the commission meeting had mixed reactions. One resident called fire service valuable, while another questioned why cutting personnel pay was not among the options. Commissioners also expressed differing views on how to respond if the reform passes. Commissioner Edward Ciampi said the county would do more belt tightening and slashing of budgets elsewhere. Commissioner Eileen Vargas said the county has only so many dollars to go around and needs to tighten up.

No decisions were made Tuesday. The presentation was an opportunity to gather information so the county can plan accordingly ahead of the November vote.

hero.headline: 108 animals rescued in Martin County hoarding case, more than a dozen adopted
hero.teaser: More than a dozen animals from a Martin County hoarding case have found forever homes and the total number of rescued dogs and cats has climbed to 108.
hero.body:

Sarah Fisher of the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast said the shelter needs community support to keep up with the growing number of animals in its care. Donations have been pouring in as staff perform spay and neuter surgeries, microchip animals, and clear them medically for adoption every day.

The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast recommends checking their website for the most up-to-date adoption listings. Those interested in adopting can call or visit the shelter for a meet and greet.

cards.headline: Martin County Fire Chief warns homestead exemption expansion could cut $16.5 million from Fire Rescue budget
cards.body:
Martin County Fire Chief Chad Cianciulli told commissioners Tuesday that a proposed expansion of Florida's homestead exemption could cut $9.5 million from Fire Rescue's annual budget in the first year and $16.5 million by the second year, a 22 percent reduction from the department's current budget. The measure goes before Florida voters in November and could lower property tax bills for homeowners, but local governments have warned it could reduce revenue for public services.

Under the scenario presented at Tuesday's Martin County Commission meeting, Fire Rescue could close Station 18 on Britt Road, Station 33 in Hobe Sound, and Station 23 on Kanner Highway. The department could be forced to lay off as many as 116 firefighters by the second year, equivalent to one of the department's three shifts. The funding loss could also force Martin County to eliminate specialized teams responsible for hazardous materials incidents, technical rescues and dive operations.

Cianciulli said the department could then have to request assistance from neighboring agencies in Palm Beach or St. Lucie counties, potentially increasing response times. He pointed to the deadly Camp Mystic flooding in Texas as an example of delays that can occur when a community must rely on outside resources. Cianciulli said those responders faced a 14-hour response time to start addressing that scene.

One resident and a commissioner questioned whether reducing employee salaries could help address the potential shortfall. Cianciulli responded that Martin County already has difficulty recruiting trained firefighter-paramedics because departments farther south offer better compensation. When the department's last class graduated, only about three paramedics completed training out of 22 open positions, with the rest being firefighter EMTs. Cianciulli advised residents to learn as much as possible about the proposal and its potential effects before casting their ballots in November.

cards.headline: Martin County Fire Rescue could lose 116 firefighters under proposed homestead exemption
cards.teaser: Martin County commissioners heard a presentation Tuesday on how a proposed expansion of Florida's homestead exemption could affect Fire Rescue operations.
cards.body:
Martin County Fire Rescue projects it could lose 116 firefighters over the next two years, about one-third of its workforce, because of reduced property tax revenue tied to a proposed constitutional amendment on the November ballot. Martin County Commissioner James Blake Capps said the county has been accustomed to the very best in fire rescue services and he would hate to see the level of service suffer greatly.

Fire Rescue leaders discussed potential operational changes if revenue reductions occur. Previous county projections have outlined possible station closures, reductions to specialized teams including HAZMAT, Technical Rescue, the dive team and LifeStar, and delays in replacing equipment. County leaders have said the department has few options to absorb the projected revenue loss because about 93 percent of the Fire Rescue budget is dedicated to personnel.

Capps said a no-overtime policy for all fire rescue personnel would mean no backfilling of stations, which would result in randomized brownouts of stations. He also warned that higher insurance premiums could result if fire stations close, because residents within five miles of a fire station receive a break on homeowner's insurance while those farther away pay higher premiums. No vote on firefighter layoffs or fire station closures was expected during Tuesday's meeting.
cards.article_text: Martin County commissioners are expected to hear a presentation Tuesday outlining how a proposed expansion of Florida’s homestead exemption could affect Martin County Fire Rescue if voters approve the constitutional amendment on the November ballot. The presentation is expected to focus on the projected financial impact of the proposed tax changes and what they could mean for the department’s budget, staffing, operations and emergency response. See the presentation in the gallery above. "As a public servant, I will be glad to honor the will of the voters, whatever they decide regarding the proposed constitutional amendment. But, we do have some concerns about the depth of the cuts that would be needed as they relate to a number of areas of government operations, particularly fire rescue," said Martin County Commissioner James Blake Capps, District 3. According to county documents, Martin County Fire Rescue projects it could lose 116 firefighters over the next two years about one-third of its workforce because of reduced property tax revenue tied to the proposed amendment. "We in Martin County have been used to the very best in fire rescue services, and I would hate to see our level of service suffer greatly. It seems to me that we would be in for that if this constitutional amendment were to pass," said Capps. Fire Rescue leaders are also expected to discuss potential operational changes if those revenue reductions occur. Previous county projections have outlined possible station closures, reductions to specialized teams including HAZMAT, Technical Rescue, the dive team and LifeStar, and delays in replacing equipment. County leaders have previously said the department has few options to absorb the projected revenue loss because about 93% of the Fire Rescue budget is dedicated to personnel. Officials have also warned the proposed cuts could lead to longer emergency response times and affect specialized emergency services provided throughout Martin County. "There would also have to be a no-overtime policy for all of our fire rescue personnel. That doesn't sound so bad initially, but when you think about the consequences, it means no backfilling of stations with personnel, which would result in randomized brownouts of stations," said Capps. Tuesday’s discussion comes as commissioners consider several other agenda items, including final solid waste assessment rates, proposed changes to fishing rules on county-owned property, development proposals, and conservation land purchases. "Another serious consequence for Martin County residents would be higher insurance premiums. If you're within five miles of a fire station, you receive a break on your homeowner's insurance. But if you're farther than five miles away, you pay higher premiums. If we shut down three fire stations, a lot of people would end up paying more for homeowner's insurance. There would also be consequences for our level of service and our comprehensive plan," said Capps. No vote on firefighter layoffs or fire station closures is expected during Tuesday’s meeting. Instead, commissioners will receive the presentation as they continue evaluating the potential local impacts of the proposed homestead exemption expansion. "I think it could be rather severe. When you think about three fire stations disappearing, response times for the people living near those stations would increase, which could have very serious consequences for residents," said Capps. Voters will have the final say on the constitutional amendment during the November general election. The meeting starts at 9 a.m. CBS12 News will have a team inside. This is a developing story, check back for updates.
