hero.headline: Three arrested in Fort Pierce baby death case after year-long investigation reveals severe neglect
hero.body:
Three people have been arrested and charged with aggravated manslaughter and child abuse in connection with the death of a three-month-old boy in Fort Pierce last August. The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office announced charges against Nicole Maxwell, the infant's mother, her father Robert Maxwell, and his girlfriend Vikki Koon after an investigation revealed the baby died from dehydration and malnutrition. The medical examiner ruled the death a homicide.

Detectives described finding horrific conditions inside the mobile home where the child lived. Detective Jennifer Diaz said the house was extremely hot with a bug infestation, lack of food, and unsafe walking conditions. Investigators found holes in the floor covered with plywood. A neighbor named Suzan who lives across the street said she had given food and drinks to two of the boys from the home because they appeared hungry and starving. She said she had been inside the mobile home and found it unlivable.

The investigation took nearly a year because of its complexity, requiring outside medical expertise and months of additional testing. Detective Diaz said the medical examiner had to seek outside experts to examine the child, and those results took several weeks to months. On August 20, 2025, the baby was rushed to the hospital after the grandfather messaged the mother saying the child was sick, but it was too late. The autopsy revealed the infant was emaciated with a sunken abdomen and widespread lesions consistent with severe dehydration and malnutrition.

Four other children of Nicole Maxwell also needed medical attention at the time and are now in foster care. Sheriff Richard Del Toro said child protective services had previously been called to the home. He urged the public to report any suspected child abuse or neglect, saying one phone call can be the difference between a child receiving help and a life being saved. The sheriff's office said families facing difficult circumstances have resources and assistance available.
hero.article_text: Lucie County Sheriff’s Office is sharing new details about the investigation into the death of a three-month-old boy in Fort Pierce, including why it took nearly a year to make arrests and the conditions investigators say they found inside the mobile home where the child lived. The infant’s mother, Nicole Maxwell, her father Robert Maxwell, and his girlfriend Vikki Koon were arrested and charged with aggravated manslaughter and child abuse. Investigators say the baby died from dehydration and malnutrition last August, and the medical examiner later ruled the death a homicide. Detectives say the case was complex, requiring outside expertise and months of additional testing before they could move forward with charges. "It takes an extended amount of resources, and due to the medical examiner, who did great job in this investigation, they had to seek out outside experts to provide an examination for the child and based on results, they could take several weeks even months," said Detective Jennifer Diaz with the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office. See also: ICE-held Lake Worth bakery owner faces up to 10 years in prison on illegal reentry charge A neighbor, Suzan, who lives across the street from the home, says she had concerns about the children’s living conditions and believes the arrests are long overdue. "It was just a blessing in disguise because now I know the kids are safe," she said. "I'm going to keep them in prayer." Suzan said two of the boys would knock on her door and she would give them food and something to drink. The kids were so hungry and starving. The child, clothes didn't ever get changed," Suzan said. I love children." Suzan said sheets of plywood covered holes in the mobile home's floor. "I've been inside the house and it was unlivable," she said. "The boards that's out there now, are the boards that was on the floor." Detective Jennifer Diaz was one of the investigators who worked on the case. She described the horrific conditions inside the mobile home. "The house was extremely hot," she said. "There was a bug infestation in the home, lack of food in the home, and the home was unsafe for walking." Investigators said on Aug. 20, 2025, the three-month old was rushed to the hospital after the boy's grandfather messaged the mother saying the child was sick but it was too late. "This was one that I think was very hard," Diaz said. "The way the child ended one of their last days of life was probably the saddest for me." Investigators say Maxwell’s four other children also needed medical attention at the time and are now in foster care. The sheriff’s office says child protective services had previously been called to the home and is reminding the public to report any suspected child abuse or neglect. Sheriff Richard Del Toro sent a statement following the arrests that reads in part: While justice is essential, our shared responsibility must be preventing these tragedies before they occur. Protecting children is not solely the responsibility of law enforcement or the child welfare system. It is a responsibility we all share. If you see signs that a child may be neglected, abused, or living in unsafe conditions, do not assume someone else will intervene. One phone call can be the difference between a child receiving the help they need and a life being saved. This case also reminds us that families facing difficult circumstances are not alone. Resources, support, and assistance are available. My commitment remains unwavering: to seek justice for victims, hold offenders accountable, and work alongside our community to protect our most vulnerable. By recognizing the warning signs, speaking up, and connecting families with the help they need, we can work together to prevent tragedies like this from happening again.

hero.teaser: A neighbor who lived on Silverstream Circle in Fort Pierce for more than a decade said the community worried about how the 3-month-old was being treated but never thought it was that bad.
hero.body:
Tee McMillan, who lived near the Maxwell home on Silverstream Circle in Fort Pierce for more than a decade, said the death of the infant boy is heartbreaking and haunts her. McMillan said when that baby boy died it was just the worst of the worst. She said everyone in the neighborhood worried about how the child was treated but never knew it was that bad.

McMillan said the community never thought that a baby boy would die. She said all anyone wants is justice for the baby. Deputies, detectives and crime scene investigators responded to Lawnwood Regional Medical Center after the child was brought to the emergency room by the child's grandparents and medical personnel advised responding deputies that the child had been pronounced deceased and exhibited injuries and conditions consistent with possible neglect.
hero.article_text: A 27-year-old Fort Pierce woman is now charged with killing her own 3-month-old child. https://www.facebook.com/stluciesheriff/posts/pfbid02vUPd5tQjx8AeP3auG9GcEcqfarpDFc4qhM4Af8AJHhWsCzjTopGC7kEkFoe5qq9il The arrests come nearly a year after the unnamed boy was rushed to the hospital on Aug. The boy's mother, Nicole Maxwell, his grandfather, Robert Maxwell, 61, and the grandfather's girlfriend, Vikki Koon, 38, are facing felony charges in connection with the child's death. Nicole Maxwell was arrested in Indian River County and is in the jail there. Robert Maxwell and Koon are in the St. "It's heartbreaking, and it haunts me," said Tee McMillan, a neighbor who lived near the Maxwells' home of Silverstream Circle for more than a decade. "When that baby boy died — I'm trying real hard not to cry — because that was just the worst of the worst," McMillan said. Deputies, detectives and crime scene investigators responded to Lawnwood Regional Medical Center after a child was brought to the emergency room by the child's grandparents. Medical personnel advised responding deputies that the child had been pronounced deceased and exhibited injuries and conditions consistent with possible neglect. The child's name hasn't been released. Investigators went to the boy’s home on Silverstream Circle in Fort Pierce and searched inside and outside the home. Detectives said the medical examiner determined the child died from malnutrition and dehydration, meaning he was not given enough food or water. McMillan said everyone in the neighborhood worried about how the child was treated but never knew it was that bad. "We never thought that a baby boy would die. We never, never thought that," McMillan said. All three suspects are officially charged with aggravated manslaughter of a child and aggravated child abuse. "Let's just get justice for this baby. That's all any of us want: justice for this baby," McMillan said. The bond for all three suspects was set at $1.5 million. Jennifer Diaz led the investigation. "The death of a child is a tragedy that affects our entire community,” Sheriff Richard Del Toro said in a post on Facebook. “I commend Detective Corporal Diaz for her leadership and thank the detectives, crime scene investigators, professional support staff, the Medical Examiner’s Office, and our State Attorneys, whose commitment and teamwork led to these arrests. Our responsibility is to pursue the truth, protect those who cannot protect themselves, and hold those responsible accountable." cards.headline: St. Lucie County firefighter says anonymity not upheld after sharing hazing videos
cards.teaser: A St. Lucie County firefighter who provided videos of alleged hazing at Station 1A said he was promised anonymity but that assurance was not upheld.
cards.body:
A St. Lucie County firefighter said his promised anonymity was not upheld after he shared videos of alleged hazing that resulted in three terminations and two suspensions within the fire district. In a deposition conducted by independent investigator J.K. Keller, the firefighter explained he was told it would be anonymous and he would stay out of it. The videos reportedly show firefighters at Station 1A using a modified bug zapper to administer electric shocks to newer employees.

The firefighter said he was shocked once while walking when someone got him in the back. He cited two reasons for sharing the videos, saying he did it because the activity sometimes went too far and there is a stigma about speaking up, and also because the guys were in a jam. Despite assurances of confidentiality, the firefighter expressed frustration, saying if it wasn't anonymous he wouldn't have done it and that he was put in a tough spot. He also voiced concerns about retaliation, stating he felt like he got back-doored.

Two of the terminated firefighters, Jordon Hutchinson and Doug Boudrias, defended their actions, calling the videos comradery-building. The union president said he has been communicating with the district chief and is working to ultimately get the terminated firefighters their jobs again while avoiding a long-term court battle.

The videos reportedly show firefighters at Station 1A using a modified bug zapper to administer electric shocks to newer employees. "I think it was used on me once. Despite assurances of confidentiality, the firefighter expressed frustration, saying, "If it wasn’t anonymous, I wouldn’t have done this, so you put me in a tough spot." He also voiced concerns about retaliation, stating, "I feel like I got back-doored here." During the deposition, the firefighter identified many of the individuals in the videos as those who were disciplined. When asked by Keller whose idea it was to engage in the hazing, the firefighter responded, "I don’t know, I was just there." cards.headline: Three arrested in Fort Pierce infant death from severe dehydration and malnutrition
cards.body:
Three people were arrested in connection with the death of a 3-month-old boy in Fort Pierce in August 2025, after an autopsy revealed the infant died from severe dehydration and malnutrition. Nicole Maxwell, 27, the baby's mother, along with his grandfather Robert Maxwell, 61, and the grandfather's girlfriend Vikki Koon, 38, all face charges of aggravated manslaughter of a child and aggravated child abuse. The infant had been living with Robert Maxwell and Koon at a home on Silverstream Circle in Fort Pierce while Nicole Maxwell lived with a boyfriend in Vero Beach.

The investigation began when St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office detectives were called to Lawnwood Regional Medical Center after the baby was brought to the emergency room by his grandparents and pronounced dead. According to an arrest affidavit, Koon told deputies she believed a newborn should have two ounces per feeding twice a day, and when she ran out of formula, she would fill the bottle with regular milk and add water. hero.headline: Martin County School District cuts 3 bus routes, saving $255,000
hero.teaser: The Martin County School District has approved a consolidation of bus routes that officials say will save $255,000 without affecting students or eliminating any driver positions.
hero.body:
The Martin County School District has approved a consolidation of bus routes that officials say will save $255,000 without affecting students or eliminating any driver positions. The school board voted Tuesday unanimously to reduce the number of bus routes by 3, bringing the total from 58 to 55 ahead of the upcoming school year. District officials say all bus stops will remain the same and students will not be impacted by the change. Superintendent Michael Maine said the district now has 55 routes and roughly 56 drivers, so all routes are covered.

The $255,000 in savings reflects a reduced transportation budget and will not be redirected to a specific expense, according to the school district. Transportation Director Ruth Spires confirmed that no drivers were let go as part of the consolidation. She said the routes that were consolidated were already being covered by existing drivers due to a shortage last year. Drivers will be paid for any additional hours they work as a result of the consolidation, Spires explained.

Michael Skinner, the President of the local AFSCME labor union chapter, voiced concerns during public comment on behalf of the bus drivers, saying their feedback indicated buses are always full and cutting routes is not a good idea. Spires pushed back on that concern, noting that the buses hold a maximum of 77 passengers and are not operating at capacity. The district said it is confident it will maintain the same level of service with fewer buses on the road.

cards.headline: Martin County Fire Chief warns homestead exemption expansion could force station closures, firefighter layoffs
cards.body:
Martin County Fire Chief Chad Cianciulli warned Tuesday that a proposed expansion of Florida's homestead exemption could reduce Fire Rescue funding by $9.5 million in the first year and $16.5 million annually by the second year, potentially forcing the closure of three fire stations and the layoff of 116 firefighters. The measure, which will go before Florida voters in November, could lower property tax bills for homeowners but also reduce revenue used to pay for public services. During Tuesday's Martin County Commission meeting, Cianciulli presented a planning exercise outlining how his department could respond to the projected revenue loss.

Under the scenario, Fire Rescue could close Station 18 on Britt Road, Station 33 in Hobe Sound, and Station 23 on Kanner Highway. The $16.5 million annual loss by the second year represents a 22 percent reduction from the department's current budget. The chief said the department could be forced to lay off as many as 116 firefighters by the second year, equivalent to one of the department's three shifts.

Cianciulli warned the funding loss could force Martin County to eliminate specialized teams responsible for hazardous materials incidents, technical rescues and dive operations. The department could then have to request assistance from neighboring agencies in Palm Beach or St. Lucie counties, potentially increasing response times. In an interview after the meeting, Cianciulli pointed to the deadly Camp Mystic flooding in Texas as an example of the delays that can occur when a community must rely on outside resources. He said Martin County already has difficulty recruiting trained firefighter-paramedics because departments farther south offer better compensation.

County leaders have previously said the department has few options to absorb the projected revenue loss because about 93 percent of the Fire Rescue budget is dedicated to personnel. Martin County Commissioner James Blake Capps said higher insurance premiums could result from station closures, as residents living more than five miles from a fire station pay higher homeowner's insurance. Cianciulli advised residents to learn as much as possible about the proposal and its potential effects before casting their ballots in November.

hero.headline: Florida judge considers challenge to Amendment 3 ballot language on property taxes
hero.body:
A Leon County circuit judge heard arguments Wednesday over whether the ballot title and summary for Amendment 3, a November property-tax measure, fairly explains the proposal or amounts to political advocacy. The amendment would increase the non-school homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028 for people who establish permanent Florida residency by Dec. 31, reduce the annual assessment-growth cap on non-homestead property from 10% to 5%, and require local governments to spend remaining property-tax revenue on public needs such as public safety, schools, infrastructure and natural resources.

Leon County Circuit Judge David Frank heard arguments in three consolidated lawsuits challenging the title and summary scheduled to appear on November ballots. The challengers include the nonprofit Save Our Voters From Misleading Ballot Language, several former mayors, former Republican state Sen. Jeff Brandes and former Democratic U.S. Rep. Al Lawson Jr. They argue the amendment's title, 'Save Our Homes From Excessive Property Taxes,' and phrases promising to benefit taxpayers, protect small businesses, preserve core services and ensure fairness are biased, inaccurate and designed to persuade voters. Plaintiffs' attorney Jamie Cole told the court the language crosses a line and called it the worst example of a biased ballot question he has seen. Frank did not immediately rule, instead ordering attorneys to submit proposed decisions by 5 p.m. Monday.

Attorneys representing the attorney general, secretary of state and Department of State urged Frank to uphold the language. State attorney Ben Gibson argued the title and summary must be read together and that Florida law requires them to explain only the amendment's chief purpose, not every possible consequence or implementation detail. The challengers must prove the title and summary are clearly and conclusively defective, not merely that different wording could have been better, Gibson said. The Legislature approved the proposal during a June special session, passing it 75-26 in the House and 30-9 in the Senate. Because it is a proposed constitutional amendment, it was not subject to the governor's signature or veto. It needs support from at least 60% of voters in November.

A July analysis by Florida's Revenue Estimating Conference projected the quantifiable portions of the amendment would reduce local property-tax collections by nearly $4.93 billion in the 2027-28 fiscal year. The modeled recurring impact is approximately $11.83 billion annually. Election officials told the court that county supervisors may begin printing ballots Aug. 27, adding urgency to the case and any appeal. If Frank finds all of the ballot statements defective and appeals are declined or exhausted, Florida law gives Attorney General James Uthmeier 10 days to submit corrected wording.

Frank did not immediately rule, instead ordering attorneys to submit proposed decisions by 5 p.m. Monday.WATCH WPTV'S COVERAGE BELOW:The challengers include the nonprofit Save Our Voters From Misleading Ballot Language, several former mayors, former Republican state Sen. Jeff Brandes and former Democratic U.S. Al Lawson Jr.They argue the amendment's title — "Save Our Homes From Excessive Property Taxes" — and phrases promising to benefit taxpayers, protect small businesses, preserve core services and ensure fairness are biased, inaccurate and designed to persuade voters.Plaintiffs' attorney Jamie Cole told the court the language crosses a line."This is probably the worst example of a biased ballot question and an inaccurate ballot question that we've seen," Cole said. "This is really just a political campaign flyer."Cole argued that "save" is an emotionally loaded word suggesting homeowners face an immediate threat. He pointed to a previous Florida Supreme Court decision rejecting a proposed amendment titled "Save Our Everglades" and noted that the state's existing Save Our Homes assessment cap was originally presented to voters in 1992 under the more neutral title "Homestead Valuation Limitation."The current Amendment 3 proposal would not change that 3% Save Our Homes assessment cap for homesteaded properties.Brandes, speaking outside the courtroom, said the language gives voters the benefits without fully explaining the potential costs or consequences."They've rolled a live grenade into the Constitution here with this amendment, and people need to be very cognizant of what's going on," Brandes said.The official ballot summary says the amendment would ensure funding for core services by requiring local governments to spend remaining property-tax revenue on public needs such as public safety, schools, infrastructure and natural resources.Plaintiffs argued that restricting how remaining revenue may be spent does not guarantee that enough money will remain to fund those services.They also challenged the promise of protecting small businesses. The amendment would reduce the annual assessment-growth cap on non-homestead property from 10% to 5%, but that change would apply broadly to commercial property, rental homes and second homes — not specifically to small businesses.Another dispute centers on language promising a "schedule for full elimination" of non-school homestead property taxes. The amendment's full text instead directs lawmakers to create a uniform procedure allowing counties and municipalities to increase the exemption up to a home's remaining assessed value. A state fiscal analysis notes that the proposal sets no timeline for those future increases.Plaintiffs also argue the summary fails to explain a potentially significant shift in control over local property-tax revenue. The amendment would add categories describing how cities and counties may spend those dollars while allowing the Legislature to prohibit some expenditures through state law.At one point, Frank questioned whether disagreement among the plaintiffs about the effect of that provision supported their broader argument that the measure is unclear."If the lawyers for both these groups can't figure out what it is, doesn't that sort of support that argument?" Frank said.Attorneys representing the attorney general, secretary of state and Department of State urged Frank to uphold the language.State attorney Ben Gibson argued the title and summary must be read together and that Florida law requires them to explain only the amendment's chief purpose — not every possible consequence or implementation detail."The summary is supposed to be written for voters, not for lawyers," Gibson said.Gibson argued the title identifies what homes would supposedly be saved from — excessive property taxes — and therefore does not leave voters to imagine an undefined threat. He also said the summary makes clear that only "remaining" property-tax revenue would be reserved for core services, rather than guaranteeing a particular amount of funding.The state further argued that small businesses would benefit from the lower non-homestead assessment cap even if other property owners receive the same protection.Ultimately, Gibson said, the challengers must prove the title and summary are "clearly and conclusively defective," not merely that different wording could have been better.The Legislature approved the proposal during a June special session, passing it 75-26 in the House and 30-9 in the Senate. Because it is a proposed constitutional amendment, it was not subject to the governor's signature or veto. It needs support from at least 60% of voters in November.For people who establish permanent Florida residency by Dec. 31, the proposal would increase the non-school homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. It would be adjusted for inflation beginning in 2029.People establishing residency after that cutoff would receive a smaller exemption for 4 years before becoming eligible for the larger amount in the fifth year. School district property taxes would remain unaffected.The amendment would also reduce the assessment-growth cap on non-homestead property from 10% to 5%.A July analysis by Florida's Revenue Estimating Conference projected the quantifiable portions of the amendment would reduce local property-tax collections by nearly $4.93 billion in the 2027-28 fiscal year. The modeled recurring impact is approximately $11.83 billion annually, although the estimate does not account for future policy changes by local governments or referendums authorized by the amendment.Election officials told the court that county supervisors may begin printing ballots Aug. 27, adding urgency to the case and any appeal.If Frank upholds the current language, it would remain on the ballot unless an appellate court intervenes. If he finds all of the ballot statements defective and appeals are declined or exhausted, Florida law gives Attorney General James Uthmeier 10 days to submit corrected wording.Any rewritten title or summary could also face another expedited challenge before the same court.

hero.headline: Martin County could cut 116 firefighters, close stations under property tax reform on November ballot
hero.body:
Martin County Fire Chief Chad Cianciulli warned commissioners Tuesday that proposed property tax reform on the November ballot could force the department to cut as many as 116 firefighters over the next two years and close firehouses across the county. The reform would expand homestead exemptions, potentially reducing the department's budget and forcing major reductions in service.

Among the potential cuts outlined by Cianciulli are closing firehouses, ending hazmat, dive, and technical rescue programs, grounding the department's critical care helicopter, and using firefighting tools past their operational lifetime. The chief said the department would have to call outside agencies when incidents exceed the capabilities of remaining crews and equipment.

Residents who attended the commission meeting expressed mixed reactions. One resident called fire service valuable, while another questioned why cutting personnel pay was not considered as an option. Commissioners also expressed differing views, with Commissioner Edward Ciampi suggesting belt tightening and slashing budgets elsewhere, while Commissioner Eileen Vargas said the county only has so many dollars to go around.

No decisions were made Tuesday. The presentation was an opportunity to gather information so the county can plan accordingly ahead of the November vote.

hero.headline: Martin County Fire Rescue could lose 116 firefighters if property tax amendment passes
hero.body:
Martin County commissioners heard a presentation Tuesday outlining how a proposed expansion of Florida's homestead exemption could force Martin County Fire Rescue to cut 116 firefighters over the next two years if voters approve the constitutional amendment in November. The cuts would eliminate about one-third of the department's workforce because of reduced property tax revenue tied to the proposed amendment.

Fire Rescue leaders discussed potential operational changes if those revenue reductions occur. Previous county projections have outlined possible station closures, reductions to specialized teams including HAZMAT, Technical Rescue, the dive team and LifeStar, and delays in replacing equipment. County leaders have previously said the department has few options to absorb the projected revenue loss because about 93 percent of the Fire Rescue budget is dedicated to personnel.

Martin County Commissioner James Blake Capps said the cuts could lead to serious consequences for residents. Officials have warned the proposed cuts could lead to longer emergency response times and affect specialized emergency services provided throughout Martin County. Capps said a no-overtime policy for all fire rescue personnel would result in randomized brownouts of stations. He also said higher homeowners insurance premiums would affect residents if stations shut down, since people living within five miles of a fire station receive a break on their insurance.

No vote on firefighter layoffs or fire station closures occurred during Tuesday's meeting. Commissioners received the presentation as they continue evaluating the potential local impacts of the proposed homestead exemption expansion. Voters will have the final say on the constitutional amendment during the November general election.

But, we do have some concerns about the depth of the cuts that would be needed as they relate to a number of areas of government operations, particularly fire rescue," said Martin County Commissioner James Blake Capps, District 3. According to county documents, Martin County Fire Rescue projects it could lose 116 firefighters over the next two years about one-third of its workforce because of reduced property tax revenue tied to the proposed amendment. "We in Martin County have been used to the very best in fire rescue services, and I would hate to see our level of service suffer greatly. It seems to me that we would be in for that if this constitutional amendment were to pass," said Capps. hero.headline: Three arrested in death of 3-month-old from severe dehydration and malnutrition in Fort Pierce home
hero.body:
St. Lucie County authorities have arrested three people in connection with the death of a 3-month-old infant in Fort Pierce, describing the case as one of the worst they have encountered. The baby had been living with his grandfather, Robert Maxwell, and Robert Maxwell's girlfriend, Vikki Koon, in a Fort Pierce mobile home while his mother, Nicole Maxwell, resided with a boyfriend in Vero Beach. An autopsy revealed the infant was emaciated and had a sunken abdomen and widespread lesions consistent with severe dehydration and malnutrition.

According to an arrest affidavit, Koon told deputies she believed a newborn should have two ounces per feeding twice a day. She said when she ran out of formula, she would fill the bottle with regular milk and add water. In the days leading up to the infant's death, Koon and Robert Maxwell contacted the baby's mother and biological father, who lives out of state, via Messenger, stating, "I need you to come to Florida, something's going on with the baby. I don't know what's going on but he has marks all over him."

Investigators found the mobile home in poor condition. "The house was extremely hot. There was a bug infestation in the home, lack of food in the home and the home was unsafe for walking. There wasn't an entryway that we could safely make entry into the home," said St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office investigator Diaz. A St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office investigator said, "Based on what I observed in my 20 years of law enforcement, this is one of the worst cases I have ever worked."

All three suspects are facing several charges, including aggravated manslaughter. St. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro released a statement saying, "The loss of a child is heartbreaking. Cases like this weigh heavily on everyone involved, from our investigators and first responders to the members of our community who mourn the death of a vulnerable child." Del Toro urged the public to report signs of child abuse, stating, "If you see signs that a child may be neglected, abused, or living in unsafe conditions, do not assume someone else will intervene. One phone call can be the difference between a child receiving the help they need and a life being saved."

cards.headline: St. Lucie County firefighter says promised anonymity not upheld after sharing hazing videos
cards.teaser: A St. Lucie County firefighter says his promised anonymity was not upheld after he shared videos of alleged hazing that resulted in three terminations and two suspensions within the fire district.
cards.body:
A St. Lucie County firefighter says his promised anonymity was not upheld after he shared videos of alleged hazing that resulted in three terminations and two suspensions within the fire district. In a deposition conducted by independent investigator J.K. Keller, the firefighter explained why he decided to come forward with the videos. "I was told that it would be anonymous, and I would stay out of it," the firefighter said. The videos reportedly show firefighters at Station 1A using a modified bug zapper to administer electric shocks to newer employees.

The firefighter cited two reasons for sharing the videos. "I did it for two reasons. One of them was, obviously, you watch it and goes too far sometimes. And there's a stigma here, so you dont want to say. Thats pretty much what it is. And then the other thing was, the guys were in a jam," the firefighter said during the deposition. Despite assurances of confidentiality, the firefighter expressed frustration, saying, "If it wasnt anonymous, I wouldnt have done this, so you put me in a tough spot." He also voiced concerns about retaliation, stating, "I feel like I got back-doored here."

Two of the terminated firefighters, Jordon Hutchinson and Doug Boudrias, defended their actions, calling the videos "comradery-building." The union president said he has been communicating with the district chief and is working to ultimately get the terminated firefighters their jobs again, while avoiding a long-term court battle.

cards.headline: Martin County Fire Chief warns homestead exemption could force station closures, 116 firefighter layoffs
cards.body:
Martin County Fire Rescue could lose $9.5 million in the first year and $16.5 million annually by the second year if voters approve a proposed expansion of Florida's homestead exemption in November, Fire Chief Chad Cianciulli told county commissioners Tuesday. The department projects it would need to lay off 116 firefighters by the second year, equivalent to one of the department's three shifts, and close three fire stations.

Under the scenario presented during Tuesday's Martin County Commission meeting, Fire Rescue could close Station 18 on Britt Road, Station 33 in Hobe Sound, and Station 23 on Kanner Highway. The $16.5 million annual loss would represent a 22% reduction from the department's current budget. Cianciulli said about 93% of the Fire Rescue budget is dedicated to personnel, leaving few options to absorb the projected revenue loss.

The funding loss could force Martin County to eliminate specialized teams responsible for hazardous materials incidents, technical rescues and dive operations. The department would then have to request assistance from neighboring agencies in Palm Beach or St. Lucie counties, potentially increasing response times. Cianciulli pointed to the deadly Camp Mystic flooding in Texas as an example of delays that can occur when a community must rely on outside resources. "They had to call for outside assets, a 14-hour response to start mitigating that scene," Cianciulli said. "We're in a position in the county, if we have any incident here, we are able to do an immediate mitigation. We're not wasting any second."

Cianciulli responded to suggestions about reducing employee salaries by saying Martin County already has difficulty recruiting trained firefighter-paramedics because departments farther south offer better compensation. "When we did our last class that we had, we had roughly 22 open positions; I only had about three paramedics that actually graduated that class," Cianciulli said. "The rest were firefighter EMTs. It's because the compensation package for a firefighter medic that is already trained is much higher down south." Cianciulli advised residents to learn as much as possible about the proposal and its potential effects before casting their ballots in November.

hero.headline: Martin County fire chief warns property tax reform could force closure of firehouses, cut 116 firefighters
hero.body:
Martin County Fire Chief Chad Cianciulli warned commissioners Tuesday that a property tax reform measure on the November ballot could force sweeping cuts to fire and rescue operations. The reform would expand homestead exemptions, potentially reducing the department's budget and forcing major reductions in service.

The potential cuts outlined by Cianciulli include closing firehouses, ending hazmat, dive, and technical rescue programs, grounding the department's critical care helicopter, and using firefighting tools past their operational lifetime. The department could be forced to cut as many as 116 firefighters over the next two years. Cianciulli told commissioners the changes would affect the department's ability to properly respond to emergencies, forcing them to call outside agencies for help.

Residents who attended the commission meeting had mixed reactions. One resident called fire service valuable, while another questioned why cutting personnel pay was not among the options. Commissioners also expressed differing views on how to respond if the reform passes. Commissioner Edward Ciampi said the county would be doing more belt tightening and slashing of budgets elsewhere, while Commissioner Eileen Vargas said the county should tighten up and that there are only so many dollars to go around.

No decisions were made Tuesday. The presentation was an opportunity to gather information so the county can plan accordingly ahead of the November vote.

hero.headline: Martin County School District cuts 3 bus routes, saves $255,000 with no impact to students
hero.teaser: The Martin County School District approved consolidating bus routes from 58 to 55 ahead of the upcoming school year, saving $255,000 without affecting students or eliminating driver positions.
hero.body:
The Martin County School District school board voted Tuesday unanimously to reduce the number of bus routes by 3, bringing the total from 58 to 55 ahead of the upcoming school year. District officials say all bus stops will remain the same and students will not be impacted by the change. Superintendent Michael Maine said the district has 55 routes and roughly 56 drivers, so all routes are covered. The $255,000 in savings reflects a reduced transportation budget and will not be redirected to a specific expense, according to the school district.

Transportation Director Ruth Spires confirmed that no drivers were let go as part of the consolidation. "We were already challenged with a shortage last year. So the routes that were merged consolidated yes, the drivers were already covering. So no one was cut at all," Spires said. Drivers will be paid for any additional hours they work as a result of the consolidation, Spires explained.

Michael Skinner, the President of the local AFSCME labor union chapter, voiced concerns during public comment on behalf of the bus drivers. "As what my feedback from the bus drivers were is that their routes or their buses are always full and cutting routes are not actually a good idea," Skinner said. Spires pushed back on that concern, noting that the buses hold a maximum of 77 passengers and are not operating at capacity.

So we have all of our routes covered," Superintendent Michael Maine said. The $255,000 in savings reflects a reduced transportation budget and will not be redirected to a specific expense, according to the school district. Parents have mixed reactions. Marino Reyes and Tiffany Gugumuck expressed support for the financial decision. "I think that's a great thing. A quarter million dollars that's a lot of money just for that one situation there. So many other needs that we can put the money towards," Reyes and Gugumuck said. Parent Ken Winstanley wondered what the change means for the budget. "Where's the money gonna go to?" Winstanley said. Michael Skinner, the President of the local AFSCME labor union chapter, voiced concerns during public comment on behalf of the bus drivers. "As what my feedback from the bus drivers were is that their routes or their buses are always full and cutting routes are not actually a good idea," Skinner said. Transportation Director Ruth Spires pushed back on that concern, noting that the buses hold a maximum of 77 passengers and are not operating at capacity. Spires also confirmed that no drivers were let go as part of the consolidation. "We were already challenged with a shortage last year. So the routes that were merged—consolidated—yes, the drivers were already covering. So no one was cut at all," Spires said. Drivers will be paid for any additional hours they work as a result of the consolidation, Spires explained. The district said it is confident it will maintain the same level of service with fewer buses on the road. cards.headline: Martin County Fire Rescue could lose 116 firefighters if homestead exemption amendment passes
cards.body:
Martin County commissioners heard a presentation Tuesday outlining how a proposed expansion of Florida's homestead exemption could force Martin County Fire Rescue to cut 116 firefighters over the next two years if voters approve the constitutional amendment in November. The cuts would eliminate about one-third of the department's workforce due to reduced property tax revenue tied to the proposed amendment.

Fire Rescue leaders discussed potential operational changes if those revenue reductions occur. Previous county projections have outlined possible station closures, reductions to specialized teams including HAZMAT, Technical Rescue, the dive team and LifeStar, and delays in replacing equipment. County leaders have previously said the department has few options to absorb the projected revenue loss because about 93% of the Fire Rescue budget is dedicated to personnel.

Martin County Commissioner James Blake Capps, District 3, warned of serious consequences for residents. "There would also have to be a no-overtime policy for all of our fire rescue personnel. That doesn't sound so bad initially, but when you think about the consequences, it means no backfilling of stations with personnel, which would result in randomized brownouts of stations," Capps said. He also noted that station closures could lead to higher insurance premiums for residents who would end up living more than five miles from a fire station.

Officials warned the projected cuts could lead to longer emergency response times and affect specialized emergency services provided throughout Martin County. No vote on firefighter layoffs or fire station closures occurred during Tuesday's meeting. Voters will have the final say on the constitutional amendment during the November general election.
cards.article_text: Martin County commissioners are expected to hear a presentation Tuesday outlining how a proposed expansion of Florida’s homestead exemption could affect Martin County Fire Rescue if voters approve the constitutional amendment on the November ballot. The presentation is expected to focus on the projected financial impact of the proposed tax changes and what they could mean for the department’s budget, staffing, operations and emergency response. See the presentation in the gallery above. "As a public servant, I will be glad to honor the will of the voters, whatever they decide regarding the proposed constitutional amendment. But, we do have some concerns about the depth of the cuts that would be needed as they relate to a number of areas of government operations, particularly fire rescue," said Martin County Commissioner James Blake Capps, District 3. According to county documents, Martin County Fire Rescue projects it could lose 116 firefighters over the next two years about one-third of its workforce because of reduced property tax revenue tied to the proposed amendment. "We in Martin County have been used to the very best in fire rescue services, and I would hate to see our level of service suffer greatly. It seems to me that we would be in for that if this constitutional amendment were to pass," said Capps. Fire Rescue leaders are also expected to discuss potential operational changes if those revenue reductions occur. Previous county projections have outlined possible station closures, reductions to specialized teams including HAZMAT, Technical Rescue, the dive team and LifeStar, and delays in replacing equipment. County leaders have previously said the department has few options to absorb the projected revenue loss because about 93% of the Fire Rescue budget is dedicated to personnel. Officials have also warned the proposed cuts could lead to longer emergency response times and affect specialized emergency services provided throughout Martin County. "There would also have to be a no-overtime policy for all of our fire rescue personnel. That doesn't sound so bad initially, but when you think about the consequences, it means no backfilling of stations with personnel, which would result in randomized brownouts of stations," said Capps. Tuesday’s discussion comes as commissioners consider several other agenda items, including final solid waste assessment rates, proposed changes to fishing rules on county-owned property, development proposals, and conservation land purchases. "Another serious consequence for Martin County residents would be higher insurance premiums. If you're within five miles of a fire station, you receive a break on your homeowner's insurance. But if you're farther than five miles away, you pay higher premiums. If we shut down three fire stations, a lot of people would end up paying more for homeowner's insurance. There would also be consequences for our level of service and our comprehensive plan," said Capps. No vote on firefighter layoffs or fire station closures is expected during Tuesday’s meeting. Instead, commissioners will receive the presentation as they continue evaluating the potential local impacts of the proposed homestead exemption expansion. "I think it could be rather severe. When you think about three fire stations disappearing, response times for the people living near those stations would increase, which could have very serious consequences for residents," said Capps. Voters will have the final say on the constitutional amendment during the November general election. The meeting starts at 9 a.m. CBS12 News will have a team inside.
